title: fix(webvh): key records follow the document's verification-method ids, and a repair for the ones that don't
body:
Found from the browser plugin's Keys pane: a room host's keys were listed as `#key-0` / `#key-1` while its published DID document declares `#key-1` / `#key-2`.

## The defect

A key record's id **is** a verification-method id. `save_entity_key_records` says so in its own name, and `vta_sdk::did_secrets::select_secret_kid` rule 1 depends on it — the kid a mediator matches inbound JWE recipients against is the record id, on the reasoning that "the DID document decided what the key is called".

Create never read the document to find out. It named records `{did}#key-0` / `{did}#key-1` while the document was whatever the caller or the template said — and `room.json` and `room-host.json` number their methods from `#key-1`. On every room and room host this VTA has minted:

| | signing (ed25519) | key agreement (x25519) |
|---|---|---|
| published document | `#key-1` | `#key-2` |
| key records | `#key-0` | `#key-1` |

- **`#key-1` names two different keys.** The signing key to every resolver; the x25519 key to the agent holding it. Hand the id the document publishes to `keys/sign` — the natural thing, having read it off the document — and the oracle fetches an x25519 record for an EdDSA signature.
- **The published `keyAgreement` matches no record.** An authcrypt message addressed to `#key-2` finds no local secret: the storm.ws outage of #337 reached from the other side. There a decorative label overwrote the right kid; here the right kid was never stored.
- **`next_fragment_id` was the constant 2**, so a room's first rotation allocates `#key-2` — over the id its key-agreement method is already published under.

Room credentials still verify, which is why this stayed quiet: `RoomKeySigner` hardcodes `{room_did}#key-1` to match the template and the public keys line up positionally, so the proof names a method that resolves to the key that signed it. Everything that addresses a key **by name** is what breaks.

(`ai-agent-peer.json` also numbers from 1 and is correct — `did:peer` fragments are 1-based by spec. Only the two `webvh` room templates are affected.)

## Commit 1 — create reads the document it just published

`document::minted_vm_ids` matches methods to the minted keys on `publicKeyMultibase` and takes the ids it finds. Matching on key material rather than position or a `#key-N` shape is what makes it total: right for a template numbering from 1, for `vta-admin` (method id `{DID}#{SIGNING_KEY_MB}`), and for a hand-written document.

Renumbering the two templates instead would have been smaller and wrong twice: `RoomKeySigner`'s hardcoded `#key-1` would then name a method the new documents lack, and the next custom template reintroduces the whole thing.

Also: `next_fragment_id` comes from the document's highest `#key-N`, and delete cleans up every `#key-N` the record allocated instead of exactly two — which had been leaking the records of every rotated DID too.

## Commit 2 — a repair for the DIDs already out there

`keys/rename` cannot do it, deliberately: its gate exists so a rename is "not a back door into VM-shaped or namespace-colliding names" (`rename_key_rejects_separator_shaped_new_key_id` pins it), and the reason is real — a caller who can write `{someone-elses-did}#key-0` as a store key can squat the kid of a DID that has not minted its keys yet. An operator attempting the obvious repair is told their new name is 86 bytes against a limit of 64, with no second attempt that works. Worse, the rename that *is* accepted detaches the record from the document permanently, because the id it had cannot be given back.

So the agent computes the names: `POST /webvh/dids/{did}/realign-keys` (admin, scoped to the DID's context), `pnm did-mgmt dids realign-keys <did> [--dry-run]`. Every target comes from the DID's own log — read locally, because a repair that depends on the network cannot run when the network is what is broken — and records are matched to methods by `publicKeyMultibase`. No caller-supplied string becomes a store key, which is what makes this safe where widening `keys/rename` would not be. Matching on key material also recovers a key already renamed away from its method id, which nothing else can name again.

It plans, then applies: nothing is written until every move is known safe. The moves **interleave** — `#key-0` → `#key-1` and `#key-1` → `#key-2`, so one destination is held by the other record in the same plan, and the general case is a cycle — so the conflict check refuses a target held by a key that is *not* moving, rather than any occupied target. Destinations are written before sources are dropped, so an interrupted run leaves a duplicate the next run collapses, never a key whose record is gone.

REST-only, and the client method says so rather than timing out on a DIDComm message nothing answers.

## Checks

- `cargo test -p vta-service --lib` — **1119 passed**, 0 failed
- `cargo test -p vta-keys` — 42 passed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all`

15 new tests. The five on `minted_vm_ids` run against the **real** built-in templates rather than a fixture — the defect was not misreading a document, it was never reading one, so a fixture of my own choosing would have agreed with the broken code — and are verified non-vacuous: three fail against the old behaviour while the builder and fallback tests stay green. Two of the ten realign tests are cases that would otherwise be found in production: the interleaved move (which the first draft of the conflict check refused outright — the tests caught it) and a key already renamed away from its method id.

## Companion

Plugin-side: OpenVTC/vta-browser-plugin#243, merged — the console now applies the agent's identifier rule before sending a rename, so this refusal arrives as a sentence under the field instead of a raw `malformed request`.

title: fix(webvh): key records follow the document's verification-method ids, and a repair for the ones that don't (#1466)
body:
fix(webvh): key records follow the document's verification-method ids, and a repair for the ones that don't (#1466)

* fix(webvh): name a created DID's key records after the document it published

A key record's id **is** a verification-method id. `save_entity_key_records`
says so in its own name, and `vta_sdk::did_secrets::select_secret_kid` rule 1
depends on it: the kid a mediator matches inbound JWE recipients against is the
record id, on the reasoning that "the DID document decided what the key is
called".

Create never read the document to find out. It named the records `{did}#key-0`
and `{did}#key-1` while the document was whatever the caller or the template
said — and the `room` and `room-host` built-in templates number their methods
from `#key-1`. So on every room and every room host this VTA has ever minted:

- the document's `#key-1` is the **signing** key and the keystore's `#key-1` is
  the **x25519** one. One name, two keys, no error anywhere. Hand the id the
  document publishes to `keys/sign` — the natural thing to do, having read it
  off the document — and the oracle fetches an x25519 record for an EdDSA
  signature;
- the document's `keyAgreement` (`#key-2`) matches no record at all, so an
  authcrypt message addressed to it finds no local secret. That is the storm.ws
  outage of #337 reached from the other side: there a decorative label
  overwrote the right kid, here the right kid was never stored;
- `next_fragment_id` was stored as the constant 2, so the DID's first rotation
  allocates `#key-2` — over the id its key-agreement method is already
  published under.

Room credentials still verify, which is why this stayed quiet: `RoomKeySigner`
hardcodes `{room_did}#key-1` to match the template, and the public keys line up
positionally, so the proof names a method that resolves to the key that signed
it. Everything that addresses a key *by name* is what breaks.

## The fix reads the document rather than renumbering the templates

`document::minted_vm_ids` matches methods to the minted keys on
`publicKeyMultibase` and takes the ids it finds. Matching on key material rather
than on position or on a `#key-N` shape is what makes it total: it is right for
a template that numbers from 1, for `vta-admin` (whose method id is
`{DID}#{SIGNING_KEY_MB}`), and for a document an operator wrote by hand.

Renumbering `room.json` / `room-host.json` to `#key-0` / `#key-1` would have
been smaller and wrong twice over: `RoomKeySigner`'s hardcoded `#key-1` would
then name a method the new documents do not have, and the next custom template
someone writes reintroduces the whole thing.

`next_fragment_id` now comes from the document's highest `#key-N`, and the
delete path cleans up every `#key-N` the record allocated instead of exactly
two — which had been leaking the records of every rotated DID as well.

## Tests

Five, driven through the **real** built-in templates rather than a fixture:
the defect was not misreading a document, it was never reading one, so a
document of my own choosing would have agreed with the broken code. Verified
non-vacuous — three fail against the old behaviour, and the two that pin the
builder's own `#key-0` / `#key-1` and the no-such-key fallback stay green,
which is what says the change is narrow.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(webvh): realign a DID's key records with the methods it publishes

The previous commit fixes DIDs minted from now on. Every room and room host
already published carries records the document does not name, and there is no
caller-facing call that can repair one.

`keys/rename` cannot, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight — its
gate exists so that a rename is "not a back door into VM-shaped or
namespace-colliding names", with `rename_key_rejects_separator_shaped_new_key_id`
pinning it. The reason is real: a caller who can write `{someone-elses-did}#key-0`
as a store key can squat the kid of a DID that has not minted its keys yet. So
an operator who tries the obvious repair — rename the record to the id the
document publishes — is told their new name is 86 bytes against a limit of 64,
and there is no second attempt that works.

Worse, trying leaves things further from repair than before: the rename that
*is* accepted (`vdr-host-key-2`, say) detaches the record from the document for
good, because the id it had cannot be given back.

## So the agent computes the names

`POST /webvh/dids/{did}/realign-keys`, admin, scoped to the DID's own context.
Every target comes out of the DID's own published log — read locally, because a
repair that depends on the network cannot run when the network is what is
broken — and records are matched to methods by **`publicKeyMultibase`**. No
caller-supplied string becomes a store key, which is what makes this safe where
widening `keys/rename` would not be.

Matching on key material is also what recovers a key someone has already
renamed away from its method id. That record is otherwise unreachable: nothing
can name it again.

## Two things the shape is doing

**It plans, then applies.** Nothing is written until every move is known to be
safe, so a conflict leaves the keystore exactly as it was rather than
half-moved. `--dry-run` returns that plan without applying it.

**The moves interleave, and the check accounts for it.** A room's records move
`#key-0` → `#key-1` and `#key-1` → `#key-2`, so one destination is occupied by
the *other record in the same plan* — and the general case is a cycle, which no
ordering unpicks. A per-move "is the target free?" test therefore refuses the
exact shape this exists to repair. What is refused is a target held by a key
that is **not** moving. Destinations are written before sources are dropped, so
an interrupted run leaves a duplicate record that the next run collapses, never
a key whose record is gone.

`pnm did-mgmt dids realign-keys <did> [--dry-run]` prints what moved, what was
already right, and any method this agent holds no key for — reported rather
than skipped, because "nothing to move" and "that key is not here" are
different answers and only one means the repair is complete.

REST-only, and the client method says so rather than timing out on a DIDComm
message nothing answers: the agent computes everything from the DID, so there
is nothing for a wire format to carry, and repairing local key custody is an
operator standing at their own agent.

## Tests

Ten, against a real published log whose document numbers its methods from
`#key-1`. Two of them are the cases that would otherwise be found in
production: the interleaved move (which the first draft of the conflict check
refused outright — the tests caught it), and a key already renamed away from
its method id, which is the state an operator reaches by trying to fix this by
hand.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(room-host)!: do not open an HTTP port nobody asked for
body:
Running a host in the arrangement this design is actually about — reached by DID, through a mediator, no ingress — still produced this:

```
$ room-host --data-dir /tmp/room-host-data --mediator-did did:webvh:…:mediator \
            --vta-did did:webvh:…:glenn-vta --vta-context vdr --secrets secrets.toml

host DID: did:webvh:…:vdr-host
INFO room_host: room host ready … listen=127.0.0.1:8300
```

Nobody passed `--listen`. It defaulted to `127.0.0.1:8300`, bound a port, and announced an address the operator never chose.

That contradicts the rule this crate already applies one field further down. `--mediator-did` is opt-in, and the `didcomm` feature is opt-in, with the reasoning stated in both places: *a host that is not asked to be reachable opens no socket and mints no identity*. HTTP was the one surface exempt from it, by accident of a clap default.

## Change

`listen: Option<String>`, bound only when given.

- **Neither `--listen` nor `--mediator-did`**: refuses to start, naming both flags. Previously it came up serving HTTP on a port the operator had not asked for; a host asked to serve nobody should say so.
- **`--mediator-did` only**: no listener, and the process awaits the mediator task — so losing that connection ends the process rather than leaving it up with nothing served. With a listener the two stay independent, because there something is still being served; that asymmetry is deliberate.
- **`--allow-origin` without `--listen`**: warns that there is no HTTP surface for it to apply to.

## Verified

Against a live `did:webvh` mediator, mediator-only:

```
INFO room_host: room host ready — reachable by DID only, with no HTTP listener
INFO room_host::didcomm: reachable at a mediator — serving Trust Tasks over DIDComm and TSP
```

`lsof -p <pid> | grep -c LISTEN` → **0**. Builds with default features and with `didcomm,onboarding,config-session,tsp`; tests green.

## BREAKING

A deployment relying on the default now serves no HTTP. Pass `--listen 127.0.0.1:8300` to keep it — which the HTTP mode needs regardless, since that is how `sample-room` registers rooms with the host.

Worth knowing when deciding whether to keep a listener at all: `GET /health` is a static `ok` that reports only that the process is listening. It stays `200` while the mediator leg is dead, which is the state that actually matters, so a load-balancer check against it will hold a target in service that no member can reach.

Follows #1459.

title: Add DTG nodeType property
body:
The [WD02 base structure for DTG credentials](https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-cred-spec/#base-structure) still does not include a property identifying the type of DTG node to which a credential is being issued.

This is how all DTG participants can have an unambiguous shared understanding of the types of nodes with which they have relationships — and apply policy against this metadata (canonical example: applying [proof of personhood](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.07892) policies to a `person`).

Proposal: in WD03 (aka WD 0.3.0) under the `CredentialSubject` property, add a subproperty following the `id` property

- `nodeType` (string, REQUIRED): MUST include exactly one of `"person"`, `"device"`, `"agent"`, `"VTC"`, or `"VTN"`.

title: fix(pnm-cli): anchor TEE bootstrap connect by DID and PCR0
body:
Add mutually exclusive --vta-did and --vta-url targets. Resolve WebVH locally without guessing a URL on failure, preserve the advertised REST endpoint, and reject credentials for a different VTA DID.

Accept a pinned PCR0 as the online connect trust anchor without requiring the server-generated digest or an opt-out warning. Preserve explicit digest opt-out warnings, conflicting-flag errors, and mandatory offline digest verification.

Add regression tests for target selection, strict endpoint resolution, credential identity checks, and anchor combinations. Update the PNM quick start and TEE bootstrap guide.

title: fix(pnm-cli): anchor TEE bootstrap connect by DID and PCR0 (#1454)
body:
fix(pnm-cli): anchor TEE bootstrap connect by DID and PCR0 (#1454)

* fix(pnm-cli): anchor TEE bootstrap connect by DID and PCR0

Add mutually exclusive --vta-did and --vta-url targets. Resolve WebVH locally without guessing a URL on failure, preserve the advertised REST endpoint, and reject credentials for a different VTA DID.

Accept a pinned PCR0 as the online connect trust anchor without requiring the server-generated digest or an opt-out warning. Preserve explicit digest opt-out warnings, conflicting-flag errors, and mandatory offline digest verification.

Add regression tests for target selection, strict endpoint resolution, credential identity checks, and anchor combinations. Update the PNM quick start and TEE bootstrap guide.

Signed-off-by: oleksii <oleksii.p@affinidi.com>

* fix(pnm-cli): validate PCR0 pins before bootstrap requests

Expose the SDK's existing Nitro PCR validator and reuse it before connect performs DID resolution or the single-use bootstrap POST. Reject malformed PCR0 even when a digest or explicit opt-out is also supplied.

Require exactly 96 hexadecimal characters after supported prefix, whitespace, and case normalization. Add SDK and connect regressions for malformed pins, valid normalized pins, and validation before network access.

Signed-off-by: oleksii <oleksii.p@affinidi.com>

* fix(pnm-cli): guard DID-advertised bootstrap endpoints

Apply the SDK endpoint policy to DID-resolved REST URLs before bootstrap connections. Cover public and private destinations, metadata endpoints, and credential redaction with regression tests.

Signed-off-by: oleksii <oleksii.p@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-tee): advertise REST endpoints for DID-first bootstrap

Include the configured public REST base URL in signed first-boot DID documents when REST is enabled, preserving host, port, and path.

Keep signed updates later than the existing log head so TEE identities can be repaired without rewriting genesis. Cover actual generated-log discovery, append-only repair, and restart preservation; document authenticated recovery for existing deployments.

Signed-off-by: oleksii <oleksii.p@affinidi.com>

* fix(pnm-cli): close three gaps in DID-anchored bootstrap connect

**Validate both PCR pins before spending the carve-out.**
`/bootstrap/request` writes `BOOTSTRAP_CARVEOUT_CLOSED_KEY` server-side
before it returns the bundle, so the VTA's one and only first boot is
already spent by the time the client reaches `check_pcrs`. That is what
makes pre-flight validation of a client-side pin load-bearing rather than
a nicety, and it is why `validate_connect_anchor` checks `--expect-pcr0`
before any network I/O. `--expect-pcr8` was not checked, so a truncated or
mistyped PCR8 survived to `check_pcrs` and was rejected after the POST —
leaving a closed carve-out, no installed credential, and no second attempt.
A typo in an optional defence-in-depth flag became an unbootstrappable VTA.
Validate it on the same rule as PCR0.

**Stop offering `--vta-url` as the remedy for an endpoint-guard failure.**
`resolve_connect_url` wrapped every error, guard rejections included, with
"explicitly use --vta-url <URL>". But `--vta-url` is not guarded, so for a
DID advertising a private address, cloud metadata, or a non-HTTP scheme the
message told the operator to route around the control. The guard already
carries its own remedy (`--allow-private-endpoints` /
`VTA_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS`); surface that and nothing else. Guard
failures are now a separate arm, asserted to name the DID, to keep naming
the guard's remedy, to keep redacting URL userinfo, and not to mention
`--vta-url`. The `file://` case moves to the guard test, where it belongs.

**Say that bootstrap resolution is local-only.** It deliberately ignores
`PNM_RESOLVER_URL` / `[resolver_url]`, which `main.rs` documents as
reaching every `DIDCacheClient` in PNM — the right call here, since the
resolved document picks the endpoint that mints a super-admin credential
against a single-use carve-out. But the error said "Retry once its DID log
is published", which is the wrong diagnosis for an operator whose egress
reaches only a resolver sidecar and whose log is already published. Name
the exception in the error and in the docs.

Also repoints the `bootstrap open` operator hint, which still printed the
identity-unpinned `--vta-url` form plus an `--expect-digest` this PR
establishes cannot be known before the call.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-tee): read public_url once for both advertised services

The new `VTARest` block trimmed whitespace off `public_url`; the
`TeeAttestation` block beside it did not. `trim_end_matches('/')` strips
nothing from a string that ends in whitespace, so
`public_url = "  https://host/  "` produced a usable REST endpoint and,
next to it in the same signed genesis document, a TeeAttestation endpoint
of `"  https://host/  /attestation/report"`. The genesis is not rewritten
on reboot, so that lands in the log permanently.

Read the field once, trimmed and empty-filtered, and use that value in
both branches. The discovery test gains the padded-URL case with
`embed_in_did` on — previously it exercised padding only with the
attestation service off, which is exactly the combination that hid this —
and now asserts no advertised `serviceEndpoint` carries surrounding
whitespace, so a third service added later cannot reintroduce it.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs: record the bootstrap-connect anchor exception in CLAUDE.md

CLAUDE.md lists "digest pinning is mandatory at the CLI" under the
sealed-transfer invariants marked *do not relax*, and this branch relaxes
it for `pnm bootstrap connect`. The relaxation is sound — that bundle is
minted during the call, so no out-of-band digest can exist beforehand and
the rule was in practice forcing every operator onto `--no-verify-digest`
— but an invariant that has an exception needs the exception written down
next to it, or the next reader applies the rule as stated and the one
after that treats the divergence as precedent.

State it as one named exception with its reason and its boundary: PCR0 is
accepted there because it is pre-computable and enforced against the quote
by `check_pcrs`, every other path still requires a digest or the
warning-bearing opt-out, and an anchor is only substitutable when the
substitute is checked.

Also updates the TEE Mode B entry point, which still read
`--vta-url <url>`, with the mutual exclusion, the local-only resolution,
PCR8's status as an additional pin rather than an anchor, and the ordering
consequence of the carve-out closing before the bundle is returned.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: security(deps): take rustls 0.23.45 for RUSTSEC-2026-0285, and drop five ignores nothing matches
body:
`cargo deny check advisories` fails on **main**, and has since RUSTSEC-2026-0285
was published — no commit made it red, so it is not a regression from any PR
currently open. Reproduced on a clean checkout of 688c7445.

## The advisory

[RUSTSEC-2026-0285](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0285): rustls
accepted TLS 1.3 handshake messages sent at the wrong encryption level when they
followed a key-changing message in the same record — a plaintext
`EncryptedExtensions` packed into the same record as the `ServerHello` was taken.
RFC 8446 §5.1 requires the connection be closed with `unexpected_message`
instead. The transcript stays authenticated, so this does not let a
network-position attacker alter or complete a handshake; the effect is that a
peer can send in plaintext what should have been encrypted. Functionally the same
bug as Go's CVE-2025-61730.

The advisory names **>= 0.23.45** as the fix. `rustls = { version = "0.23", … }`
already admits it, so only the lockfiles move:

| Lockfile | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| workspace | 0.23.43 | 0.23.45 |
| `deploy/nitro/enclave-proxy` | 0.23.44 | 0.23.45 |

rustls reaches the workspace through `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` and the
TDK, so every service that speaks TLS resolved the affected version. #1460 bumped
the enclave-proxy to 0.23.44, which the advisory also names — and that workspace
is the enclave's TLS proxy, the one place in the tree whose whole job is
terminating TLS. Those are the only two lockfiles in the repo.

## Five ignores that match nothing

The same run reported five `advisory-not-detected` warnings. Each entry names the
condition it should be dropped on, and each condition has been met:

- **RUSTSEC-2026-0098 / -0099 / -0104** (rustls-webpki 0.101.x name constraints,
  and the CRL parse panic) — "drop when AWS SDK retires the rustls 0.21 code
  path". It has: the lockfile holds `rustls-webpki` 0.103.15 only, and no rustls
  0.21 at all.
- **RUSTSEC-2026-0258** (h2 queues empty DATA frames without limit) — "drop when
  AWS SDK moves off hyper 0.14". It has: `h2` is 0.4.19, past the 0.4.16 fix, and
  `hyper` is 1.11.1 with no 0.3 or 0.14 left.
- **RUSTSEC-2025-0141** (bincode 1.3.x unmaintained, via uniffi_macros) — "drop
  when uniffi updates to bincode 2.x or drops it". It has: `bincode` is not in
  the graph at all.

An ignore that matches nothing is not harmless: it is a documented exception to a
security policy that no longer describes the tree, and the next reader has to
re-derive that before trusting any of it. The four entries that still match are
left exactly as they are, and no remaining entry cross-referenced a removed one.

## Checks

- `cargo deny check advisories bans sources licenses` — **clean, and now with no
  warnings at all** (it was `advisories FAILED` before)
- `cargo metadata --locked` resolves in both workspaces
- `scripts/check-lockfile-self-pins.sh`, `check-nitro-copies-every-member.py`,
  `check-workspace-version-reqs.py` — all pass
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- The two CI test jobs were still running locally when this was opened; CI runs
  both here.

Unblocks the red `cargo-deny` on #1465 and #1467, neither of which touches Rust.

title: fix(manager): a key's new name is a name, and the field is where the key is
body:
Renaming a key in the console could not succeed. The field opened pre-filled with the key's current id, which for every DID-bound key is a DID URL — and `keys/rename` will not take one. The agent's gate is `vti_common::identifier::validate_identifier`: `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`, at most 64 bytes, because a key id lands as a store key and a caller who can inject `:` collides with an adjacent keyspace. The only thing pressing Save could produce was:

```
keys/rename/0.1 failed: malformed request: validation error: new_key_id is 86 bytes; maximum is 64
```

…with nothing on screen saying what would have worked. The specification cannot help: `keys/rename/0.1` declares `newKeyId` as a non-empty string and leaves the shape to the agent, so the narrower rule is the agent's and this console has to know it.

## The rule, applied before the send

`key-name.ts` is that rule, phrased for the person typing — a **pre-flight, not the decision**. The agent still answers and its refusal still renders; nothing here may widen the rule, because a value this accepts and the agent refuses is a message the operator can act on, while the reverse is a name the agent would have taken and the console pretended it would not.

A DID-bound key opens with an **empty** field and a derived name as its *placeholder* — `vdr-host-key-0` from `did:webvh:QmRqx…:webvh.storm.ws:vdr-host#key-0`. A placeholder rather than a value on purpose: a pre-filled suggestion is one press away from a rename nobody chose, and this rename is a one-way door. The id a DID document addresses the key by contains `:` and `#`, so the agent cannot be given it back, and the editor says so rather than leaving it to be discovered.

## And the field is under the key now

It rendered inside the actions column, the narrowest in the table, which showed about eight characters of an 86-byte value. `Table` already has `expanded` for exactly this — a detail rendered in the flow beneath the row it belongs to — so the editor goes there, full width, with focus moved into the field and Escape closing it.

## Tests

`keys-pane.render.test.mts` is rendered rather than unit, because both defects are ones a person sees and a model does not: the type checker was happy with a field that could only fail, and `key-name.ts`'s own tests would pass with the editor still drawing in a 190px column.

`manager-form-state.test.mts`'s prop-seed detector only matched a prop read as the whole `useState` argument, so `useState(nameable ? record.keyId : "")` read as a component with no state at all. Widened to find the prop anywhere in the call — it flags no existing component, which is the point: the narrow match was missing seeds, not tolerating them.

## Noted, not fixed here

`rooms-create.tsx` gains a note on something found while confirming the above: for a templated mint the key record's id and the DID document's verification method disagree by one — `room` / `room-host` number VMs from `#key-1`, the create path saves records from `#key-0` — so the document's `#key-1` names the signing key and the keystore's names the x25519 one. That is a VTA-side fix and is being opened against `verifiable-trust-infrastructure`. The offer in `rooms-create.tsx` is by `{did}#` prefix and `keyType !== "x25519"`, never by fragment number, so it is unaffected.

## Checks

`npm test` — 620 extension tests pass (1338 across the workspace); `npm run build` clean.

title: fix(room-host): speak TSP to the VTA, and stop hiding why a start failed
body:
Standing a `room-host` up against a live VTA — `did:webvh` identity, `did:webvh` mediator, TSP and DIDComm both advertised — hit four separate walls. Each one is a one-liner; what they have in common is that none of them said what was wrong.

## 1. `room-host` could not speak TSP to the VTA

`vtc-service`, `vta-service`, `vtc-client` and `pnm-cli` all forward `vta-sdk/tsp`. `room-host` never did, so the control leg that fetches this host's identity fell back to DIDComm with a warning — *except on the first connect*, where it is fatal:

`session::rotation_endpoint` matches the TSP arm first and takes it unconditionally (there is a test asserting that ordering), and `connect_tsp_bounded` on a build without the feature returns

```
VTA '…' advertises TSP, but this build of the SDK/CLI was compiled without the `tsp`
feature, so it cannot connect over it.
```

with nothing to fall back to. A session waiting to rotate is exactly the state a host is in the moment after it has been granted — so enrolment fails, every later connect would have worked, and it reads as intermittent.

Adds `tsp = ["onboarding", "vta-sdk/tsp"]`.

## 2. The reason a start failed was replaced by the fallback's complaint

`fetch_identity` reads its cached bundle only when the VTA could not be reached — then let the cache's own failure replace the reason it was consulting the cache. With a misconfigured secret store this produced, on consecutive runs against the same box:

```
Error: read the cached VTA bundle: … AccessDeniedException …
Error: read the cached VTA bundle: … failed to decode hex seed from AWS: Odd number of digits
```

Two errors, apparently two problems, actually neither: the VTA connect was failing both times and the reason went in the bin with the `?`. Every arm now carries the connect error and says which of the two is the one to fix.

## 3. The VTA client was dropped with a live session

`fetch_identity` never called `client.shutdown()`. The SDK's leak guard is a `debug_assert`, so a **debug build panics on a successful fetch**:

```
thread 'main' panicked at vta-sdk/src/didcomm_session.rs:127:13:
DIDComm session for `did:key:…` dropped without shutdown()
```

and a release build leaves an auto-reconnecting socket competing with the one `didcomm::serve` opens moments later for the host's own DID — which the SDK's warning says will fight on the mediator and time out round-trips. Shut down on both the success and failure paths.

## 4. Two error messages that named the wrong thing

- `session-keyring` compiled but nothing installed a platform store, so it died at the first session read with `keyring entry error: No default store has been set, so cannot search or create entries` — the keyring crate's internals rather than the missing call `vti-secrets`' own feature comment asks the consuming binary to make. Installs it, and points at `config-session` when there is no keyring to install (a container, a headless server).
- Losing the mediator connection ends a spawned task while `axum::serve` carries on, so the process stays up, a health check on `--listen` keeps passing, and every member addressing the host by DID times out. The log line now says the host is unreachable and does not retry, instead of leaving that to be discovered.

## Testing

`cargo test -p room-host --features didcomm,onboarding,config-session,tsp` — green.

Verified against a live VTA and mediator: with `tsp` compiled in, a pending-rotation session reaches the VTA over TSP and gets a real authorization answer (`acl/swap-key failed: DID not in ACL` for an ungranted test key) where the same session previously failed with the TSP feature error.

## Not fixed here

Two things found alongside these, left alone as separate concerns:

- **The mediator leg never retries.** Item 4 makes the failure legible; it does not add backoff. A host that loses its mediator connection stays up and unreachable until restarted.
- **`SecretEntry.key_type` is ignored** by `to_secrets`, which passes `private_key_multibase` straight to `Secret::from_multibase` as `did_secrets.rs` prescribes. That is correct for the bundles we saw, but it means a bundle carrying an Ed25519 seed under an X25519 kid — a shape that field's own doc comment describes — would be silently unusable.

title: fix(webvh): clamp versionTime against the previous log entry
body:
## Summary

Fixes TEE VTA `did:webvh` identities becoming unresolvable after their first update.

## Problem

PR #600 introduced `backdated_version_time` for the standard VTA genesis and update paths. The TEE genesis path was not updated and continued relying on `didwebvh-rs`'s default `Utc::now()` timestamp.

As a result:

1. TEE genesis received a real current `versionTime`.
2. The first runtime update received a timestamp backdated by one day.
3. The update timestamp was earlier than genesis.
4. `didwebvh-rs` rejected the chain because `versionTime` must be strictly increasing.

This affected mediator connection, DIDComm operations, backup export, and other flows that resolve the VTA's DID.

## Solution

Reuse the PR #600 backdating policy for TEE genesis:

```rust
.version_time(backdated_version_time(0))
```

The helper is now owned by `vta-support::version_time` so both `vta-service` and `vta-tee` use the same implementation without creating a dependency cycle.

The policy remains:

```text
versionTime = now - 1 day + entry_index * 1 minute
```

This keeps timestamps safely in the past and strictly increasing at the whole-second precision required by `did:webvh`.

## Testing

- Shared `vta-support` version-time regression test passes.
- `vta-service` did:webvh test suite passes.
- `vta-tee` test suite passes: 35 tests.
- Clippy passes for `vta-support` and `vta-tee`.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` passes.

title: fix(webvh): clamp versionTime against the previous log entry (#1456)
body:
fix(webvh): clamp versionTime against the previous log entry (#1456)

* fix(tee): backdate WebVH genesis versionTime

The TEE genesis path used the library's current-time default while
runtime updates used PR #600's backdated timestamps. This caused the
first update to have a lower versionTime than genesis, making the DID
unresolvable.

Apply the shared PR #600 backdating policy to TEE genesis and move the
helper into vta-support so both TEE and service paths use one implementation.

Signed-off-by: Yaroslava Kurash <yaroslava.k@affinidi.com>

* fix(webvh): clamp versionTime against the previous log entry

Backdating TEE genesis fixes DIDs minted from now on. It does nothing for
the ones already out there, because `backdated_version_time` derived its
timestamp from the entry index alone — which silently assumes every
earlier entry in the chain was stamped by this same policy.

For a TEE VTA provisioned before that fix the assumption is false. Its
genesis carries a real `Utc::now()`, so its first runtime update is
computed as `now - 1 day + 1 min`: earlier than genesis. didwebvh-rs
checks monotonicity only at resolve time (`log_entry/read.rs:378`), never
at write time, so the entry is signed, appended and published to the host
before anyone can find out. The log is append-only, so no later update
can repair it and the DID is permanently unresolvable — an operator
upgrading an existing Nitro VTA runs `pnm services didcomm enable`, is
told it succeeded, and loses mediator connection, DIDComm and backup
export with no way back.

`next_version_time(existing_entry_count, previous)` replaces it and takes
the previous entry's timestamp, clamping to `previous + 1s` whenever the
backdated value would not be strictly later. Three consequences:

- Chains whose genesis predates the fix recover on their next update
  instead of bricking on it.
- A backwards clock step larger than the one-minute index spacing — an
  NTP correction on the host a Nitro enclave took its clock from — no
  longer yields a non-increasing entry.
- The index offset is capped at 1439 minutes. Uncapped, `now - 1 day +
  N minutes` overtakes `now` at N = 1440 and the entry is rejected as
  future-dated: the same unresolvable DID, reached from the other side,
  and just as silent at write time. Past the cap the clamp carries strict
  increase instead of the index.

Comparisons are made on whole seconds, the only precision that survives
serialisation. Comparing at full precision let two saturated entries a
few microseconds apart pass the clamp and then serialise to the identical
timestamp — the exact collision this helper exists to prevent.

Regression coverage now sits on the path that actually broke. The TEE
genesis builder is extracted as `build_genesis_create_config` so a test
can assert the config it produces carries a backdated versionTime, that
`create_did` stamps that value on the entry, and that the first update
after such a genesis is strictly later. Both tests fail if the
`.version_time(..)` call is removed; each of the five helper tests fails
with its own fix reverted.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(pnm): confirm before `vta remove`, with a --force opt-out
body:
`pnm vta remove <slug>` deleted the stored VTA connection **and** its keyring credential with no prompt. A mistyped slug is not recoverable from the config file, so the command now confirms first.

```
About to remove VTA 'my-vta':
  Name: My VTA
  DID:  did:webvh:...
  The stored credential for this VTA will be deleted.
  This is the default VTA — the default will move.

Proceed with removal? [y/N]
```

Anything other than `y`/`yes` prints `Aborted.` and leaves the config untouched.

- The prompt reuses `vta_cli_common::commands::contexts::confirm_destructive`, so the wording matches `pnm contexts delete` rather than adding a second style of destructive prompt.
- As with that command, a non-TTY stdin reads EOF and aborts. That is the safe default and it is what `--force` is for — scripts that call `pnm vta remove` today (the `pnm setup --overwrite` error hint points operators at it) pass the flag to keep their current behaviour.
- `docs/02-vta/non-interactive-setup.md` notes the prompt and the flag on the `--overwrite` row that carries that hint.

Two parse tests pin the default-confirms / `--force` behaviour. `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p pnm-cli --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo test -p pnm-cli` are green locally.

title: ZKP working draft: trust-graph implementation guide and construction catalogue
body:
This draft introduces an implementation-oriented ZKP specification for decentralized trust graphs. It starts with the outcome an application needs—membership eligibility, a private relationship, selective disclosure, common control, accepted status or delegated authority—and connects it to credential inputs, constructions, verifier checks and reproducible evidence. Personhood and liveness are important use cases and sources, rather than the specification's entire scope.

The contribution contains twelve construction records, the ADR-001 crosswalk, four proving-system entries and portable conformance generation. Records remain informative at their existing evidence states. ADR-001 is the flagship community-anchored use case; a credential-bound membership presentation is proposed as the first implementation milestone supporting it. Existing component tests do not establish the complete composition.

The reading order now leads with an implementation guide and trust-graph lifecycle. Detailed cryptographic background follows the operational material. The book explains construction fit and paper relationships from the same technical records. Explicit WG review notes mark proposals, open technical questions and evidence requests; they do not imply ratification.

The draft clarifies private witness custody, credential authenticity, offline voucher linkage, distinct members versus distinct people, root authority, transcript encoding and the separation of proof verification, policy acceptance and action completion. It documents the lab's domain-separated, length-prefixed transcript hash and BN254 conversion, with a comparison vector. Strict transcript types and semantic checks remain proposed implementation work, rather than claims about the current lab validator.

Near the end, an informative maintenance note describes how surveys of related DTG, Trust over IP, VTC and First Person Project work may produce traceable updates. An agent handoff lists twelve verification tasks with use-case fit, dependencies and expected evidence. The companion research/verifier-worklist.json makes that queue reusable.

Validation performed locally: all 17 conformance files validate; generated sections and terms match regeneration; Spec-Up-T renders with its two configured external glossary sources; the framed/plain transcript comparison digests were separately reproduced. Existing record states and histories were preserved. These checks are not a circuit audit or independent reproduction of the complete proof.

Review requested: general scope and first milestone; credential/witness contracts; canonical wire profile; construction comparisons; book organization; and the evidence required for future recommendations or adoption.

The author’s CC BY 4.0 grant for the adapted background is recorded in Appendix A. The renderer’s Windows branch-metadata fallback remains a known local rendering limitation. The draft also leaves exact cross-repository implementation baselines and several wire-profile decisions open. No construction or proving system is proposed as adopted merely by opening this PR.

title: docs: fix seven mermaid blocks that fail to render on GitHub
body:
## What

Seven mermaid blocks across three docs pages render as **"Unable to render rich display"** on GitHub. `docs/02-vta/task-consent.md` — the DTTE ceremony page — is the one that prompted this.

Two independent causes, both invisible locally because nothing parses these blocks before they are pushed.

### 1. A semicolon terminates a mermaid statement

In a sequence message it is not text:

```
V->>V: PDP → requireConsent; compute payload_digest
```

parses as a message, then `compute payload_digest` as a fresh statement, which then hits the *next* line's arrow:

```
Parse error on line 7:
...mpute payload_digest    V-->>R: rejecte
-----------------------^
… got 'NEWLINE'
```

Two lines in `task-consent.md`, one in `03-vtc/trust-registry.md`. Replaced with commas.

### 2. `[/` opens a shape, not a label

`API[/v1/*]` is read as the parallelogram form `[/text/]`, so in `03-vtc/website-and-admin.md` every node named after a route path (`/v1/*`, `/admin/*`, `/health`, `/`) broke its diagram — five blocks. Quoting the label (`API["/v1/*"]`) fixes it; two decision nodes carrying parentheses needed the same treatment.

## Verification

Parsed **every** mermaid block in the repo with mermaid 11.17.2 under jsdom — **43 blocks, 0 failing**. Reverting the first hunk reproduces GitHub's error text character for character, so the harness is measuring the right thing.

Worth adding as a CI gate: this class is only visible after a push, and these have been broken since they were written.

## Also: one known-gap correction

`task-consent.md` read "**No Rust client crate can sign a decision**" one sentence after naming `vta-mobile-core/src/consent.rs` — a Rust crate in this workspace that does exactly that. The real constraint is that it is a UniFFI crate for the mobile bindings and no CLI depends on it (`pnm-cli` has no such dependency and no approve command), so approval is remote-only. Reworded in both places it appears.

The other three gaps were re-checked against the code and hold as written:

- no pending-status task exists under `task-consent/` — only `request/0.1`, `decision/0.1`, `granted/0.1`
- `policy/evaluate/0.3` is still unserved by the VTA (the `vtc-service` mention is a different service)
- the three ceremony families are still separate: `auth/step-up/approve-response/0.3`, `task-consent/decision/0.1`, `consent/decision/1.0`

Docs only — no code, no behaviour change.

title: Specify the Verifiable Trust Network
body:
Adds a chapter specifying the Verifiable Trust Network, rendered after the Verifiable Trust Community and before the membership lifecycle.

## What a VTN is

A VTN aggregates communities. It curates a published set of VTCs and of other VTNs, under an identified owner and a governance framework, so that a relying party can discover many communities through one list rather than through a relationship with each of them. The comparison the chapter uses is the autonomous system: the unit at which a set is aggregated, announced and found.

It sits above the VTC in **aggregation**, not in **authority**. A VTN is not a parent of the communities it lists — it creates no trust contexts, derives no keys, and does not decide who is a member of anything. Removing a community from a network's list takes nothing away from that community's members.

## The asymmetry the chapter turns on

A listing is the network's to make. A VTN may list a party that never asked to be listed, where community membership requires both sides to agree. That one-sidedness is what makes curation possible at all — a curator who must negotiate every entry curates nothing — and it is also what makes a list easy to misread, since *they list us* and *we joined* are different facts about different numbers of parties.

The cost is paid explicitly:

- `VTI-VTN-011` — every entry states whether the listed party acknowledged it;
- `VTI-VTN-012` — a listed party can repudiate, and the network publishes the repudiation alongside the entry;
- `VTI-VTN-013` — an unacknowledged entry is not membership, and gets no membership credential.

## What a listing does not establish

A network invites exactly the shortcut `VTI-REG-024` refuses: one relationship standing in for a hundred. `VTI-VTN-022` keeps listing non-transitive with recognition; `VTI-VTN-023` allows a relying party to accept everything a network lists, but only as an explicit policy naming the network and the framework version it rests on. A decision can be withdrawn when the framework changes; an inference cannot, because nobody recorded making it.

Networks nest without limit (state → national → global) and are expected to overlap — nothing stops three parties curating the same subject. Neither changes what an entry establishes, and `VTI-VTN-041` refuses the arithmetic of treating several overlapping networks as corroboration without establishing their independence, per `VTI-CMP-071`.

## The open question

Whether a VTN is a distinct node type or a VTC operating in a curation role is not settled, and the chapter says so rather than deciding it. The requirements state what a network must do, not what it is built from, so either resolution is reachable without disturbing a requirement identifier. The conformance target is marked provisional until the working group closes it. Recorded as **D9** and **D10** in `STRUCTURE.md`.

## Contents

- `spec/11a-vtn.md` — the chapter: 29 requirements in area `VTN`, plus an informative open-question subsection and illustrations (a software foundation's communities, three-level health networks, a conformance body such as Ayra, the First Person Network).
- Architecture — a provisional target row and a subsection placing the VTN against the VTA and VTC.
- Conformance — a `Network` profile, the VTN target with a note on its provisional status, and the `VTN` area.
- Introduction — nodes list, vocabulary paragraph, structure table, and a row in the reading table for curating communities into a network.
- Terminology — `VTN` and `listing`.
- References — the autonomous system model, Ayra, and the First Person Network, all informative.
- A pointer from the registries chapter, since a network's answers bind under it.

## Notes for review

- The file is named `11a-vtn.md` rather than renumbering everything after it: `markdown_paths` in `specs.json` fixes the rendered order, and renumbering costs the history of every file it touches for nothing. The convention is now written down in `STRUCTURE.md`.
- No implementation exists. This is specification-first in the strong sense, and the chapter opens by saying so.
- The organisations named in the illustrations are there to make the shapes concrete; the chapter states that naming one is neither recognition nor endorsement.
- `npm run render` was not run locally (`node_modules` is not installed); CI renders it. Checked by script instead: every `[[ref:]]` resolves to a definition, and every cited `VTI-XXX-nnn` exists.

transitive with recognition (VTI-VTN-022); a relying party may still accept
everything a network lists, but as an explicit policy naming the network and
the framework version, never as an inference. Networks nest without limit and
are expected to overlap, and neither changes what an entry establishes.

Whether a VTN is a distinct node type or a VTC operating in a curation role is
not settled. The chapter states what a network must do rather than what it is
built from, so either resolution is reachable without disturbing a requirement
identifier; the conformance target is marked provisional until the working
group closes it. Recorded as D9 and D10 in the structure record.

The chapter renders after the VTC and before the membership lifecycle. It is
specification-first in the strong sense: no implementation exists.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: Create the DTG predicate vocabulary as a repo-driven registry
body:
## Summary

#47 introduces the verifiable statement credential (VSC), whose meaning is carried by a predicate from a governed vocabulary, and says that predicates beyond the two core profiles will be defined in a planned "DTG Predicate Vocabulary" specification. Review has already produced the first candidates (#50 identity vetting; presentation/custody in the #47 thread), and the question of where they go is blocking. This issue proposes the answer: **a repo-driven registry, on the model of the ToIP glossary, not a specification** — and lays out what the repository needs to contain so that it can be created and populated without further design work.

The proposal was discussed against the alternative of growing the credential spec, or a dedicated vocabulary spec, and rejected both on cadence: a ToIP specification moves WD → Implementers Draft → Approved Deliverable, and a vocabulary needs to add an entry the week a community needs it. A generated registry governed by pull request is the only shape that matches how the content changes.

Assumption for this issue: ToIP is amenable to hosting the namespace and the published artifacts, at least for now. The IRIs below are placeholders until #48 is decided.

## Three things that were being called "the vocabulary"

| | What it is | Nature | Home |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. The rules** | what a predicate definition must contain, how it is published, immutability, NFC, labels, admission criteria | normative, changes rarely | the credential spec's *Predicate Profiles* section for now (it already states the nine required members); split out into a small "DTG Vocabularies" spec if and when the definition format needs its own normative home |
| **B. WG-curated predicates** | `endorses`, `witnessed`, and whatever the WG agrees to define under the DTG namespace | content, grows one entry at a time | **this repository** |
| **C. Community predicates** | terms a VTC or VTN defines under a namespace it controls | content, not ours to hold | the community's own namespace, referenced from its governance framework; published in the same format as B so tooling works for both |

The credential spec's *Community-Defined Predicates* section keeps one illustrative example and no more; every real predicate goes to B or C.

## The repository

Proposed name: `trustoverip/dtgwg-predicate-vocab`. Same tooling philosophy as `ctwg-main-glossary`: one source file per entry, a generator, a published output, PR governance.

```
dtgwg-predicate-vocab/
├── README.md                     what this is, how to propose a predicate
├── GOVERNANCE.md                 admission criteria, review, statuses, versioning
├── predicates/                   one file per predicate — the source of truth
│   ├── endorses.jsonld
│   ├── witnessed.jsonld
│   ├── identity-vetting.jsonld   from #50
│   └── presented.jsonld          from the #47 review thread
├── schemas/                      JSON Schema for each predicate's `value` payload
│   └── identity-vetting.schema.json
├── meta/
│   ├── predicate.schema.json     the definition format (mirrors the nine points in the credential spec)
│   └── meta-context.jsonld       JSON-LD context for the definition files themselves
├── tools/                        generator: validates predicates/ against meta/, builds dist/
└── dist/                         generated, published at the namespace; never hand-edited
    ├── vocab.jsonld              all active and deprecated terms, additive
    ├── index.html                human-readable vocabulary document
    ├── accept-list.json          machine-readable list verifiers can import
    └── context/
        └── v1.jsonld             frozen context for the additional members of core profiles
```

## The definition format

One JSON-LD document per predicate. The members are the nine points a profile MUST state under *Predicate Profiles* in #47, plus registry metadata. `witnessed`, as it would appear:

```json
{
  "@context": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab/meta-context.jsonld",
  "id": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab#witnessed",
  "type": "Predicate",
  "status": "active",
  "since": "2026-10-01",
  "label": {
    "en": "witnessed",
    "de": "bezeugt",
    "nl": "getuige geweest van"
  },
  "definition": {
    "en": "The issuer observed the subject issue the credential the object names, under the conditions of a specific trust task exchange."
  },
  "classification": "evidence",
  "weighedBy": "The community whose witnessing policy the attestation is issued under.",
  "objectKind": ["digestMultibase"],
  "subjectObjectRelationship": "credentialSubject.id MUST be the issuer of the credential object.digestMultibase names; a verifier holding that credential MUST check it.",
  "additionalMembers": {
    "witnessContext": {
      "required": false,
      "schema": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab/schemas/witness-context.schema.json"
    }
  },
  "taskContextRequired": true,
  "minimumIssuerScope": "directed",
  "issuer": "A member, or a VTA acting according to VTC policy.",
  "establishes": "That the issuer attests that, in the exchange identified by taskContext, it observed the subject issue the credential whose claims digest to object.digestMultibase.",
  "doesNotEstablish": [
    "that the referenced credential is currently valid or unrevoked",
    "that the referenced credential's claims are true",
    "that the exchange reached its terminal state (Outcome Interpretability applies)",
    "that the witness is a member of any community",
    "that any consequential action is authorized"
  ],
  "definedIn": "https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-cred-spec/#the-dtgwitnessed-profile-vwc",
  "governedBy": null
}
```

The presentation/custody predicate from the #47 thread, showing the case where the observed party is the referenced credential's *subject*:

```json
{
  "@context": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab/meta-context.jsonld",
  "id": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab#presented",
  "type": "Predicate",
  "status": "proposed",
  "label": { "en": "presented" },
  "definition": {
    "en": "The issuer observed the subject present the credential the object names. The subject is the holder; the credential's issuer need not have been present."
  },
  "classification": "evidence",
  "objectKind": ["digestMultibase"],
  "subjectObjectRelationship": "credentialSubject.id MUST be the credentialSubject.id of the credential object.digestMultibase names.",
  "taskContextRequired": true,
  "minimumIssuerScope": "directed",
  "issuer": "A member, or a VTA acting according to VTC policy.",
  "establishes": "That the issuer attests that, in the exchange identified by taskContext, the subject presented the credential whose claims digest to object.digestMultibase.",
  "doesNotEstablish": [
    "that the presented credential is valid, unrevoked, or was issued to the subject",
    "that the presented credential's claims are true",
    "that the subject controls the presented credential's subject identifier",
    "that any consequential action is authorized"
  ]
}
```

A community predicate uses the same format under its own namespace, with `governedBy` pointing at the governance framework that defines who may issue it and how it is weighed. That is what makes one generator, one validator and one accept-list format serve both tiers.

## Generated outputs

| Artifact | Consumer | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `vocab.jsonld` | tooling, RDF consumers, `rdfs:label` lookups | additive; a term is never removed or altered once active, only deprecated |
| `index.html` | people | the human-readable vocabulary, one section per predicate, labels in every language supplied |
| `accept-list.json` | verifiers | the active IRIs with their machine-checkable constraints (object kinds, `taskContextRequired`, minimum scope, schema URLs), for import into verifier configuration at configuration time |
| `context/v1.jsonld` | credentials under core profiles | the JSON-LD terms for additional members such as `witnessContext`; frozen per version, as VC contexts must be |

An `accept-list.json` entry, so the shape is concrete:

```json
{
  "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab#witnessed": {
    "status": "active",
    "objectKind": ["digestMultibase"],
    "taskContextRequired": true,
    "minimumIssuerScope": "directed",
    "additionalMembers": { "witnessContext": { "required": false } }
  }
}
```

## Versioning and immutability — two different rules

This is the part that needs to be got right before anything is published, and it feeds #48.

- **Predicate IRIs are unversioned and term-immutable.** `…/vocab#witnessed` never changes meaning and is never deleted; adding `#presented` does not touch it. Versioning the namespace (`…/vocab/v1#witnessed` → `…/vocab/v2#witnessed`) would change every predicate's IRI whenever any predicate is added, and break byte-exact matching for every issued credential. So the namespace IRI decided in #48 **must carry no version segment**. The current placeholder in #47 (`https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1#witnessed`) has one and should not be the final form.
- **Contexts are versioned and frozen.** A JSON-LD context that credentials list must not change after publication, so `context/v1.jsonld` is frozen and additions go in `v2`. This is fine because credentials do not need the vocabulary context to carry a predicate — predicates are absolute IRIs — only to carry a core profile's additional members.

Releases are git tags. `dist/` at a tag is the published state; the namespace serves the latest tag's `vocab.jsonld` and `index.html`, and every `context/vN.jsonld` ever released.

## Governance

`GOVERNANCE.md`, drawing on the credential spec's rules:

- **Admission to the DTG namespace.** A proposed predicate is accepted when it (1) is complete against `meta/predicate.schema.json`, including the establishes / does-not-establish block; (2) is on the *attests* side of the statement/establishment test — it is not a predicate whose PASS a verifier would act on as representation, authority, membership, admission, governed status or task completion; (3) is unilateral; (4) is not meaningful only inside one exchange; (5) has no existing term with the same meaning — one identifier per concept; (6) has an NFC IRI and at least an English label; and (7) is either needed by a DTG specification or in use, or credibly about to be, by more than one community.
- **Statuses.** `proposed` (merged, not yet in a release), `active`, `deprecated` (kept forever, marked, with a pointer to any replacement). Nothing is ever deleted.
- **Review.** Two WG approvals for a new `active` term; one for editorial changes to labels or definitions that do not alter meaning; meaning changes are not permitted — deprecate and add.
- **Equivalence.** The registry MAY record that a community term has the same meaning as a DTG term, as information for people configuring verifiers. Verifiers never follow it (Predicate Handling in #47).

## Relationship to the credential spec

- The credential spec keeps the statement mechanism, Predicate Handling, What Verification Establishes, Predicate Profiles (which is where the definition format's requirements live for now), and — for WD03 — the `endorses` and `witnessed` profiles, because they replace WD02 normative text and need a published home. Once this repository has a release, those two move here and the credential spec references them; nothing on the wire changes.
- The `dtg:` notation in the credential spec resolves to this repository's namespace once #48 is decided.
- *Related Specifications* in the credential spec should describe this as a registry, not a specification.
- #50 should target this repository rather than the credential spec's example section, as the first entry.
- #47's reviewer request for a core presentation/custody profile is answered by `presented.jsonld` above rather than by a third profile in the credential spec.

## Sequencing

1. Create the repository with `README.md`, `GOVERNANCE.md`, `meta/`, and an empty `predicates/`; decide #48 so the placeholder IRIs can be replaced.
2. Add the generator (validation against `meta/predicate.schema.json`, build of `dist/`), and CI that fails a PR whose definition is incomplete.
3. First entries: `identity-vetting` (#50), `presented`. Mirror `endorses` and `witnessed` as `proposed` so the format is exercised against the two real profiles.
4. First release once the credential spec reaches WD03; then move `endorses` and `witnessed` here for WD04 and update the credential spec's references.

## Open questions

- Which ToIP deliverable type a repo-driven registry is, and whether the glossary's process and tooling can be borrowed wholesale. (A question for ToIP staff.)
- Whether this repository should also carry the other community-defined vocabularies the DTG already depends on — VDC `scope` terms, VAC `actions`, the VEC endorsement vocabulary — since they are the same kind of thing with the same publication gap. If so, "DTG Vocabularies" is the better name. Flagged, not proposed here.
- Namespace and hosting: #48.

Refs #45, #47, #48, #50, #51.

title: Add the verifiable statement credential (VSC)
body:
## Summary

Adds the **Verifiable Statement Credential (VSC)**: one `StatementCredential` type carrying a subject, an absolute-IRI predicate drawn from a governed vocabulary, and an object. The WD02 `EndorsementCredential` and `WitnessCredential` subtypes become its first two **predicate profiles** (`dtg:endorses`, `dtg:witnessed`); future predicates are added as profiles, not types. Implements the design settled in #45, including the fail-closed rule, the "what does PASS mean" bound on every profile, and the predicate-handling rules raised in that thread.

Type count goes from eight to seven. The type strings `EndorsementCredential` and `WitnessCredential` are removed — a VSC carries exactly one channel of meaning, its `predicate`.

## What changed

- **New `VSC` section** (`spec/body.md`, replacing the VWC and VEC sections):
  - *Statements and Establishment* — the profile/type test, stated once; statements are evidence, governance turns evidence into establishment
  - Schema — `credentialSubject.id` / `predicate` / `object` (`id` | `digestMultibase` | `value`), the unilateral rule
  - *Predicate Handling* (normative) — reject anything not an absolute IRI; reject any predicate not in a configured vocabulary; no equivalence-following; NFC; identifier vs `rdfs:label`; resolve at configuration time, never at verification time; vocabularies immutable once published
  - *What Verification Establishes* (normative) — type-level bound (representation, authority, membership, admission, governed status, task completion) and the per-profile "establishes / does not establish" requirement; a profile classifies shape and narrows no cross-cutting obligation
  - *Predicate Profiles* (normative) — the nine things a profile MUST state; artifact rule; non-nested-task rule; editor's note on the planned **DTG Predicate Vocabulary** spec
  - *Statements in the Graph* — the credential is the unit of attribution; informative RDF-reification note; editor's note on context terms (`predicate` as `@id`, `object.value` as `@json`)
  - `dtg:endorses` (VEC) and `dtg:witnessed` (VWC) profiles with PASS blocks; community-defined predicate example
- **Generic wording** in Digest Encoding (statement `object` replaces the VWC line; predicate named as a #38 blinding target), Trust Task Context Binding ("currently only the VWC" → profiles that require it), VDC "differs in kind" list, ZK predicate list, Security (#6 generalised, new #7 on predicate acceptance), Governance #4, Internationalization, Conformance targets, References
- **`intro.md` / `header.md`** — eight → seven; VEC/VWC listed as VSC profiles; DTG Predicate Vocabulary added to Related Specifications
- **Glossary** — new VSC term; VEC, VWC and DTG annotation credential definitions updated

Renders cleanly with `npm run render`; no undefined terms or broken `[[ref]]`s.

## Judgment calls — please review these specifically

1. **Absolute IRIs only; no CURIEs on the wire.** The strawman allowed CURIEs. Dropping them removes the silent-failure case (undefined prefix → VC 2.0's issuer-dependent `@vocab`), makes predicate matching a byte comparison that needs neither `@context` nor a JSON-LD processor, and gives each predicate exactly one representation for digests and blinding. `dtg:` is declared as documentation notation only.
2. **Direction binding generalised to every VWC.** WD02 required "subject = issuer of the referenced credential" only for bidirectional exchanges; the profile requires it always. Editor's note in the profile presents the WD02 alternative.
3. **VEC/VWC kept as the names of the two profiles** so existing prose (witness scope, DID methods, privacy) still reads; only the type strings are gone.
4. **VSC placed under Annotation Credentials provisionally.** It annotates a node, not an edge. Category reshaping is left to #28; editor's notes in the taxonomy and the section say so.
5. **Non-nested-task rule stated here** as a constraint on profiles, with nesting semantics deferred to the trust task spec (#11). Could equally live there.
6. **Core profiles stay in this spec for WD03** because the vocabulary spec doesn't exist yet; the editor's note says they move once it does, and that nothing on the wire changes when they do.
7. **`specs.json` still says "seven"** — it was stale before and is now correct, so it's untouched.

## Decision needed: the home of the DTG namespace

Mandating absolute IRIs means the core predicates are now written out in full, and this PR writes them as the context URL plus `#`:

```
https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1#witnessed
```

That's a default, not a decision. The namespace is where every predicate this WG defines will live, and it's the IRI communities will copy. It should be controlled by whoever governs the vocabulary — which, if the DTG Predicate Vocabulary becomes a ToIP spec, may not be `firstperson.network`. Changing it later is a find-and-replace in the spec but a migration for every issued credential.

**We need to decide this soon — ideally now, and at the latest before this specification bumps to an Implementers Draft**, since that's the point at which issued credentials start to matter. Options as I see them: keep `firstperson.network`, move to a ToIP-controlled IRI (e.g. under `trustoverip.org` or a `w3id.org` redirect the WG controls), or a `w3id.org` indirection now so the hosting decision can be made separately from the identifier.

## Pre-existing issue noticed, not fixed here

spec-up-t generates heading ids with parentheses and percent-encoded colons (`vac-(verifiable-authority-credential)`) while every internal link in the spec uses GitHub-style slugs (`#vac-verifiable-authority-credential`). This predates the branch and affects all existing links; this PR follows the existing convention. Worth checking whether anchors resolve on the published site.

Refs #45, #28, #38, #11.
