title: chore(deps): take the resolver line that guards did:webvh resolution
body:
`affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` 0.8.37 named directly as a floor, and
`affinidi-did-web` 0.1.5 / `affinidi-net-guard` 0.1.0 in the lockfile behind it.

## What changes for an operator

**A signer DID on a non-public host stops resolving, so its commits report
`unresolvedSigner` instead of being fetched.**

`verify-trust` resolves DIDs that the author of the commits under review chose.
The `Signed-by-DID:` trailer, and the committer header it falls back to, are
whatever the commit object says — fully attacker-supplied on a fork pull
request. Resolving `did:webvh:<scid>:<host>` is an outbound fetch of `<host>`.

Until this bump `did:webvh` was the unguarded method in this graph. `did:web`
(`affinidi-did-web`) and agent-name lookups (`agent-names`) already refused
non-public targets; `didwebvh-rs` 0.6.1 built its client with a timeout and
`redirect::Policy::none()` and no address check at all, so
`did:webvh:<scid>:localhost%3A<port>` was fetched over plain `http://` and any
other name was fetched from whatever address it resolved to. On a GitHub-hosted
ephemeral runner there is little behind that. On a **self-hosted runner with
internal reachability** it was an SSRF primitive that a pull request could aim,
one DID at a time, reading the answers off the per-signer resolution errors in
the report. `max_signers` bounded how many it could try, not where they pointed.

After this bump, resolution refuses before any request is sent: the names
`localhost`, `*.localhost`, `*.local`, `*.internal`, `home.arpa` and
single-label names, and any name whose resolved addresses include a loopback,
private, carrier-grade-NAT, link-local (cloud metadata), unique-local,
multicast or reserved address. It then connects only to the addresses it
checked, which closes DNS rebinding; it follows no redirect; and it ignores
proxy environment variables, since a proxy would resolve the name itself,
outside these checks.

**There is deliberately no opt-out.** A DID on an internal host is not an
identity this verifier can be asked to trust, and a commit claiming one now
fails as `UNRESOLVED` (`unresolvedSigner`) with a `BlockedHost` reason —
visibly, in the report, rather than silently. If a community genuinely publishes
its signer DIDs on an internal host, the fix is to publish them where the
verifier can reach them, not to widen the verifier.

## Why the floor is stated in the manifest

`affinidi-tdk` reaches this crate as `^0.8`, which silently admits 0.8.36 —
where the webvh half of the guard is simply absent. So
`affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk = "0.8.37"` is named directly in
`[workspace.dependencies]` and taken by `verify-trust`, and `build_resolver`
states `HostPolicy::PublicOnly` rather than relying on the default. That makes a
downgrade a compile error — `with_host_policy` does not exist before 0.8.37 —
instead of a quiet reopening of the fetch.

It is a normal dependency and not a dev-dependency on purpose: a floor in
`[dev-dependencies]` does not travel with the published crate, and
`did-git-sign`, the crate OpenVTC consumes, resolves through the same graph.
No feature is chosen — `affinidi-tdk` already takes this crate with its default
features, so the line adds a version requirement and nothing else.

`affinidi-did-web` moves 0.1.4 → 0.1.5 in the lockfile only (it is not a direct
dependency here). That is the did:web half of the same guard: its classifier and
DNS-pinning resolver move into the shared `affinidi-net-guard` 0.1.0 crate with
its public API unchanged, so this workspace's behaviour is unaffected except
that a wider set of addresses is refused.

`didwebvh-rs` 0.6.1 stays in the graph alongside 0.7.0 because `vta-sdk` 0.36
declares `"0.6"`. Nothing here names a `didwebvh-rs` type, and the copy the
**resolution** path holds is the 0.7.0 one:
`cargo tree -i didwebvh-rs@0.7.0` shows
`didwebvh-rs 0.7.0 → affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk 0.8.37 → verify-trust`.
It collapses when VTI takes 0.7 and releases.

## Tests

`crates/verify-trust/tests/verify_trust_e2e.rs`:
`a_signer_did_on_an_internal_host_is_refused_without_being_fetched`. A real
sshsig-signed commit claims `did:webvh:<scid>:localhost%3A<port>:agent` while a
TCP listener stands in for the internal service. The test runs the real path —
`build_resolver` then `resolve_signer_keys`, exactly as `handle_verify_trust`
does — and asserts the report marks the signer `unresolvedSigner` with a
`BlockedHost` reason, that the range fails, and that the listener accepted
**zero** connections. A refusal raised after connecting would already have told
the author that something is listening.

## Version

No version bump. `0.4.9` was released in #43 and this repo bumps the workspace
version in its own `chore(release):` commit; #44 and #45 likewise landed on main
without one. This needs to go out in a release for consumers to pick it up.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace` — all pass, including the 16 `verify_trust_e2e` tests
- `cargo test -p did-git-sign --features insecure-policy-bypass` — 2 passed
- `cargo tree -i didwebvh-rs@0.7.0` — resolution path on 0.7.0 as above

title: fix(vgi-core): find the Signed-by-DID trailer block the way git does
body:
`vgi-core` located the `Signed-by-DID:` trailer with its own rules: walk up from
the end of the message while each line looks like `key: value`. Git's rules are
not that, and the two disagreed in both directions.

Nothing here was exploitable on its own — every trust decision already fails
closed. The identity comes out of the signed payload, the claimed DID has to
publish the key that actually signed, the signature has to verify over that
payload, and the registry has to authorize the DID. What was left is a
**display** differential: a reviewer reads the DID that `git log`, `git
interpret-trailers` and every git-based review UI report for a commit, so when
`vgi-core` read a different trailer, the DID that got verified was not the DID
that was shown.

## What the differential found

A property test comparing `signer_did` against both of git's own trailer views
found seven disagreements. Three had `vgi-core` reading a claim git does not show
as a trailer at all, which is the direction that matters: the commit is
attributed to a DID a reviewer cannot see in the trailer block.

1. **A trailer-shaped line inside a prose paragraph.** Git takes the final
   paragraph as trailers only when every line in it is a trailer, or when one of
   git's own trailers is present and trailers are at least 25% of it.
   `Signed-by-DID: …` appended to a paragraph of prose is not a trailer to git;
   it was a claim here.
2. **A trailer-shaped line in the title paragraph.** Git never reads trailers
   from the first paragraph, so `Signed-by-DID: …` as the subject, or as the
   line directly under the subject with no blank line between, is not a trailer.
   Both were claims here.
3. **Blank lines before the subject.** `git log` reads trailers from the subject
   onward — pretty.c's `parse_commit_message` runs `skip_blank_lines` first — so
   in a message beginning with a blank line the trailer-shaped line that follows
   *is* the subject. It was a claim here. (This one is also why the two git
   commands disagree with each other on such a message: `interpret-trailers`
   reads plain text and does no such normalization. The commit view is the one
   that matters, since that is what `vgi-core` and reviewers both read.)
4. **Whitespace before the colon.** Git's key scan allows spaces and tabs
   between the key and the colon and trims them, so `Signed-by-DID : did:…` is
   the trailer to git. `vgi-core` did not recognize the key, and — because the
   line then failed its "is this a trailer line" test — stopped treating the
   whole block as a trailer block.
5. **Key case.** `%(trailers:key=…)` matches case-insensitively, so
   `signed-by-did: did:…` is the claim to git. `vgi-core` compared the key
   exactly.
6. **A folded value.** Git folds a continuation line (one starting with
   whitespace) into the value above it and displays the joined text. To
   `vgi-core` a continuation line was not a trailer line, so the entire block
   stopped being a trailer block and the claim disappeared.

7. **Whitespace before a fold.** Git leaves the whitespace that precedes the
   newline alone and adds one space for the fold, so `Signed-by-DID: did:…com   `
   with a continuation line under it reports four spaces where this reported
   one. Both values are unresolvable DIDs, so unlike the others this is cosmetic
   rather than a difference in *which* trailer is read — but the text git reports
   is the text a reviewer sees. It only surfaced at case 3674 of a deep local
   run, which is the argument for generating these rather than listing them.

Cases 4–6 lose a claim rather than invent one, so `signer_did` fell back to the
committer identity and verification failed closed — but a reviewer still saw a
`Signed-by-DID` that nothing had checked.

Git's 25%-non-trailer allowance and its treatment of `(cherry picked from commit
…)` — which counts as one of git's own trailers even though it contains no
separator at all — had no equivalent here in either direction.

## What changed

`crates/vgi-core/src/commit.rs` now ports git's rules from `trailer.c` rather
than approximating them:

- `trailer_block_start` follows `find_trailer_block_start`: the title paragraph
  is excluded, only the final paragraph can be a block, and it qualifies when
  every line is a trailer or when one of git's generated prefixes is present and
  `trailer_lines * 3 >= non_trailer_lines`. Comment lines are skipped, and
  whitespace-led lines count as continuations or non-trailers depending on what
  sits above them.
- `separator_pos` follows `find_separator`: an alphanumeric-and-`-` key, then
  optional spaces or tabs, then a colon that may not be the first character.
- `last_trailer_value` follows `trailer_block_get`: the block is split into
  entries, a whitespace-led line continues the entry above it only when that
  entry had a separator, keys match case-insensitively, and values are unfolded
  the way `unfold_value` does it.
- Blank lines before the subject are skipped, matching the commit view.

Two behaviour changes worth calling out, both narrowing:

- A `Signed-by-DID:` line that is not in git's trailer block is no longer a
  claim. `did-git-sign` writes the trailer with `git interpret-trailers`, so
  commits it produced are unaffected; the shapes that stop being claims are the
  ones git does not present as trailers either.
- The **last** `Signed-by-DID` trailer wins, and it is a claim only if its value
  is a DID. Previously a later non-DID trailer was skipped in favour of an
  earlier DID-valued one, which let the checked DID hide behind the trailer a
  reader sees last.

Deliberate, documented divergences: this code reads no git configuration, so
`core.commentChar`, `trailer.separators` and `trailer.<token>.key` are git's
defaults here. A repository that changes them can have git see a block this does
not — which loses a claim and fails closed, never the reverse. The comments in
`commit.rs` say so at each site.

## Tests

- `crates/vgi-core/tests/trailer_differential.rs` — the differential. It builds
  commit objects in a throwaway bare repository and compares `signer_did`
  against `git interpret-trailers --parse` **and** `git log -1
  --format='%(trailers:key=Signed-by-DID,valueonly,unfold,separator=%x00)'`. No
  expected DID is hard-coded: git is the oracle, and the test also fails if
  git's two views disagree with each other. 31 fixed shapes always run
  (including the 25% boundary on both sides, which a generated message lands on
  only by luck), plus generated messages built from awkward trailer shapes:
  spaces and tabs before the colon, key case, continuation lines, several
  `Signed-by-DID` lines, trailing whitespace, comment lines, non-trailer
  paragraphs after the block, and trailer-shaped subjects.
  - The case count is capped at 64 and shrinking at 64 iterations, since each
    case spawns three git processes; the whole file runs in about 6 s. It was
    run at 4000 cases locally while writing this, which is where the seventh
    disagreement above turned up, at case 3674.
  - Git is invoked with `GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1` and `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL`/`SYSTEM`
    pointed at a path that does not exist, so the defaults the port follows are
    the ones git uses. Nothing beyond `git init --bare` and `hash-object` is
    needed — no commit, so no `user.name`/`user.email` — which is why it works on
    a plain hosted-runner git.
  - `failure_persistence` is off, so a failure writes nothing into the tree; it
    prints the shrunken message instead, and shapes worth keeping go in the
    fixed list.
- Eleven unit tests next to `trailer_did` assert each rule above directly. They
  need no `git` on PATH and run in microseconds, so the semantics stay pinned
  even where the differential is skipped.
- `proptest` is a new dev-dependency (workspace `proptest = "1"`, resolved to
  1.11.0); `tempfile` was already in the workspace.

## `.github/CODEOWNERS`

Second commit, unrelated to the parser: this repository had no CODEOWNERS, and
no rule requiring review. The file covers `/.github/` (the workflows holding the
crates.io OIDC permission and Releases write access, plus the published
composite action), `/crates/did-git-sign/src/policy.rs` (the signing gate),
`/crates/verify-trust/` (the CI authorization gate) and the manifests, with a
catch-all first so later entries win.

Teams are the ones CLOWarden maintains for this repository from
`OpenVTC/governance` `config.yaml`: `@OpenVTC/openvtc-admins` (admin) and
`@OpenVTC/openvtc-maintainers` (maintain). `lf-staff` is deliberately not used —
it holds no grant on this repository, and a team without write access makes the
whole file invalid.

**This file alone changes nothing that is enforced.** It makes GitHub *request*
those reviews; it blocks nothing until an admin adds a `pull_request` rule to a
ruleset on `main`:

- `required_approving_review_count: 1`
- `require_code_owner_review: true`
- `dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push: true`
- `require_last_push_approval: true`

Today `main` carries only the org `DCO` ruleset, and recent PRs merged with zero
reviews, so that setting is the half of this item that actually closes it.

## Not in this PR

The audit-log fail-open work belongs on top of `did-git-sign/src/policy.rs`,
which #44 rewrote. #44 has since merged (it is in `origin/main` at `d103f98`),
so that item can follow now without conflicting.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace` — 157 passed, 0 failed, across all 11 targets. The
  `vgi-core` lib tests are 37 of those (eleven new), and
  `tests/trailer_differential.rs` is the pair that shells out to git — 31 fixed
  shapes plus 64 generated cases — in 2.3 s.

title: security(audit)!: report failed audit writes, and record use of the signing oracle
body:
Two findings from the same triage row, both about the audit trail being quieter
than it looks.

## 1. Failed audit writes were discarded

27 call sites in `vta-service/src/operations/` wrote `let _ = audit::record(..)`.
The intent was right and stays right — a failed audit write must not fail the
operation it records, since refusing to revoke a key because the log is full
protects nobody. But `let _ =` implements "must not fail the operation" as
"must not be mentioned". The row was gone, the process knew, and it said
nothing, so the only symptom was an absence.

That got worse when the VTA's log became a **hash chain** (#1420). A failed
append is then not one missing line: it is the point past which the chain
cannot be extended, and whoever runs `verify` weeks later cannot distinguish
"the sink was unavailable on Tuesday" from "somebody removed an entry" — the
exact case the chain exists to detect. A dropped error turns tamper-evidence
into a false-positive generator.

`vta-audit` gains `record_best_effort` and `record_with_detail_best_effort`.
Same "never fails the caller" contract; on `Err` they emit `tracing::error!` on
a **distinct target**, `audit.write_failure` (`AUDIT_WRITE_FAILURE_TARGET`),
carrying action, actor, resource, outcome, channel, context id and the error —
enough to reconstruct the row by hand, because nothing retries it — and
increment `audit_sink_write_failures_total` (`AUDIT_WRITE_FAILURES`), labelled
by action.

The target is deliberately not `audit`: that one carries the events, this
carries the news that one of them is missing, which is worth routing and
alerting on separately. Filtering still works from either end, since EnvFilter
matches target prefixes — `RUST_LOG=audit=error` picks it up too.

`detail` is deliberately **not** logged: it is operator free text up to
`DETAIL_MAX_CHARS`, and this line goes to the ordinary log stream.

All 27 sites now call the new helpers (`operations/keys.rs` ×8, `did_templates.rs`
×6, `acl.rs` ×5 — two of them the `_with_detail` variant — `device.rs` ×5,
`audit.rs`, `seeds.rs`, `provision_integration/mod.rs`). No `let _ = audit::record`
remains in the workspace.

`metrics` is added to `vta-audit` as a **facade only**. With no recorder
installed (the offline CLIs, tests) incrementing is a no-op; the Prometheus
exporter stays in `vta-service`, where the HTTP surface is.

## 2. Key signing left no row in the queryable trail

**The question asked in triage — does the trust-task dispatch layer already
audit key signing? — is answered: no.** `handle_sign`
(`trust_tasks/keys.rs`) had no audit call of any kind. Its sibling
`handle_derive_and_sign` records `keys.derive-and-sign` explicitly, and the
dispatch spine's `DispatchAudit::record` returns early for a non-vault
*success* (by design — "its handler owns the row"), recording only refusals as
`task.refused`. So a successful signature reached neither. An incident review
could establish that a key existed and that nobody exported it, and not that it
had signed four thousand times.

`operations/keys::sign_payload` now records `keys.sign` (actor, key id as
resource, channel, the key's context id) via `record_best_effort`.

**Placed at the oracle, not in the four handlers.** `sign_payload` is the
chokepoint all callers reach signing through — the Trust Task, REST, DIDComm,
and the rooms signer (`RoomKeySigner`/`VtaKeySigner`). A handler-level row
would have to be remembered four times, and again for the fifth caller; here a
new caller is audited by construction. The action name matches the sibling
oracle `keys.derive-and-sign` rather than this module's older `key.*` rows.

The payload is not recorded: it is the caller's bytes, may carry anything, and
the trail answers "which key signed, for whom, over what transport", not "what
did it say".

**Success only, deliberately.** A refusal returns from one of the four gates
above the signing code, and for Trust Tasks the spine already records those as
`task.refused`. REST and DIDComm refusals are a real remaining gap, but the fix
belongs wherever those transports grow a spine of their own — not spread across
eight early returns here. Flagging it rather than smuggling it in.

### Volume

`keys.sign` is the highest-frequency key operation, and each row is an append
plus a chain hash, so this is worth stating rather than discovering.

I have **not** added sampling or aggregation, and recommend against sampling:
an audit log that records one signature in N cannot answer "did this key sign
at time T", which is the only question it is here for, and it muddies what the
chain's completeness claims. Aggregation (one row per key per bucket, with a
count) keeps volume bounded and evidence intact, but loses per-signature
timestamps and complicates chain semantics — worth doing if measurements
justify it, not before.

Two existing mechanisms already bound this. Per-context policy quotas
(`enforce_daily_quota(.., "sign", limit)`) cap signatures per context per day,
so the row rate has a configured ceiling wherever a quota is set. And retention
(`cleanup_expired_logs` + `PruneWatermark`, #1423's chain-safe sweep) is the
designed answer to log growth. My suggestion: ship per-signature rows, watch
`audit_sink_write_failures_total` and store growth, and revisit with numbers.

## Breaking change

`sign_payload` takes a new `audit: &vta_audit::SharedAuditSink` parameter and
`room_issuance::SigningContext` a new `audit` field. Both are `pub` in a
published crate, hence the `!`. The sink is **required, not optional**: a caller
able to opt out of the trail could sign unrecorded, which is the whole gap.

This is the same shape as `ec9fc6ef` (`security(keys)!`), which added
`SigningDomain` to this function. Callers updated: `trust_tasks/keys.rs`,
`routes/keys.rs`, `messaging/handlers.rs`, `operations/room_issuance.rs`, plus
the `SigningContext` builders in `trust_tasks/room_owner.rs` and
`trust_tasks/room_group.rs`, and 12 test call sites.

On the release machinery: `vta-audit` has `semver_check = false` in
`release-plz.toml` (nothing consumes it directly), so its bump comes from the
conventional commit — the `!` is what makes that correct. `vta-service` keeps
the check, because `openvtc-core` dev-depends on it for `MockVta`, so
release-plz will force a compatibility-breaking bump there from the same
signal. CI's `semver report` job is `continue-on-error: true` and
informational, so it will flag this and not block.

## Tests

`vta-audit/src/lib.rs` gains a `best_effort` module with a failing `AuditSink`
stub and a capturing `tracing_subscriber` layer:

- a refused write is reported on `audit.write_failure` at **ERROR**, carrying
  the action, actor, resource, context id and the sink's error;
- a refused write still returns normally to the caller — asserted because the
  fix would be worthless if it had turned audit failures into operation
  failures;
- a healthy write reports nothing on that target.

The runtime is built *inside* `with_default` on purpose: that guard is
per-thread, so holding it across an `.await` that resumed elsewhere would emit
where nothing is listening — a test passing for the wrong reason, in the one
place where a false pass means the reporting silently is not there.

`tracing-subscriber` is a **dev**-dependency only. A test that merely checked
the function returned would pass with the log line deleted.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt -p vta-audit -p vta-service --check` — **clean**.
- `cargo clippy -p vta-audit -p vta-service --all-targets -- -D warnings` —
  **clean**.
- `cargo test -p vta-audit` — **15 passed, 0 failed**.
- `cargo test -p vta-service` — **1514 passed, 0 failed, 6 ignored** across 31
  test binaries (lib: 1115 passed, 1 ignored, 402s). Notably green: the
  `audit_coverage` census (every consequential dispatched task must leave an
  audit entry) and the `audit_sink` integration test, both of which sit
  directly over this change.

`Cargo.lock` carries exactly two added edges (`metrics`, `tracing-subscriber`
under `vta-audit`) and nothing else.

## Coordination

Touches only `vta-audit/` and `vta-service/`, so it stays clear of the open PRs
— #1437 (`vta-sdk/src/session.rs`, `vta-cli-common`, `cnm-cli`) and #1438
(backup files, `vti-common`).

title: security(audit)!: report failed audit writes, and record use of the signing oracle (#1443)
body:
security(audit)!: report failed audit writes, and record use of the signing oracle (#1443)

27 call sites in vta-service/src/operations wrote let _ = audit::record(..). The intent was right and stays right: a failed audit write must not fail the operation it records, since refusing to revoke a key because the log is full protects nobody. But let _ = implements that as "must not be mentioned", so the row was gone, the process knew, and it said nothing. With the log now a hash chain, a failed append is the point past which the chain cannot be extended, and whoever runs verify later cannot tell an unavailable sink from a removed entry, which is the case the chain exists to detect.

vta-audit gains record_best_effort and record_with_detail_best_effort: the same never-fails-the-caller contract, but on Err they log at ERROR on a distinct target (audit.write_failure) carrying enough of the row to reconstruct it by hand, and increment audit_sink_write_failures_total labelled by action. All 27 sites now call them, and no let _ = audit::record remains. detail is deliberately not logged, being operator free text bound only by DETAIL_MAX_CHARS. metrics is a facade only: with no recorder installed the increment is a no-op, and the Prometheus exporter stays in vta-service.

Second, key signing left no row in the queryable trail. handle_sign had no audit call at all, its sibling handle_derive_and_sign records explicitly, and the dispatch spine returns early for a non-vault success, recording only refusals as task.refused. So a successful signature reached neither. sign_payload now records keys.sign, placed at the oracle rather than in the four handlers because it is the chokepoint the Trust Task, REST, DIDComm and the rooms signer all reach signing through, so a new caller is audited by construction. Success only: a refusal returns from one of the gates above, and the REST and DIDComm refusal rows are a separate gap left for follow-up. The payload is not recorded, since the trail answers which key signed and for whom, not what it said.

BREAKING: sign_payload takes a required audit sink, and room_issuance::SigningContext gains an audit field; both are pub in a published crate. Required rather than optional, because a caller able to opt out of the trail could sign unrecorded. Same shape as the SigningDomain addition in ec9fc6ef.

Tests: a failing AuditSink stub plus a capturing tracing layer assert that the refusal is reported at ERROR with the row it lost, that the caller still returns normally, and that a healthy write reports nothing on that target. tracing-subscriber is a dev-dependency only, because a test that merely checked the return value would pass with the log line deleted.

title: security(vtc-admin-ui): render a plugin icon as an image, not as markup (#1442)
body:
security(vtc-admin-ui): render a plugin icon as an image, not as markup (#1442)

PluginIcon passed plugin.icon to dangerouslySetInnerHTML, putting a third-party plugin string into the document as live DOM. script-src self stops a script element in it from executing, but an onload or onerror attribute is not script-src business, and the icon reaches the shell from plugin JavaScript the shell does not control.

A string starting with <svg now renders as an img with a data:image/svg+xml URL. Nothing inside an img executes, and img-src self data: is already in the CSP, so this needs neither a sanitiser nor a new dependency. Any other string renders as text, so markup that is not an SVG appears as its own characters rather than as elements.

PluginIcon is exported and covered by src/App.test.tsx: an SVG carrying onload renders as an img with no on* attribute anywhere and no inline svg in the document, a legitimate SVG survives the round trip byte for byte, and non-SVG markup renders as text. The icon doc comment in plugin-api.ts now states the rendering and its consequence for authors, that an img inherits neither currentColor nor the shell 1.75 stroke width.

A .nav-icon img rule keeps the 16px box that the .nav-icon svg rule no longer sizes.

title: security(enclave-proxy): resolve nitro-cli by absolute path, not through $PATH
body:
`detect_enclave_cid` spawned the privileged helper as the bare name
`nitro-cli`, so `$PATH` decided which binary ran (CWE-426). `nitro-cli` is the
thing that tells the proxy which enclave CID to bridge vsock traffic to, and
the proxy believes it.

## What changed

`deploy/nitro/enclave-proxy/src/detect.rs` gains `nitro_cli_path()`, which
returns an absolute path or nothing:

- `NITRO_CLI`, when it is absolute, an existing regular file, and not writable
  by group or others;
- otherwise the first of `/usr/bin/nitro-cli`, `/usr/local/bin/nitro-cli` that
  passes the same check;
- never a bare name, and `$PATH` is never consulted.

The chosen path is logged at INFO. A `NITRO_CLI` that fails vetting is logged
at WARN **with the reason**, then ignored in favour of the standard locations —
an operator who set it and saw nothing happen previously had no way to
distinguish that from "no enclave is running".

The child also gets a minimal environment: `.env_clear()` plus
`PATH=/usr/bin:/bin`. So a `PATH` (or `LD_PRELOAD`, or `IFS`) that influenced
the proxy cannot influence whatever `nitro-cli` itself executes.
`describe-enclaves` reads local state and needs no AWS credentials or region,
so nothing worth inheriting is lost — worth a reviewer's attention anyway,
since it is the one behavioural change beyond path resolution.

## Severity, and why this is not urgent

Low. Two independent reasons:

1. Exploiting it needs write access to a directory on the proxy user's `PATH`,
   which already implies code execution as that user.
2. **The shipped deployment never reaches this code.** `deploy/nitro/deploy-enclave.sh`
   launches the proxy with `--enclave-cid 16` (`:388`, and again at `:426`), and
   auto-detection runs only when `enclave_cid == 0`
   (`deploy/nitro/enclave-proxy/src/main.rs:113-124`). `deploy/nitro/README.md`
   documents pinning the CID in the same way. So this is hardening of a path
   that the shipped scripts do not take.

## Tests

Four unit tests in `detect.rs`, `#[cfg(all(test, unix))]`. The main one plants
an executable `nitro-cli` in a temp directory that writes a marker file,
prepends that directory to `$PATH`, and asserts:

- `nitro_cli_path()` does not return the planted binary, and returns only one
  of the vetted absolute candidates;
- `NITRO_CLI` naming a group/world-writable file is refused;
- **the marker file does not exist after `detect_enclave_cid()`** — the
  load-bearing assertion, because a later refactor back to
  `Command::new("nitro-cli")` would leave a path-only assertion passing.

The three smaller tests pin the `vet_helper` refusals (relative path, missing
file, directory). All the environment mutation is in one test on purpose:
`$PATH` and `NITRO_CLI` are process-global, and `cargo test` would otherwise
interleave them across threads — a flake in the one place where a false pass
means the hardening silently is not there.

## Verification

Run in `deploy/nitro/enclave-proxy`, which is a **standalone workspace**
(excluded from the root one because `tokio-vsock` is Linux-only), so it needs
its own cargo invocation:

- `cargo test` — **23 passed, 0 failed**, including the 4 new `detect::tests`.
- `cargo fmt --check` — fails, **identically to `origin/main`**: the same 6
  files (`channels.rs`, `config.rs`, `main.rs`, `protocol.rs`, `resolve.rs`,
  `storage.rs`). `detect.rs` is not among them.
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` — fails, **identically to
  `origin/main`**: the same 6 locations (`channels.rs:332`, `config.rs:162`,
  `config.rs:195`, `protocol.rs:266`, `storage.rs:47`, `storage.rs:185`).
  None in `detect.rs`.

Both baselines were taken by stashing only `detect.rs` and re-running, so the
comparison is against this crate at `origin/main`. This crate is not built by
CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s `enclave` job checks `vta-enclave`, a
different crate), which is presumably how the pre-existing fmt/clippy debt
accumulated. Cleaning it up is a separate change — it would bury this one.

title: ci: pin every action to a commit SHA, drop write-all, and add Dependabot
body:
`ci.yml` and `verify-trust.yml` between them used **34** `uses:` refs, not one of
them pinned, and `ci.yml` had no `permissions:` block at all — so every job
inherited the repository default of write-all and handed that token to
third-party actions, one of which (`rustsec/audit-check`) is explicitly given
`secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN`.

## What changed

**Pinning.** The 25 refs that remain now name a full-length commit SHA with the
tag it resolved from in a trailing comment. SHAs were resolved with `gh api`,
dereferencing annotated tags:

| Action | Pin |
|---|---|
| `actions/checkout` | `11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262` # v4.4.0 |
| `Swatinem/rust-cache` | `6323deb102c322ba6fcbdcafc7e3dddab59af2b6` # v2.9.2 |
| `rustsec/audit-check` | `69366f33c96575abad1ee0dba8212993eecbe998` # v2.0.0 |
| `EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny-action` | `3c6349835b2b7b196a839186cb8b78e02f7b5f25` # v2.1.1 |
| `taiki-e/install-action` | `9534c84618278caac52cb373bb164ed464dbd8af` # v2.87.11 |
| `actions/upload-artifact` | `ea165f8d65b6e75b540449e92b4886f43607fa02` # v4.6.2 |
| `…/verify-trust` (VGI) | `d4186e5d819c2cbd1247a4d0e6cbd373d25dd0b2` # v0.1.1 |

`git grep -nE 'uses: *[^ .][^ ]*@' -- .github | grep -vE '@[0-9a-f]{40} '` is
now empty.

**The toolchain action is gone.** The nine `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable` /
`@1.95.0` refs were branch refs, and pinning a branch tip would leave Dependabot
nothing to follow. They are nine plain `rustup` steps now — the hosted runners
already ship rustup. The MSRV job stays on 1.95.0, the workspace's
`rust-version`; move both together. `taiki-e/install-action@cargo-llvm-cov` (a
tool tag upstream re-points on every release) becomes a versioned tag plus
`with: tool: cargo-llvm-cov`, which gives Dependabot a semver tag to track.

**Permissions.** Top-level `contents: read` on `ci.yml`. The `audit` job declares
`contents: read` + `checks: write`: that is what `rustsec/audit-check` needs to
publish advisories as check-run annotations (its README documents `checks: write`
for the check run, and `issues: write` only for the issue-filing mode this
workflow does not use). A job-level block replaces the top-level one rather than
adding to it, which is why `contents: read` is repeated there for the checkout.
`persist-credentials: false` on every checkout; none of them push.

**Dependabot.** New `.github/dependabot.yml` for `github-actions` (weekly,
grouped, `cooldown.default-days: 7`, `ci(deps)` prefix) and `cargo` (weekly,
grouped, `cooldown.default-days: 7`, `chore(deps)` prefix). Dependabot bumps the
SHA and its version comment together, which is what keeps the pins from going
stale. Security updates bypass the cooldown.

## The verify-trust action stays on v0.1.1 for now

This repo consumes
`OpenVTC/verifiable-git-infrastructure/.github/actions/verify-trust`, whose
input-injection issue is fixed in **0.4.9**. `gh release list --repo
OpenVTC/verifiable-git-infrastructure` shows the latest release is **v0.4.8**
(2026-09-10), so there is nothing to move to yet. The ref is pinned to the v0.1.1
commit and carries a TODO in the workflow, because the upgrade is a SHA bump
*plus* an input migration: 0.4.x renames `authority:` to `vtc-did:`. Worth a
follow-up issue once VGI cuts 0.4.9.

## Verification

- `python3 -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(...)"` parses all three files; `ci.yml`
  still has its 11 jobs.
- The pinning grep above is empty.
- Not exercised on a runner from this branch. The nine rustup steps and the
  `install-action` `tool:` input want a green CI run before merge — including on
  `windows-latest`, where the multi-line `run:` executes under pwsh.

## Note for reviewers

Rebased onto `8c23834`, so it includes #305 and #307. That matters: #305 added a
`test-dev-overrides` job to `ci.yml` after this work started, and it arrived with
three unpinned refs of its own. A plain merge would have left them unpinned and
quietly defeated the point, so that job is pinned here too — `checkout` and
`rust-cache` by SHA, and its `rust-toolchain@stable` (with `components: clippy`)
converted to the same rustup step as the `clippy` job.

Touches only `.github/`, so there is no overlap with the Rust changes in #305 or
with the sibling branch for the debug-log, unlock-file and PIN items.

title: fix(cli): a debug log only its owner can read, a passphrase file instead of argv, and no literal PIN
body:
Three small, independent hardening items, one commit each.

## 1. The `OPENVTC_DEBUG_LOG` file

Opened with `create().append()` and nothing else, so the file was created with
the process umask — on a default 022 that leaves a **world-readable** trace of
DIDs, profile names and message metadata in whatever directory the operator
named, often a shared `/tmp`.

- Created `0600` on unix. An existing file is tightened through the open handle
  rather than the path, so there is no window between the check and the change,
  and a log left loose by an earlier run does not stay readable.
- A **symlink at the path is refused**. Creating through a link planted in a
  world-writable directory would append this process's log to a file of the
  planter's choosing. `symlink_metadata` does not follow the final component, so
  this sees the link rather than its target; a missing path is still fine.
- The default filter was a bare `"debug"`, which also turned on every dependency
  — hyper, the SDKs — and buried the openvtc trace in transport noise while
  widening what reached the file. Now `info,openvtc=debug,openvtc_core=debug`.
  `RUST_LOG` still wins.
- Enabling the log says so on stderr, and says the file carries identifiers,
  because the moment to tell someone that is before they attach it to an issue.

A spot-check for secret *values* reaching `debug!` found only message strings,
so no redaction layer is added here.

## 2. `--unlock-code-file <PATH|->`

`--unlock-code` puts the passphrase in argv, readable by any local user through
`ps` or `/proc`. It stays — scripts use it — but is marked DEPRECATED in its help
text, and the existing runtime warning now names the replacement.

The new flag reads the first line of `PATH`, trimmed, or standard input when
`PATH` is `-`. clap refuses both flags at once. An empty first line is an error
rather than an empty passphrase, and the path is read before the profile is
opened so a bad one fails with a clear message rather than mid-unlock.

The process-list warning is gated on where the passphrase came from: warning
about the route that exists to avoid the problem is how a warning gets trained
out of people. That is what the new `SuppliedUnlockCode { passphrase, from_argv }`
carries.

## 3. No literal PIN in the binary

`get_user_pin()` sets `.allow_empty_password(false)`, so its
`if user_pin.is_empty() { "123456" }` branch was dead — deleted. `load_fast`
also built a literal `"123456"` placeholder for every non-Token protection type,
where no card is ever used; `DeferredLoad.user_pin` becomes an `Option` and that
case is `None`. The two `load_step2` call sites pass an empty secret for the
argument the non-token path never reads, which is the idiom already used in
`dispatch_util.rs` and `setup_sequence/config.rs`.

Hygiene, not a live vulnerability — the branch was unreachable — but it stops the
scanners re-reporting a hardcoded PIN, and no PIN literal is compiled in.

## Tests

- `open_debug_log` extracted as a function: the created file is `0600`, a loose
  pre-existing file is tightened without truncating it, and a symlink is refused
  with `InvalidInput` and nothing written through the link.
- `--unlock-code-file -` parses; `--unlock-code` alongside it is an
  `ArgumentConflict`; the first line of a temp file is read and trimmed, a second
  line is ignored, and an empty or missing file is an error.

## Verification

On this branch: `cargo fmt --all --check` clean, `cargo clippy --workspace
--all-targets -- -D warnings` clean, `cargo test -p openvtc-core -p openvtc`
green (560 + 625 unit tests plus the integration suites), and `cargo check -p
openvtc --no-default-features` clean — the `user_pin` change sits behind
`#[cfg(feature = "openpgp-card")]`, so the feature-off shape is checked too.

## Note for reviewers

Branched from `0dd3cab` — `main` as it stood when #304 merged. `main` has since
moved to `8c23834` with #305 and #307 in it. This branch merges into that
cleanly: `main.rs` and `state_handler/mod.rs` both auto-merge, with no conflict.

That merge was tested rather than assumed. On the merged tree, the gate #305 added
to CI — `cargo clippy -p openvtc --all-targets --features dev-overrides -- -D
warnings` and `cargo test -p openvtc --features dev-overrides` — is clean and
passes 584 tests.

One local patch was needed to get that far, and it is **not** from this branch:
`main` at `8c23834` does not compile on its own. `main.rs` calls
`style(notice).color256(CLI_ORANGE)`, and no `CLI_ORANGE` exists in `colors.rs`
(`color256` also wants a `u8`, where the roles are `Role`). That is what the open
#308 fixes; I patched it locally to `.themed(CLI_CAUTION)` for the duration of
the check only. Worth landing #308 before this.

title: fix(cli): a debug log only its owner can read, a passphrase file instead of argv, and no literal PIN (#309)
body:
fix(cli): a debug log only its owner can read, a passphrase file instead of argv, and no literal PIN (#309)

* fix(logging): the debug log is owner-only, never a symlink, and quieter

OPENVTC_DEBUG_LOG was opened with `create().append()` and nothing else, so
the file was created with the process umask — on a default 022 that leaves a
world-readable trace of DIDs, profile names and message metadata in whatever
directory the operator named, often a shared /tmp. It is now created 0600,
and an existing file is tightened through the open handle rather than the
path, so there is no window between the check and the change and a log left
loose by an earlier run does not stay readable.

A symlink at the path is refused. Creating through a link planted in a
world-writable directory would append this process's log to a file of the
planter's choosing.

The default filter was a bare "debug", which also turned on every dependency
— hyper, the SDKs — and buried the openvtc trace in transport noise while
widening what reaches the file. It now defaults to
`info,openvtc=debug,openvtc_core=debug`; RUST_LOG still wins.

Enabling the log says so on stderr, and says the file carries identifiers,
because the moment to tell someone that is before they attach it to a bug
report.

The opener is a function so the mode and the symlink refusal can be tested.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(cli): read the unlock passphrase from a file or standard input

`--unlock-code` puts the passphrase in argv, where any local user can read it
out of `ps` or /proc. The flag stays, because scripts use it, but it is marked
DEPRECATED in its help text and the runtime warning now names the replacement.

`--unlock-code-file <PATH|->` is that replacement: the first line of PATH,
trimmed, or standard input when PATH is `-`. clap refuses both flags at once —
one passphrase, one source, because taking both and silently preferring one is
how the wrong one gets used quietly.

Only the first line is taken and both ends are trimmed. A trailing newline is
what every editor and every `echo` leaves behind, and a passphrase whose ends
are whitespace cannot be told from one whose ends are not by the person typing
it at the prompt. An empty first line is an error rather than an empty
passphrase: it almost always means the file was not written, or was written
somewhere else. The path is read before the profile is opened, so a bad one
fails with a clear message rather than mid-unlock.

The warning is gated on where the passphrase came from. `--unlock-code-file`
exists precisely to keep it out of the process list, and warning about the safe
route as well is how a warning gets trained out of people.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* refactor(config): no factory PIN literal in the binary

`get_user_pin()` sets `allow_empty_password(false)`, so its
`if user_pin.is_empty() { "123456" }` fallback could never be reached. Deleted.

`load_fast` also built a literal "123456" as a placeholder for every non-Token
protection type, where no card is ever used and the value is never read.
`DeferredLoad.user_pin` becomes an `Option` and that case is `None`, so no PIN
literal is compiled in at all. The two `load_step2` call sites pass an empty
secret for the argument the non-token path does not read — the idiom already
used in `dispatch_util.rs` and `setup_sequence/config.rs`.

Hygiene rather than a fix: the branch was unreachable and the placeholder never
used. It stops a scanner re-reporting a hardcoded PIN, and a `strings` of the
binary no longer shows one.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: security(resolver): refuse did:web/did:webvh resolution to non-public hosts
body:
security(resolver): refuse did:web/did:webvh resolution to non-public hosts

Raise affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk to 0.8.37, which moves did:webvh
resolution onto didwebvh-rs 0.7 and closes a resolver-side SSRF. This repo's
lockfile was the furthest behind in the fleet: 0.8.34 with didwebvh-rs 0.6.0
and affinidi-did-web 0.1.3, all predating the host guards.

A did:web/did:webvh identifier names the host its document is fetched from,
and the DIDComm transport resolves DIDs the gateway did not choose — every
authcrypt sender that reaches it through the mediator. Through didwebvh-rs
0.6, resolve() rejected IP-literal hosts and nothing else, so an inbound
message naming an internal host produced a GET from inside the gateway's own
network.

0.8.37 defaults to HostPolicy::PublicOnly, which refuses loopback, private,
CGNAT and link-local hosts both when a DID names one directly and when a
public-looking name resolves to one. resolver.rs now states that policy
explicitly at the one place it configures resolution, and adds
GATEWAY_DID_ALLOW_PRIVATE_HOSTS for local stacks whose VTA and mediator DIDs
are did:webvh:{SCID}:localhost%3A3000 and would otherwise fail as BlockedHost.

The version requirement is pinned to 0.8.37 rather than 0.8 so a later resolve
cannot land back on a build without the policy. Exactly one didwebvh-rs node
remains in the tree; no second, pre-policy node is reachable through
dev-dependencies here.

title: ci: pin every action to a SHA, drop the token's write scope, add Dependabot
body:
`.github/workflows/ci.yml` referenced four actions by mutable tag and asked
for no `permissions:`, so the job ran with the workflow-default token scope.
Neither is exploitable on its own; together they are the standard supply-chain
path into a repository that publishes an npm package.

## Pins

A tag is a moving pointer. `actions/checkout@v6` means "whatever `v6` points
at when this job runs", so anyone who can move that tag — upstream
maintainers, or anyone who compromises that account — runs code in this job.
Each `uses:` is now a 40-character commit SHA with the version it was as a
comment:

| Action | SHA | Was |
|---|---|---|
| `actions/checkout` | `d23441a48e516b6c34aea4fa41551a30e30af803` | `@v6` → v6.1.0 |
| `actions/setup-node` | `249970729cb0ef3589644e2896645e5dc5ba9c38` | `@v6` → v6.5.0 |
| `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` | `6bed0761d98439e5a578e2877258200ad565ba87` | `@stable` |
| `Swatinem/rust-cache` | `6323deb102c322ba6fcbdcafc7e3dddab59af2b6` | `@v2` → v2.9.2 |

Each SHA is the commit the tag resolved to at the time of pinning, so this
changes no behaviour — `rust-cache`'s tag is annotated, and the pin is the
commit it dereferences to, not the tag object. `dtolnay/rust-toolchain`
publishes no release tags (`stable` is a branch), so the comment names the
branch instead of a version; bumping it is now a deliberate edit.

## Token scope

- Top-level `permissions: contents: read`. Nothing in this workflow writes to
  the repository. A future job that needs more has to say so, at that job.
- `actions/checkout` gets `persist-credentials: false`. By default it leaves
  the job token in `.git/config`, readable by every later step — including
  `npm ci`, which runs third-party install scripts.

## Dependabot

`.github/dependabot.yml` is new; the repository had none, which is why the
tags had drifted. It watches `github-actions` and `npm` weekly with
`cooldown: default-days: 7`, so a freshly published version is held back for
a week — long enough for most compromised releases to be caught and yanked.
`tools/roundtrip-helper` (cargo) is deliberately not watched: it is test-only
(`publish = false`) and nothing it builds ships in the tarball.

## Verification

`npm test` and `npm run build:types` pass unchanged (this branch touches no
shipped file). The workflow change is exercised by this PR's own CI run: the
pinned SHAs have to resolve and the read-only token has to be enough.

No version bump — workflow and Dependabot configuration only, matching how
the test-only round-trip helper change was handled in 0.8.0. The CHANGELOG
entry is under *Unreleased* and will ship with the next release.

## Follow-up, not in this PR

A `zizmor --min-severity medium .github/workflows` or `pinact run --check`
step would keep this from regressing. It is the same job in every repository
in the org, so it belongs with that rollout rather than here.

title: fix(store): write the handle snapshot and the key files owner-only
body:
fix(store): write the handle snapshot and the key files owner-only

The store snapshot holds raw APNs/FCM device tokens and Web Push endpoints
with their p256dh/auth secrets. It was written to a predictable temp path
(path.with_extension("json.tmp")) with std::fs::write, so it landed at the
umask default with no fsync, and anything able to create files in the store's
directory could pre-plant a symlink there and have the gateway write every
device token wherever it pointed.

Write through tempfile::NamedTempFile::new_in instead — O_EXCL, mode 0600,
unpredictable name — then write_all, sync_all, persist. The rename makes the
live snapshot inherit 0600. Store::open tightens an existing snapshot that is
group- or world-readable, and warns: those tokens should be treated as leaked.

Add src/secretfile.rs for the key files. write_owner_only_new does create_new
plus mode 0600 in one open, replacing vapid-keygen's exists-then-write-then-
chmod (a race plus a world-readable window). read_secret_file warns when a
secret is readable beyond its owner, or fails when GATEWAY_STRICT_KEY_PERMS is
set; used for the identity file, VAPID key, APNs .p8 and FCM service account.

Correct the README's note on the persisted tokens: it now says what the file
is, what protects it, and what encryption at rest would and would not buy.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78

title: fix(didcomm): refuse mediator and VTA endpoints that name a non-public host
body:
A mediator's REST, auth and WebSocket URLs come out of its DID document, and
that document is not ours. A mediator DID arriving by QR, or one whose document
changed after onboarding, decided where this wallet sent its auth handshake and
the mediator JWT it gets back, and the only check was the scheme. An extension
fetch is not CORS-bound and the wallet runs in the user's browser, so
`https://127.0.0.1`, `https://169.254.169.254` or `https://printer.local` in a
mediator document was a request from inside the user's own network with the
wallet's credentials attached. A VTA's REST base URL is the same shape of input,
written from a document (or a QR code) at onboarding, and it is the one channel
that carries a bearer token.

`@openvtc/vti-didcomm-js` 0.8 adds the guard (`net-guard.js`) and threads a
`netPolicy` through `resolveMediator`, `authenticateToMediator`,
`MediatorSession` and VTA REST auth. This bumps `packages/core` to `^0.8.0`
(the only package that depends on it — `packages/tsp-js` does not) and adopts
it.

## What decides, and where it is passed

`walletNetPolicy` (`extension/src/net-policy.ts`) is the only place the policy
is chosen, and it keys off the build: `npm run dev` builds with
`--mode development`, so `import.meta.env.DEV` is set and the policy carries
`allowInsecure` **and** `allowPrivate`. Every packaged build — `npm run build`,
which is what CI and the Web Store zip run — gets neither. Outside a vite build
`import.meta.env` is absent and that reads as production, so a test has to ask
for the dev policy rather than inherit it.

It reaches every call site that reaches the library:

- `resolveMediatorEndpoint` — the transport diagnosis and the connection
  self-test, so the self-test resolves under the policy the real path honours
  rather than passing a check the wallet will not.
- `connectMediatorSession` — onboarding (twice), the warm holder session and the
  approver session. It hands the policy to `authenticateToMediator` *and* to
  `MediatorSession`, so the socket that carries the JWT is held to the same
  terms as the handshake; the session re-checks the endpoint before every open.
- `RestChannel` — its `baseUrl` reaches `getVtaBearer` and the dispatcher POST
  through `guardedFetch`, so every URL built from it is vetted before it is
  dialed and no request follows a redirect. One exported
  `vtaRestEndpointPolicy` serves both, rather than two policies that happen to
  match. `swapAclRest` takes the policy too, so the deprecated REST swap path
  is not the one place that cannot reach a dev VTA.

## What developers must change locally

**A local stack now needs two flags, not one.** `allowInsecure: true` no longer
implies that private hosts are allowed, so a dev setup pointed at a mediator or
VTA on `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` must pass:

```js
netPolicy: { allowInsecure: true, allowPrivate: true }
```

- **Building the extension:** nothing to change by hand — but you must build
  with `npm run dev` (or `npm run dev:extension`). A wallet built with
  `npm run build` will refuse a mediator or VTA on loopback, and the refusal is
  deliberate: tying the opt-outs to the build is what stops a packaged wallet
  carrying them.
- **Calling `@openvtc/pnm-core` directly** (a script, the PWA, a test): the
  `allowInsecure` option is **gone**, not deprecated — nothing is deployed, so
  there is no compatibility fold. Replace `allowInsecure: true` with the
  `netPolicy` above on `connectMediatorSession`, `resolveMediatorEndpoint` and
  `WalletSession.fromDids`, and pass the same to `RestChannel` /
  `getVtaBearer` (and anything built on them, e.g. `vaultList`) when the VTA is
  local. Passing nothing is the strict, production policy.
- **A local mediator whose document advertises `https://127.0.0.1`** is refused
  by `allowInsecure` alone. If a dev build suddenly cannot reach a stack it used
  to, that combination is why.

## Surfacing a refusal

A refusal carries `code: "E_BLOCKED_ENDPOINT"`. `isBlockedEndpointError`
(`core/src/did/egress-guard.ts`) matches the code, not the class: there are now
two guards carrying one code — the library's, and this package's did:webvh one —
and an `instanceof` would silently miss whichever it was not written against
(R3.7).

`transport-diagnosis.ts` classifies it first, as `mediator/blocked-endpoint`,
and deliberately ignores the reachability probe. Nothing was contacted, so "the
mediator is up and refused this request" would be a claim about a request that
was never made, and it would send the reader to a mediator's CORS config instead
of to the address in its document. The network pane and the pasted self-test
report render that line as-is; the mediator-resolve check in the self-test
reports it too, since it now resolves under the same policy.

0.8 also stops copying a response body into the error message — from a hostile
endpoint that is attacker-chosen text, and these strings end up in logs, a
pasted report and the UI — and puts it on `err.body` with the HTTP status on
`err.status`. The `rejected` branch reads both from the fields and bounds the
excerpt. Nothing else in this repo parsed those messages: the only
message-matching left is in tests.

## Tests

- `core/tests/didcomm.net-policy.mjs`: a mediator document advertising loopback
  is refused by default and accepted under the dev policy; `allowInsecure` alone
  is not enough, which is the 0.8 semantics the wallet now depends on; a
  `http://localhost` stack needs both flags and each alone is refused. The
  refusal reaches neither the injected `fetch` nor the injected WebSocket — the
  difference between a control and an error message. The positive control drives
  the whole path, handshake then socket, through a fake WebSocket.
- `core/tests/vta.rest-net-policy.mjs`: the same for a VTA REST base URL —
  loopback, a local-only name and plaintext on a public host, each with zero
  requests, then the dev policy completing the handshake.
- `extension/tests/transport-diagnosis.test.mts`: the blocked-endpoint case as
  the pane renders it, that a probe result cannot re-classify it, and that the
  status and body are read from the fields.

Full CI sequence run locally on Node 24: `npm run lint`, `npm run build`,
`npm test` (core 621, extension 594, tsp-js, demos — all passing), the MV3
single-bundle and dynamic-`import()` assertion, the admin / key-material /
persona bundle guards in both directions, the console single-bundle assertion,
and `scripts/package.mjs` with the Web Store zip checks.

## What it cannot do

An extension has no DNS API, so a public name that *resolves* to a private
address (`127.0.0.1.nip.io`, a rebinding domain) passes every check here.
`allowHosts` is the answer to that and needs a pinned list of hosts; this wallet
records its mediators and agents as DIDs, so it has no such list, and narrowing
to one derived from the same document would check a value against itself. The
parameter is plumbed through and left unset; pinning it belongs beside the inbox
in `config.ts`, where an operator can state it. The did:webvh resolution guard
this package already has (`did/egress-guard.ts`) is left in place — replacing it
with the library's now-published `net-guard` is a separate change, and the two
agree on ranges, names, code and reasons.

## Overlap with my other open branches

Branched from `origin/main`. None of the files `sec-4045/egress-and-input-bounds`
adds or changes are touched (`core/src/http/public-endpoint.ts`, `proxyFetch`,
`registerPushChannel`, `content.ts`, `armor.ts`). Two shared files will conflict
textually if another branch lands first: `package-lock.json` (the dependency
bump) and `CLAUDE.md` (one new bullet in the networking-rules list, after R3.7).

body:
docs(resolver): describe the cache the module actually has

The module comment still said did:key and did:peer are "cached uniformly (harmless)" after they stopped being cached at all, carried an orphaned "callers share one fetch." fragment, and repeated the tradeoff sentence. Comments are not covered by tests, so the merge that introduced this went unnoticed.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78

title: fix(resolver): bound the DID-resolution cache and stop caching offline methods
body:
`src/resolver.js` expired cache entries on a TTL but never bounded the map's
size, and it cached every method uniformly — the comment at the top said
did:key and did:peer were "cached uniformly (harmless)".

It is not harmless, because **a client resolves DIDs it did not choose**. An
inbound frame's `skid` names its own sender, and `unpackInbound` resolves an
unknown one before the frame is authenticated, so whoever can route frames to
a client through the mediator decides what that client caches. did:key and
did:peer are the sharp end: they resolve from the identifier itself with no
network I/O, so they are free and unlimited to mint, and each one was kept for
the full 5-minute TTL. The shared `defaultResolver` (process-wide) is what the
mediator transport uses, and in an MV3 service worker that is the extension's
own heap.

## Changes

- `createResolver(overrides, { maxEntries })`, default **500**. On insert,
  expired entries are dropped first and then the least recently used is
  evicted. A cache hit re-inserts its entry, so `Map` insertion order *is* the
  LRU order and no second structure is needed. `maxEntries: 0` disables
  caching, like `cacheTtlMs: 0`; a negative or non-finite bound is a
  `TypeError` rather than an unbounded cache.
- **did:key and did:peer are not cached at all.** This removes the flooding
  vector outright; the LRU bound then covers did:webvh, which is the method
  the cache exists for (an HTTPS `did.jsonl` fetch plus full log verification).
  Their handlers are cheap to re-run, so the only observable difference is
  that a rotated document is never stale for them.
- `resolver.size()` and a module-level `didCacheSize()`, plus an exported
  `DEFAULT_DID_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES`, for tests and diagnostics.
- The module header now explains both bounds and where the untrusted
  identifiers come from, since that is the part that made "harmless" wrong.

`parseMethod` now runs before the cache check rather than inside
`rawResolve` only, so a malformed DID still throws the same error on the
uncached path.

## Tests

In `test/resolver.test.js`, following the existing cache tests. These replace
the memory-measurement harness with deterministic assertions:

- 1,000 distinct `did:webvh` stubs against `maxEntries: 100` leave `size()`
  at exactly 100; 600 against the default leave it at 500.
- 1,000 distinct did:keys and 1,000 did:peers leave `size()` at 0, and every
  one of the 2,000 resolutions ran its handler.
- The real built-in did:key handler resolves twice, identically, with an empty
  cache.
- Eviction order: with `maxEntries: 2`, touching `a` before inserting `c`
  evicts `b`, not `a`.
- An expired entry is dropped to make room instead of evicting a live one.
- `maxEntries: 0` disables caching; bad bounds throw.

## Version

0.8.1. The size bound and the accessor are additive, and not caching two
offline methods is not an API change. Consumers get it after a publish and a
range bump (CLAUDE.md: a fix merged here changes nothing for them until
published).

## Not in this PR

- The stale-key window (the CWE-613 duplicate) is unchanged: `invalidate(did)`
  is still the answer after a known rotation. A shorter TTL for did:webvh
  specifically is worth considering separately.
- A DID length cap in `parseMethod` (the did:peer payload item) is a separate
  small change.

title: fix(didcomm): refuse mediator and VTA endpoints that name a non-public host
body:
fix(didcomm): refuse mediator and VTA endpoints that name a non-public host

A mediator's REST, auth and WebSocket URLs come out of its DID document, and
that document is not ours. A mediator DID arriving by QR, or one whose document
changed after onboarding, decided where this wallet sent its auth handshake and
the mediator JWT it gets back, and the only check was the scheme. An extension
fetch is not CORS-bound and the wallet runs in the user's browser, so
`https://127.0.0.1`, `https://169.254.169.254` or `https://printer.local` in a
mediator document was a request from inside the user's own network with the
wallet's credentials attached. A VTA's REST base URL is the same shape of
input, written from a document (or a QR code) at onboarding, and it is the one
channel that carries a bearer token.

`@openvtc/vti-didcomm-js` 0.8 adds the guard (`net-guard.js`) and threads a
`netPolicy` through `resolveMediator`, `authenticateToMediator`,
`MediatorSession` and VTA REST auth. This adopts it.

## What decides, and where it is passed

`walletNetPolicy` (`extension/src/net-policy.ts`) is the only place the policy
is chosen, and it keys off the build: `npm run dev` builds with
`--mode development`, so `import.meta.env.DEV` is set and the policy carries
`allowInsecure` **and** `allowPrivate`. Every packaged build — `npm run build`,
which is what CI and the Web Store zip run — gets neither. Outside a vite build
`import.meta.env` is absent and that reads as production, so a test has to ask
for the dev policy rather than inherit it.

It reaches every call site that reaches the library:

- `resolveMediatorEndpoint` — the transport diagnosis and the connection
  self-test, so the self-test resolves under the policy the real path honours
  rather than passing a check the wallet will not.
- `connectMediatorSession` — onboarding (twice), the warm holder session and
  the approver session. It hands the policy to `authenticateToMediator` *and*
  to `MediatorSession`, so the socket that carries the JWT is held to the same
  terms as the handshake; the session re-checks the endpoint before every open.
- `RestChannel` — its `baseUrl` reaches `getVtaBearer` and the dispatcher POST
  through `guardedFetch`, so every URL built from it is vetted before it is
  dialed and no request follows a redirect. One exported
  `vtaRestEndpointPolicy` serves both, rather than two policies that happen to
  match.

## Breaking for a local stack

`allowInsecure: true` no longer implies that private hosts are allowed, and the
option is gone from `@openvtc/pnm-core` rather than kept as an alias — nothing
is deployed, so there is no fold to write. `connectMediatorSession`,
`resolveMediatorEndpoint` and `WalletSession.fromDids` take `netPolicy`.

A mediator or VTA on loopback now needs both flags:

    netPolicy: { allowInsecure: true, allowPrivate: true }

In the extension that is automatic with `npm run dev`. A wallet built with
`npm run build` refuses a local mediator, which is the point of tying it to the
build rather than to a setting.

## Surfacing a refusal

A refusal carries `code: "E_BLOCKED_ENDPOINT"`. `isBlockedEndpointError`
(`core/src/did/egress-guard.ts`) matches the code, not the class: there are now
two guards carrying one code — the library's, and this package's did:webvh one
— and an `instanceof` would silently miss whichever it was not written against
(R3.7).

`transport-diagnosis.ts` classifies it first, as `mediator/blocked-endpoint`,
and deliberately ignores the reachability probe. Nothing was contacted, so "the
mediator is up and refused this request" would be a claim about a request that
was never made, and it would send the reader to a mediator's CORS config
instead of to the address in its document. The network pane and the pasted
self-test report render that line as-is.

0.8 also stops copying a response body into the error message — from a hostile
endpoint that is attacker-chosen text, and these strings end up in logs, a
pasted report and the UI — and puts it on `err.body` with the HTTP status on
`err.status`. The `rejected` branch reads both from the fields and bounds the
excerpt. Nothing else in this repo parsed those messages.

## Tests

- `core/tests/didcomm.net-policy.mjs`: a mediator document advertising loopback
  is refused by default and accepted under the dev policy; `allowInsecure`
  alone is not enough, which is the 0.8 semantics the wallet now depends on; a
  `http://localhost` stack needs both flags and each alone is refused. The
  refusal reaches neither the injected `fetch` nor the injected WebSocket —
  the difference between a control and an error message. The positive control
  drives the whole path, handshake then socket.
- `core/tests/vta.rest-net-policy.mjs`: the same for a VTA REST base URL —
  loopback, a local-only name and plaintext on a public host, each with zero
  requests, then the dev policy completing the handshake.
- `extension/tests/transport-diagnosis.test.mts`: the blocked-endpoint case as
  the pane renders it, that a probe result cannot re-classify it, and that the
  status and body are read from the fields.

## What it cannot do

An extension has no DNS API, so a public name that *resolves* to a private
address (`127.0.0.1.nip.io`, a rebinding domain) passes every check here.
`allowHosts` is the answer to that and needs a pinned list of hosts; this wallet
records its mediators and agents as DIDs, so it has no such list, and narrowing
to one derived from the same document would check a value against itself. The
parameter is plumbed through and left unset; pinning it belongs beside the inbox
in `config.ts`, where an operator can state it.

title: fix(resolver): bound the DID cache and stop caching the offline methods
body:
fix(resolver): bound the DID cache and stop caching the offline methods

The resolution cache expired entries on a TTL but never bounded its size, and
cached every method uniformly — the file said did:key and did:peer were
"cached uniformly (harmless)".

It is not harmless, because a client resolves DIDs it did not choose. An
inbound frame's `skid` names its own sender, and `unpackInbound` resolves an
unknown one before the frame is authenticated, so whoever can route frames to
a client through the mediator decides what that client caches. did:key and
did:peer are the sharp end: they resolve from the identifier itself with no
network I/O, so they are free and unlimited to mint, and each one was held for
the full 5-minute TTL. The cache in question is the process-wide
`defaultResolver`, which in an MV3 service worker is the extension's own heap.

  - `createResolver(overrides, { maxEntries })`, default 500. On insert,
    expired entries are dropped first, then the least recently used one. A
    cache hit re-inserts its entry, so Map insertion order *is* the LRU order
    and no second structure is needed. `maxEntries: 0` disables caching like
    `cacheTtlMs: 0`; a negative or non-finite bound is a TypeError rather than
    an unbounded cache.
  - did:key and did:peer are not cached at all, which removes the flooding
    vector outright and leaves the LRU bound covering did:webvh — the method
    the cache exists for, being an HTTPS did.jsonl fetch plus full log
    verification. Their handlers are cheap to re-run, so the only observable
    difference is that a rotated document is never stale for them.
  - `size()` on the resolver, `didCacheSize()` at module level, and an
    exported `DEFAULT_DID_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES`.

`parseMethod` now runs before the cache check rather than only inside
`rawResolve`, so a malformed DID throws the same error on the uncached path.

New tests, replacing the memory-measurement harness with deterministic
assertions: 1,000 distinct did:webvh stubs against `maxEntries: 100` leave
`size()` at exactly 100 and 600 against the default leave it at 500; 1,000
did:keys and 1,000 did:peers leave it at 0 with all 2,000 handlers run; the
built-in did:key handler resolves twice with an empty cache; with
`maxEntries: 2`, touching `a` before inserting `c` evicts `b` and not `a`; an
expired entry is dropped to make room instead of a live one; `maxEntries: 0`
disables caching and bad bounds throw.

0.8.1: the bound and the accessor are additive, and not caching two offline
methods is not an API change.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(vgi-core): find the Signed-by-DID trailer block the way git does
body:
fix(vgi-core): find the Signed-by-DID trailer block the way git does

The trailer was located by walking up from the end of the commit message while
each line looked like `key: value`. git's rules are not that, and the two
disagreed in both directions.

Nothing here was exploitable on its own, because every trust decision already
fails closed: the identity comes out of the signed payload, the claimed DID has
to publish the key that actually signed, and the registry has to authorize it.
What was left is a display differential — the DID a reviewer reads from `git
log` or a review UI was not always the DID that got verified.

A property test against both of git's own trailer views found seven
disagreements. Three had vgi-core reading a claim git does not present as a
trailer at all, which is the direction that matters, since the commit is then
attributed to a DID no reviewer is shown:

  - a trailer-shaped line appended to a paragraph of prose. git takes the final
    paragraph as trailers only when every line is one, or when one of its own
    trailers is there and trailers are at least 25% of it
  - a trailer-shaped line in the title paragraph, either as the subject itself
    or as the line under it with no blank line between
  - the same in a message beginning with blank lines, which git's commit view
    skips before the subject, making the trailer-shaped line the subject

Four lost a claim instead, so verification fell back to the committer identity
and failed closed, while a reviewer still saw a Signed-by-DID nothing checked:

  - spaces or tabs before the colon, which git's key scan allows and trims
  - a key differing in case, which `%(trailers:key=...)` matches anyway
  - a folded value, whose continuation line stopped the block being a block
  - trailing whitespace before a fold, where git keeps those spaces and adds one
    for the fold. Both values are unresolvable DIDs, so this last one is
    cosmetic, but the text git reports is the text a reviewer sees

git's 25% allowance, and its treatment of `(cherry picked from commit ...)` as
one of its own trailers even though it holds no separator, had no equivalent
here in either direction.

commit.rs now ports the rules rather than approximating them: trailer_block_start
follows find_trailer_block_start, separator_pos follows find_separator,
last_trailer_value follows trailer_block_get with unfold_value's folding, and
blank lines before the subject are skipped the way pretty.c does it.

Two narrowing behaviour changes:

  - a Signed-by-DID outside git's trailer block is no longer a claim. The
    commit-msg hook writes the trailer with `git interpret-trailers`, so commits
    did-git-sign produced are unaffected
  - the last Signed-by-DID wins, and counts only when its value is a DID.
    Previously a later non-DID trailer was skipped in favour of an earlier
    DID-valued one, which let the checked DID hide behind the trailer a reader
    sees last

No git configuration is read, so core.commentChar, trailer.separators and
trailer.<token>.key are git's defaults here. A repository that changes them can
have git see a block this does not, which loses a claim and fails closed, never
the reverse; the comments say so at each site.

Tests:
  - tests/trailer_differential.rs builds commit objects in a throwaway bare
    repository and compares signer_did against `git interpret-trailers --parse`
    and `git log -1 --format='%(trailers:key=Signed-by-DID,valueonly,unfold,
    separator=%x00)'`. git is the oracle; no expected DID is hard-coded, and it
    also fails if git's two views disagree with each other
  - 31 fixed shapes always run, including the 25% boundary on either side, plus
    generated messages: whitespace before the colon, key case, continuation
    lines, repeated trailers, trailing whitespace, comment lines, non-trailer
    paragraphs after the block, and trailer-shaped subjects
  - cases are capped at 64 and shrinking at 64, since each case spawns three git
    processes. Run at 4000 locally, which is where the whitespace disagreement
    turned up, at case 3674
  - git runs with GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM and the global and system config pointed at
    a path that does not exist, so the defaults the port follows are the ones git
    uses. It needs nothing beyond `init --bare` and `hash-object` — no commit, so
    no identity — so a plain hosted-runner git is enough
  - failure_persistence is off, so a failure writes nothing into the tree
  - eleven unit tests beside trailer_did assert each rule without needing git
  - proptest joins the workspace dev-dependencies

title: chore(deps): guard did:webvh resolution behind the public-host policy
body:
chore(deps): guard did:webvh resolution behind the public-host policy

affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk is named directly at 0.8.37 so the floor is stated rather than inherited as ^0.8 through affinidi-tdk, which silently admits 0.8.36 — the release where did:webvh resolution still contacts whatever host the DID names. 0.8.37 moves to didwebvh-rs 0.7, which refuses localhost, *.localhost, *.local, *.internal, home.arpa and single-label names before any request is sent, refuses a name whose resolved addresses are non-public, connects only to the addresses it checked, follows no redirect and ignores proxy environment variables.

That matters here because every DID the verifier resolves is chosen by the author of the commits under review: the Signed-by-DID trailer, and the committer header it falls back to, are attacker-supplied on a fork pull request. did:web and agent-name lookups were already guarded; did:webvh was the gap, and on a self-hosted runner with internal reachability it was an SSRF primitive whose oracle was the per-signer resolution error printed in the report. max_signers bounded how many DIDs a range could try, not where they pointed.

build_resolver states HostPolicy::PublicOnly rather than relying on the default, so a downgrade below 0.8.37 fails to compile instead of quietly reopening the fetch — which is also why this is a normal dependency and not a dev-dependency: a floor in dev-dependencies does not travel with the published crate, and did-git-sign resolves through the same graph. There is no opt-out by design. A commit claiming a DID on an internal host now fails as unresolvedSigner with a BlockedHost reason, visibly, rather than being fetched.

affinidi-did-web moves 0.1.4 -> 0.1.5 in the lockfile, taking affinidi-net-guard 0.1.0 with it: that is the did:web half of the same guard refactored onto the shared crate, with its public API unchanged.

didwebvh-rs 0.6.1 stays in the graph beside 0.7.0 because vta-sdk 0.36 declares "0.6", which excludes 0.7. Nothing here names a didwebvh-rs type, and the copy the resolution path holds is the new one: cargo tree -i didwebvh-rs@0.7.0 resolves didwebvh-rs 0.7.0 -> affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk 0.8.37 -> verify-trust. The duplicate collapses when VTI takes 0.7 and releases.

Regression test: a real sshsig-signed commit claiming did:webvh on a loopback host, run through build_resolver and resolve_signer_keys exactly as handle_verify_trust does, asserting the report marks the signer unresolvedSigner with a BlockedHost reason and that the stand-in listener accepted zero connections. A refusal raised after connecting would already have told the author that something is listening.
