* chore(deps): take the published 0.35 line and delete every patch entry

`did-git-sign` 0.4.8 is published and requires `vta-sdk ^0.35`. That is the
release six consecutive minors have been waiting on, and it makes the whole
line resolvable from crates.io for the first time since 0.23.

  vta-sdk                   0.34.1 → 0.35     (git pin → crates.io)
  trust-tasks-rs            0.18.11 → 0.19.4
  trust-tasks-capability-client  0.18.5 → 0.19.4
  affinidi-tdk              0.12 → 0.13
  affinidi-messaging-sdk    0.22 → 0.23
  did-git-sign              0.4.6 → 0.4.8     (git pin → crates.io)
  vta-service     (dev)     0.24 → 0.25
  test-mediator   (dev)     0.5.2 → 0.6

`[patch.crates-io]` is **deleted, not emptied**, so that adding one back is a
visible decision rather than a line in an existing block; `deny.toml`'s
`allow-git` list — the other half of the same change — goes with it. Both keep
a note saying what the block was for and what to do if it is ever needed again.

`trust-tasks-capability-client` was the edge that nearly got left behind: it
declares its own `trust-tasks-rs` requirement, so the first resolve produced two
copies of both while every other line looked correct. `cargo tree -i` on the old
version named it; `cargo outdated` would not have.

Zero source changes. The only API delta from 0.34.1 is an addition, which is
also the thing to be careful about — see below.

**vta-sdk 0.35 refuses an unsigned trust-task reply by default, so the VTA has
to be upgraded before this ships.** An agent predating VTI #1334/#1335 sends no
proof, and a client on 0.35 then refuses every answer it gets — a total outage
in the pane, from a change that compiles clean and passes every test here.
`vta-service` 0.25.0 is the first release that signs; 0.24.1 was published hours
before those merged and does not. The manifest note beside the `vta-sdk` line
carries this, and `trusting_unsigned_replies()` is the staging hatch if the
order ever has to be the other way round.

Verified: fmt, clippy (both feature sets), test, test --include-ignored (the
MockVta e2es, which are what actually exercise vta-service 0.25),
--no-default-features, cargo doc with -D warnings, and cargo deny across
advisories/licenses/bans/sources. One vta-sdk, one trust-tasks-rs, no git
sources.

* test(tsp): stop asserting a property of the runner's DNS

`an_unresolvable_did_web_falls_back_rather_than_failing` resolved
`did:web:nothing-seeded.example`, which is a real DNS query. The assertion
holds only when that query fails *fast*: discovery is wrapped in a 5s
timeout, and a timeout reports `Unavailable` rather than the
`NotAdvertised` the fallback produces. A resolver that answers NXDOMAIN
instantly gives one outcome and one that hangs on an unknown TLD gives the
other, so the test was pinning the environment as much as the code.

It failed on a macOS runner in this PR and passes on every machine here,
which is the shape that costs an afternoon later. Nothing in the bump
caused it: `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` 0.8.36 and `affinidi-did-web`
0.1.4 are byte-identical across it, the only networking move is a
`reqwest` patch, and the sibling test — the one using `did:example:`, which
needs no network at all — passed.

Port 1 on 127.0.0.1 is refused by the kernel with no name to look up, so
resolution still fails, still fails fast, and reaches the same fallback
branch the same way everywhere. The comment says why the address is what it
is, because the obvious "tidy-up" is to put a hostname back.

title: Draft the client and operation-surface chapters
body:
Stacked on #8 (architecture + trust contexts), which is stacked on #7 (the
outline). Retarget down the stack as each merges. `npm run render` succeeds.

Chapters 3 and 4 of the drafting sequence: the client, and the operation
surface it calls.

## Client onboarding and lifecycle — `spec/07-clients.md`

40 requirements (`VTI-CLT-*`) across the four steps, written in sequence order
because the order is what carries the security properties.

**Step 1 — mint.** The client generates its own key pair; the private key never
leaves it and a node may not require its disclosure. `did:key` is required here
specifically because this happens before the client has standing, network, or
anywhere to publish. The identifier is recorded as a *bootstrap identity*,
distinguishable in local state from a long-term one.

**Step 2 — enrol.** Least-privilege at creation, enrolling administrator must
hold act authority over the target context, bootstrap identifier treated as
low-trust because it crossed a channel outside the trust system.

Two requirements here address a threat the outline didn't: **the enrolment
channel's weak point is substitution, not disclosure.** An attacker who can
modify the message carrying the identifier can have the administrator enrol an
identifier *they* control — and rotation in Step 3 does not help, since the
substituted identifier simply rotates onto another one the attacker controls.
So: confirm the identifier over a second channel (VTI-CLT-015), and require
that a client refused for want of an entry reports that condition
distinguishably (VTI-CLT-016), so the "legitimate client never got standing"
signal reaches a human instead of looking like an ordinary connection failure.

**Step 3 — roll.** SHOULD, per D2, with the rationale tied to exposure: a
sealed provisioning bundle is a defensible reason not to roll, a DID pasted
into chat is not. The mechanism is REQUIRED of a VTA either way. Then the
sequence: mint → **prove reachability before committing** (a liveness check,
not an authorization one — before the swap the new identifier has no entry at
all; committed to an unreachable identifier the rotation is unrecoverable) →
**atomic swap** with caller-is-current-subject and new-subject-is-proven-holder
bindings and authority preserved exactly → **persist before anything else**.

VTI-CLT-029 and VTI-CLT-030 are what make a self-service operation safe to
expose to the subject itself: without the first it is a self-service
escalation, without the second it is a way to take over someone else's grant.

**Step 4 and lifecycle.** Refresh rather than re-enrol; never treat a past
authorization as evidence for a later request; surface step-up to a human and
never satisfy a consent requirement on one's own behalf; distinguish a refusal
from a transport failure; hold an idempotency key stable. Plus **one identity
per instance, including via machine images** (VTI-CLT-052) — that is how
sharing actually happens, not by a decision to share but by cloning a template
captured after enrolment — and **no entry may be moved to a subject that hasn't
proven control** (VTI-CLT-054), so a lost key is recovered by re-enrolling.

Ends with a conformance checklist splitting the client's requirements from the
node's.

## Operation surface — `spec/08-operations.md`

33 requirements (`VTI-OPS-*`), implementing D3.

- **Precedence** — canonical Trust Task wherever one exists; private interfaces
  only where none does, namespaced so they cannot collide with a future
  canonical task, discoverable, and carrying a retirement path.
- **Extension not divergence** — payloads stay closed so a misspelled member is
  refused rather than ignored; a declared extension slot is the only local
  content, and it confers no authority.
- **The operation document** — and VTI-OPS-021, which records a defect rather
  than a preference: an implementation shipped the consumer half of the rule
  while its producer built unsigned, unaddressed documents on exactly the two
  transports whose sender authentication made the guard look unnecessary. The
  same defect reported a different condition on each transport and was
  diagnosed twice. Transport authentication says who opened the connection;
  document proof says who authored this and what it covers.
- **Responses conform too** (VTI-OPS-031) — a request-only check measures its
  own fixtures. And a condition with no defined code gets a machine-readable
  discriminator rather than a generic failure, "not found" being the recurring
  case.
- **Versioning** — no 0.x exemption (VTI-OPS-041), and **enum-value changes are
  breaking** (VTI-OPS-042). The concrete case: a set of enumerated values
  renamed across two minor bumps with the payload shape untouched — invisible
  to a schema comparison, fatal to every peer. An unsupported version is
  refused explicitly and never left to time out.
- **Policy gate in front of dispatch** (VTI-OPS-050/051) — a requirement
  enforced in handlers is enforced wherever it was remembered.
- **Retry and idempotency** — classify every operation by what a repeat costs;
  unclassified is treated as the most costly class; exactly one retry owner per
  failure domain, and no application-level loop, because a hand-written loop
  cannot hold a key stable and so converts one operation retried into several
  operations performed.

## Left open

The minimum operation set per profile is still an instruction — it needs the
canonical catalogue references settled first.

title: Draft the client and operation-surface chapters (#9)
body:
Draft the client and operation-surface chapters (#9)

Client onboarding and lifecycle: 40 requirements over the four-step
sequence. Mint client-side, with the private key never leaving the
client and the identifier recorded as a bootstrap identity; enrol
least-privilege, with the bootstrap identifier treated as low-trust
because it crossed a channel outside the trust system; roll the key
(SHOULD, per D2) with reachability proven before the commit, an atomic
swap that preserves authority exactly, and nothing optional between the
commit and the persist; then steady-state use and lifecycle.

Two threats are addressed explicitly. Enrolment-channel substitution is
not solved by rotation, so it is met with second-channel confirmation
and a requirement that a client refused for want of an entry says so
distinguishably. Shared client identity is prohibited including via
machine images, which is how sharing usually happens.

Operation surface: 33 requirements. Canonical Trust Task wherever one
exists, private interfaces namespaced and temporary (D3); closed
payloads with a declared extension slot rather than local members; the
operation document, including the requirement that a sender-authenticated
transport does not relieve a producer of signing; response conformance
as well as request conformance; versioning with no 0.x exemption and
enum-value changes as breaking; the policy gate in front of dispatch;
and retry classification with exactly one retry owner per failure
domain.

Adds the CLT and OPS areas to the conformance area registry.

title: Draft the architecture and trust-context chapters
body:
Stacked on #7 (the outline), which is why the base of this PR is
`spec-outline` rather than `main`. Retarget to `main` once #7 merges.

Fills in the first two chapters the outline reserved. `npm run render`
succeeds.

## Architecture and conformance targets — `spec/02-architecture.md`

Informative, so it carries no RFC keywords: its job is to fix the vocabulary
the normative chapters are written in.

- **The problem VTI addresses** — why a set of individually conformant
  components is not a trust system, with the three failure shapes that motivate
  the composition chapter.
- **Six conformance targets** — VTA, VTC, client, mediator, host service, trust
  registry — each with a paragraph on what it is for. The VTA/VTC division of
  authority is stated here rather than left to be inferred.
- **The trust boundary is per operator, not per service**, and the consequence
  that runs through the rest of the spec: a property a relying party can check
  is worth more than one a node enforces about itself.
- **Layering**, including the rule it settles — where a requirement gets edited
  when it turns out to be wrong.
- **A request end to end** — one ordinary agent-signing operation walked
  through eight steps, each naming the chapter that governs it. Every step is
  somewhere a real system has gone wrong, which is the argument for the chapter
  list.

## Trust contexts and the authority model — `spec/03-trust-contexts.md`

Normative. 74 requirements across four areas (`CTX`, `ACL`, `APV`, `AUD`).
The load-bearing ones:

- **Ancestry is segment-wise** (VTI-CTX-016), stated as a prohibition on
  string-prefix comparison rather than as a definition, because the incorrect
  implementation is the shorter one — under it `acme` is an ancestor of
  `acme-evil`.
- **The authorization gate is pure** (VTI-CTX-018): decidable from the caller's
  verified authority and the target identifier alone, with no store traversal
  inside the security check. This is the reason for path-encoded identifiers,
  and the reason re-parenting is prohibited in this version.
- **Absent is not empty** (VTI-ACL-006/007). For the narrowed key set, absent
  means every key the scope reaches and present-but-empty means none — so the
  ordinary "omit empty collections" serialization convention turns the
  narrowest grant expressible into the widest one, on the wire, with both ends
  conforming to their own understanding of the shape.
- **Act scope is derived from (role, contexts), never from either alone**
  (VTI-ACL-020/021). An empty context set means *everywhere* for an
  administrator and *nowhere* for every other role; both known violations of
  this were privilege defects.
- **Capabilities narrow, and an unrecognised one is not granted**
  (VTI-ACL-030–034) — the pair that makes D6's extensible registry safe. A
  capability outside the role's ceiling is refused when written rather than
  silently dropped.
- **Approve is an axis independent of act** (VTI-ACL-040–042), so a
  least-privilege approver — approves in named contexts, acts nowhere — is
  expressible. An approver whose authority to approve implies authority to act
  is not a control.
- **A context listing has a direction** (VTI-ACL-060–066). *Who may act in X*
  reads up the tree; *what is granted beneath X* reads down. A subtree
  revocation asked with the first gets exactly the entries that are **not**
  being revoked — an answer that is short rather than empty, so it looks
  complete. Includes the two deliberate edges and the cursor-binding rule.
- **Revocation may not report success while a grant beneath it survives**
  (VTI-ACL-082). This has happened: a grant one level below a swept context
  kept signing while the operator was told the sweep succeeded. A containment
  control that reports success without containing anything is worse than none,
  because it ends the incident response.
- **Consent is bound to the payload digest, and MUST NOT be implemented by
  elevating the requester's session** (VTI-APV-004/005). The elevation pattern
  is consent with the binding removed: the approver believes they approved one
  change, and what they granted was a window in which every gated change
  passes.
- **An unsatisfiable approval rule is refused when written** (VTI-APV-009) —
  it is a lockout that has not happened yet.
- **Refusals are audited** (VTI-AUD-003): a trail of successes alone cannot
  distinguish a system nobody attacked from one whose gate is open.
- **Where this spec is silent about who owns an authority decision, an
  implementation refuses rather than assumes** (VTI-ACL-092).

Rationale paragraphs are kept inline and marked non-normative. They are there
because the common failure mode for these requirements is a reader reasonably
concluding that the obvious simpler formulation would do.

## Also in this PR

- **Appendix D** now holds the actual context-path ABNF and the ancestry
  definition, normatively.
- **Conformance chapter** gains the requirement-identifier area registry.
- **Glossary**: real definitions for VTI and VTC replacing the template stubs,
  and both are now referenced.

## For reviewers

The role set and per-role capability ceiling (Appendix C) are deliberately
still an instruction — that annex should be filled once the WG agrees the role
names, and the chapter is written so that it can be.

title: Draft the VTI specification outline and chapter structure
body:
## What this is

A first draft of the **structure** of the VTI specification, not its normative
text. The repo is currently the unmodified ToIP Spec-Up-T template, so this PR
proposes the chapter breakdown before anyone writes requirements — the file
split becomes the working group's unit of assignment and review, and it is much
cheaper to argue about now.

Each chapter file fixes that chapter's scope and section list. Bodies are
editorial instructions (`{{...}}`) describing what the chapter will specify.
`npm run render` succeeds; the only warning is the pre-existing dangling `VTC`
glossary definition.

## Scope proposed

VTI is the **system specification**. It defines:

1. **the common model** every node shares — trust contexts and the authority
   model over them, identity and keys, transports and delivery, sessions, the
   client lifecycle, the operation surface, credentials;
2. **the nodes** — VTA and VTC (in full), plus supporting hosts — including,
   where two nodes could each plausibly own an authority decision, which one
   does;
3. **the composition requirements** — properties that must hold across a
   complete interaction and that no single component specification can
   establish.

It does not restate identifier methods, credential data models, Trust Task
definitions, transports or governance frameworks.

## Chapters

| Part | Chapter |
|---|---|
| A — Foundations | Introduction · Terminology · Architecture and conformance targets |
| B — Common model | **Trust contexts and the authority model** · Identity, DIDs and keys · Transports, messaging and delivery · Sessions and authentication · **Client onboarding and lifecycle** · Operation surface · Credentials and presentations |
| C — Nodes | The Verifiable Trust Agent · The Verifiable Trust Community · Membership lifecycle and community credentials · Trust registries and recognition |
| D — System properties | **Composition requirements** · Operational and assurance · Considerations · Conformance · References · Appendices A–F |

Three chapters are the substance of the proposal:

- **Trust contexts and the authority model** — the chapter that exists nowhere
  today. Nested, path-encoded context identifiers with a segment-aware ancestry
  gate; the access control entry; roles as ceilings; how a super-administrator
  and a context administrator are each *spelled*; capabilities that narrow;
  the act/approve split and the least-privilege approver; approvals and step-up
  as two distinct requirements; the direction of a context query; delegation,
  revocation and audit.
- **Client onboarding and lifecycle** — the four-step flow, written in the
  order that carries the security properties: mint an ephemeral `did:key`
  client-side → enrol it in the ACL out-of-band (so the bootstrap identifier is
  low-trust by construction) → connect and roll the key (prove reachability
  *before* committing, then one atomic swap that preserves scope exactly) →
  steady-state use.
- **Composition requirements** — eleven properties of the composed
  interaction, developed from the RAHP composition work: composition integrity,
  semantic completion, authority ≠ verification, currency of state, delegation
  lineage, privacy across composition, false independence, indeterminacy,
  configuration materiality, component substitution, human control.

## Decisions this PR encodes

Recorded with rationale in `STRUCTURE.md`:

| # | Decision | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Is the VTC in scope? | In scope, **fully** |
| D2 | Post-enrolment key roll | **SHOULD**, with the mechanism REQUIRED of a VTA and an expiry required on any unrolled bootstrap entry |
| D3 | Trust Tasks vs bespoke interfaces | **Trust Task wherever one exists**; private interfaces only where none does, and they carry a retirement path |
| D4 | Who defines conformance | **VTI does** — conformance and assurance separated, with an assessment interface so multiple programmes can contribute evidence without normative authority |
| D5 | Nested contexts | **Yes**, path-encoded; re-parenting deferred |
| D6 | Capabilities | **Extensible registry**, made safe by "unrecognised MUST NOT be treated as granted" |
| D7 | Identifier methods and algorithms | **`did:webvh` and `did:key` REQUIRED**, others OPTIONAL; **Curve25519 mandatory to implement**, others OPTIONAL |
| D8 | Publish unresolved composition propositions | **Yes**, with their status visible in Appendix E |

## Also included

- **Requirement identifiers** — `VTI-<AREA>-<nnn>`, stable and never reused.
  This is what lets a test suite, a conformance claim and any number of
  independent assessments cite the same thing.
- **Ownership tags** during drafting (`COMPONENT-OWNED`, `COMPOSITION-OWNED`,
  `JOINTLY-OWNED`, `ASSURANCE-ONLY`, `UNRESOLVED`), from the RAHP composition
  work.
- `specs.json`, `spec/header.md` and `README.md` updated from template
  placeholders to VTI; `spec/body.md` removed (superseded by the chapter files).

## Open for the WG

Editors and the working group name in the IPR block are still placeholders.
The drafting sequence in `STRUCTURE.md` suggests starting with the conformance
targets, then trust contexts, then clients.

title: feat(vta): a service can fetch the keys of the DID it operates
body:
`vta/contexts/secrets/1.0`. An integration whose identity the VTA manages — a
mediator, a room-host, a did-hosting service — has to hold that DID's private
keys to decrypt what is addressed to it. It cannot ask the VTA per frame, so it
fetches them at startup.

The only path that did that was `seeds/export-mnemonic/1.0`, and it is wrong in
three ways at once: it exports no mnemonic (it is a per-key secret export that
kept the name of the thing it was migrated from), it takes one `key_id` so a
caller assembling a bundle makes one call per key, and each of those calls is
gated on **global Admin**. Being a service therefore required authority over the
whole VTA — over every other context's keys included — in order to be itself.

One request naming one context, one response carrying that context's DID and its
key material, one authorization decision about the one thing being decided.

## Application, not Admin, and what makes that safe

Reading the keys of the DID you already operate is not an administrative act.
The loosening is real and worth being explicit about: the role floor drops from
Admin to Application. What makes it sound is that the entitlement is a **scope**
and not a **rank** —

- `require_write()` is the floor: a Reader may see that keys exist and a Monitor
  may not even do that, and neither may hold one;
- `require_context()` is the scope, and it narrows Admin too. Only an *empty*
  `allowed_contexts` means "all contexts", so an Admin of some other context
  reaches nothing here.

Five tests assert that rather than describing it, including the two mistakes a
reimplementation would actually make: treating the entitlement as a privilege
level (`an_admin_of_another_context_cannot_either`), and checking existence
before entitlement (`entitlement_is_checked_before_existence`, which compares the
two refusals against each other so "no such context" cannot become an oracle for
contexts the caller may not reach).

## Delegating rather than re-walking

The operation is a thin wrapper over `build_did_secrets_bundle`, which already
existed for the offline export path. Its first draft re-walked the context
itself, and re-walking it got two things wrong that the existing traversal has
right: it passed `None` where the label belongs, silently dropping every key
whose store id is a derivation path and whose label carries the VM id (rule 2 of
`select_secret_kid`, which exists for exactly those records), and it did not page,
so a context with more keys than one page would have been truncated without
saying so. The only thing that legitimately differs between the two callers is
the role floor — the offline path runs as a local super-admin — so that is the
only thing the wrapper adds.

## The dispatch class is `Secret`

`[ None Secret false ]`. This classification, not the published registry, is what
the PDP feeds into `PolicyInput`, so it is what sets the consent bar. The first
draft said `Metadata`, which would have treated a private-key release as a
metadata read on the most disclosing task in the surface.

## Wire form

`ContextSecretsResultBody` is a wire type of its own rather than serialising
`DidSecretsBundle` directly. They are not the same thing: `DidSecretsBundle` is
the internal and on-disk form, snake_case, shared with `sealed_transfer` and with
operator exports already written to disk, while the spec is lowerCamelCase as
SPEC §4.10 requires. Renaming the existing type would rewrite a format that has
been written to disk to fix a format that has never been on the wire. `From` in
both directions, and a test that fails if anyone collapses the two.

Spec: trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#440. `every_served_uri_has_a_published_
spec_or_is_tracked_debt` fails until that merges and trust-tasks-rs releases —
deliberately not allowlisted in `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`, since the point of
that ledger is that it shrinks.

The spec for `vta/contexts/secrets/1.0` published in trust-tasks-rs 0.20.1
(trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#440), so the URI is no longer unspecced and
`every_served_uri_has_a_published_spec_or_is_tracked_debt` goes green with
nothing added to `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`.

Publishing it made two further ledgers speak up, which is them working — both
key off the registry, so neither could see the task while its spec was absent:

- **Retry safety.** `ReadOnly`. The task returns private keys, so `KeyedSecret`
  looks like the careful answer and is the wrong one: `export-mnemonic` is
  `KeyedSecret` because its export guard is one-shot, not because it returns a
  secret. This task has no guard and no side effect, so `ReadOnly` is simply
  true — and it takes the dedup path out entirely, which means no response body
  is stored at all. Same protection, reached by the honest classification.

- **A conformance witness**, built by serialising the type the service actually
  answers with rather than by hand. The risk it covers is precisely that
  `ContextSecretsResultBody` (lowerCamelCase, per SPEC §4.10) and the published
  schema drift apart while the internal `DidSecretsBundle` it converts from
  stays snake_case. A hand-written literal would be written to match the spec
  and would keep passing if the service drifted; this cannot.

## The dependency move is all of them or none

trust-tasks-rs 0.20.1 and its four sibling crates, plus `affinidi-tdk` 0.14,
`affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.24, `affinidi-messaging-mediator` 0.24 and
`affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` 0.7 — six manifests across the workspace.

None of those is optional or separable. `trust-tasks-rs` is a **public**
dependency of `affinidi-messaging-sdk`, so pinning this workspace at 0.20 while
anything still reached 0.19 puts two `trust-tasks-rs` nodes in one graph and
fails to compile on `expected MediatorAcl, found a different MediatorAcl`.

Bumping only the two obvious ones was not enough, and the way it failed is the
point: `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` 0.6 is a **dev**-dependency of
`vtc-service`, `room-host` and the e2e tests, and it dragged
`affinidi-messaging-mediator` 0.23 and `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.23 back in
behind it — a stale 0.19.4 node arriving through the test harness rather than
through anything the workspace declares directly. Verified after the fact:
`cargo tree -i trust-tasks-rs` now resolves exactly one node, 0.20.1, and the
long-standing 0.17.10 cycle (published `vta-sdk` -> `affinidi-tdk` 0.11 ->
`affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.21.1) is gone with it.

The upstream half of this is affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#786.

title: feat(vta): a service can fetch the keys of the DID it operates (#1398)
body:
feat(vta): a service can fetch the keys of the DID it operates (#1398)

* feat(vta): a service can fetch the keys of the DID it operates

`vta/contexts/secrets/1.0`. An integration whose identity the VTA manages — a
mediator, a room-host, a did-hosting service — has to hold that DID's private
keys to decrypt what is addressed to it. It cannot ask the VTA per frame, so it
fetches them at startup.

The only path that did that was `seeds/export-mnemonic/1.0`, and it is wrong in
three ways at once: it exports no mnemonic (it is a per-key secret export that
kept the name of the thing it was migrated from), it takes one `key_id` so a
caller assembling a bundle makes one call per key, and each of those calls is
gated on **global Admin**. Being a service therefore required authority over the
whole VTA — over every other context's keys included — in order to be itself.

One request naming one context, one response carrying that context's DID and its
key material, one authorization decision about the one thing being decided.

## Application, not Admin, and what makes that safe

Reading the keys of the DID you already operate is not an administrative act.
The loosening is real and worth being explicit about: the role floor drops from
Admin to Application. What makes it sound is that the entitlement is a **scope**
and not a **rank** —

- `require_write()` is the floor: a Reader may see that keys exist and a Monitor
  may not even do that, and neither may hold one;
- `require_context()` is the scope, and it narrows Admin too. Only an *empty*
  `allowed_contexts` means "all contexts", so an Admin of some other context
  reaches nothing here.

Five tests assert that rather than describing it, including the two mistakes a
reimplementation would actually make: treating the entitlement as a privilege
level (`an_admin_of_another_context_cannot_either`), and checking existence
before entitlement (`entitlement_is_checked_before_existence`, which compares the
two refusals against each other so "no such context" cannot become an oracle for
contexts the caller may not reach).

the role floor — the offline path runs as a local super-admin — so that is the
only thing the wrapper adds.

the PDP feeds into `PolicyInput`, so it is what sets the consent bar. The first
draft said `Metadata`, which would have treated a private-key release as a
metadata read on the most disclosing task in the surface.

* fix(vta-mcp): classify vta/contexts/secrets as Sensitive

The MCP bridge's guard keeps its own risk census, and a new dispatchable URI has
to be classified or `every_dispatchable_uri_has_a_known_verb` fails.

`Sensitive`, beside `vta/seeds/export-mnemonic` under "secret material,
emitted" — whose replacement this is.

Not `ReadOnly`, despite the task being a read that changes nothing. `ReadOnly`
is the class `--read-only` permits and means "safe to call on a whim", and what
comes back here is the whole authority of a context's DID. An MCP host approves
a *tool*, not a call, so a blanket `vta_call` approval must not silently cover
handing over a signing key — which is the gap this module exists to close.

Worth noting because it looks like a contradiction: this is the opposite call
from `vta-sdk`'s `retry_safety`, where the same task is `ReadOnly`. The two
ledgers ask different questions. Retry safety asks what a SECOND execution
costs, and the answer is nothing — the task is idempotent, so it needs no
dedup record, which is also what keeps a private key out of the dedup store.
The guard asks what ONE execution discloses, and the answer is everything.

title: chore(release): bring the workspace to 0.4.8 so vgi-core republishes
body:
## What

Workspace version 0.4.7 → **0.4.8**. Two lines plus the lockfile; all three crates take it through `version.workspace = true`.

No dependency or source changes.

## Why a bump rather than re-tagging 0.4.7

0.4.7 cannot be released, and not for a reason a retry fixes.

The partial `v0.4.7` run uploaded `vgi-core` 0.4.7 and then died on the `trql-client` git dependency — the failure `publish.yml`'s own header comment describes. That left crates.io in a split state:

| Crate | On crates.io | In tree |
|---|---|---|
| `vgi-core` | **0.4.7** — content predates `signer_did` / `conflicting_signer_dids` | 0.4.8 |
| `verify-trust` | 0.4.6 | 0.4.8 |
| `did-git-sign` | 0.4.6 | 0.4.8 |

`publish.yml` skips any crate already on crates.io at the workspace version. So a second `v0.4.7` tag would **skip** `vgi-core` and then build both dependents against that stale copy — and both call those two functions. That is the `E0432: unresolved imports` a dry run has been reporting all along.

The version number is the only thing that makes `vgi-core` republish, so the bump *is* the fix.

## Verification

As far as it can go before a real upload:

- `cargo publish --dry-run -p vgi-core` — packages and compiles clean ✅
- `cargo publish --dry-run -p verify-trust` — now fails **only** with:
  ```
  failed to select a version for the requirement `vgi-core = "^0.4.8"`
  candidate versions found which didn't match: 0.4.7, 0.4.6, 0.4.5, ...
  ```
  i.e. the ordinary first-in-chain ordering, which `publish.yml` handles by publishing `vgi-core` first. **No longer the stale-API error it gave at 0.4.7** — that's the signal the bump does what it needs to.

`cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo check --workspace`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace` (136 pass), `cargo +1.95.0 check --workspace` — all clean.

## What tagging this unblocks

This is step 3 of the chain OpenVTC's manifest documents:

1. ✅ Registry publishes `trql-client` — **done** (0.17.0)
2. ✅ VGI swaps its git pin back to a version — **done** (#38, #39)
3. ⬜ **VGI tags → `publish.yml` fires → OpenVTC deletes its `[patch.crates-io]` block**

OpenVTC currently consumes `did-git-sign` and `vgi-core` through git revs pinned to VGI `main`, which have to be re-pinned on every `vta-sdk` minor. A published 0.4.8 lets that block go away and the requirement be floored at a real release.

## After merge

Tag `v0.4.8` to fire `publish.yml`, which publishes all three in dependency order via crates.io Trusted Publishing. **Left for a human to push** — crates.io uploads can't be undone, only yanked.

Still outstanding and not addressed here: OpenVTC is on `vta-sdk` 0.34.1 / TDK 0.12 while this workspace leads on 0.35.

title: feat(vtc-client): any DID method can hold, and a session can carry it
body:
Every client of a VTC should be able to use this crate. Two things stopped that, and **both were in the client, not the service.**

## Signing was `did:key`-only, and it blamed the wrong side

`submit_join` called `build_signed` — the `did:key` convenience wrapper — and its own doc said the applicant *must* be a `did:key` because "the server's proof resolver accepts no other method."

That has not been true for a while. The document endpoint runs the proof through `TrustTaskVmResolver`, whose module doc says the `did:key`-only rule was removed precisely because "every DID this workspace provisions for an integration is a `did:webvh`". `resolve_holder` never had the restriction. It was this signature deriving the verification method from the identifier.

`submit_join_as` takes a `HolderKey` and signs as any method; `submit_join` is now a `did:key` wrapper over it, so no existing caller changes.

**Why it matters:** a persona minted by a VTA *is* a `did:webvh`. A client that could only sign as a `did:key` made every such holder borrow an identity it does not otherwise use — and the borrowed one is the DID that would have become the member.

## There was one transport

The holder verbs are addressed to a *community* and routed by document `type`. They were never URL-shaped; only the client was. `connect_didcomm` / `connect_tsp` put them over a mediated session, which is what a persona behind a mediator actually has.

Over a session the signing question does not arise at all: the envelope proves the sender and the VTC never reads a document proof, because `resolve_holder` short-circuits on `sender_did`.

**Delegated, not reimplemented.** Both constructors hold a `vta_sdk::client::VtaClient` pointed at the VTC's DID, which already owns session setup, `thid` demultiplexing, retry under one idempotency key, and reply-proof verification. A second copy of that here would be a second thing to keep correct.

Both are **off by default** — they pull the SDK's client and the TDK behind it, which a REST-only operator tool has no use for. `tsp` implies `didcomm`, since a TSP leg rides an existing session rather than replacing it.

## The admin verbs stay on HTTPS, and say so

Each is gated on a bearer token *and* a per-route `Trust-Task` header — a URL surface a session cannot carry. A session-only client now answers `VtcError::NoRestTransport`, naming the constructor argument it was not given, instead of requesting against an empty base and failing as a malformed URL. Guarded once in `tt`, which every admin verb already goes through.

## Found on the way: `Debug` printed the bearer token

It was derived, so `token: Option<String>` rendered in full into anything that formatted the struct — a `tracing` field, a test failure, an `unwrap` on an enclosing type. A credential that reaches a log has left. It is hand-written now and reports *whether* a token is held, never its value. (The manual impl was also forced: `VtaClient` is not `Debug`.)

## Checks

`cargo check`, `test` and `clippy --all-targets` clean on all three feature sets (default / `didcomm` / `tsp`); `cargo check --workspace` clean, so no dependent breaks; `cargo fmt --all --check` clean. 17 tests pass, including four new ones covering any-method holder keys, fragment rejection, the `NoRestTransport` guard, and that `Debug` does not leak the token.

**One pre-existing failure left alone:** `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc -p vtc-client` fails on ~20 unresolved `[`RoomSession`]` links in `vtc-client/src/rooms/`. Present on `main` before this branch and untouched by it — flagging rather than fixing, since it is someone else's module and a separate change.

## What this unblocks

OpenVTC hand-builds the join ceremony (`openvtc-core/src/join.rs` plus its half of `tsp.rs`) precisely because the library offered a transport it could not use and a signature it could not satisfy. With this it can consume `vtc-client` and delete that path — including the DIDComm-vs-TSP thread-id reconciliation, which stops being a consumer's problem.

title: WD02 merge plan: sequencing the five outstanding PRs into a consistent whole
body:
Per [#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5465297803), @stormer78 and I have the ball on assembling WD02. Five of the six open PRs can merge into a consistent document; this issue records the sequence, the per-PR work each needs before merging, and — the reason this needs its own issue — four decisions that belong to no single PR. The goal is that every merge closes the issues it can close, and nothing lands that a later PR has to un-say.

@stormer78's combined preview branch (`stormer78:preview/wd02-combined`) proved that `main` + #30 + #19 + #29 renders as one document, which is most of the confidence we need. But that preview omits #26 and #27, so the full five-PR integration has not yet been assembled by anyone — and the two it omits are the ones with a vocabulary dependency on #30's ordering. Hence the sequence below.

## Proposed merge order

**#26 → #27 → #30 → #19 → #29**

1. **#26 (edge verifiability, closes #21).** First because its new normative section is written in `[[ref: M-DID]]` / `[[ref: R-DID]]` vocabulary. If #30 merges first, those term files are deleted and #26's references dangle, forcing a semantic rewrite; if #26 lands first, #30's document-wide sweep picks the section up as ordinary prose. Needs a rebase onto current `main` first.
2. **#27 (max-of-halves privacy consideration; closes #23 together with #30).** Same vocabulary logic, and it needs the privacy-consideration renumber already flagged on the thread (#20's item 7 landed in its slot; #12 took 8).
3. **#30 (correlation scope, closes #22).** The big sweep. Its rebase re-words #26's section and shortens #27's paragraph to the one-line rule — both PR descriptions already anticipate exactly this. Housekeeping: the body says "Implements #22," which is not an auto-close keyword; add "Closes #22."
4. **#19 (VDC).** Rebased over #30's vocabulary and current `main`, review feedback folded in, undrafted. Checklist below.
5. **#29 (VAC).** Last, because it depends on the vocabulary and on the VDC existing for its cross-references. Checklist below.

**#18 stays out, deliberately.** It is parked as draft pending the vti-spec repo, per @bmiller59's plan to split it between cred-spec content and cross-cutting material. It is blocked on an external event, not on this merge — so it is not a gap in WD02. #11 stays open with it; #17 mostly resolves inside this merge (see D-A).

## Pre-merge work per PR

**#19 (VDC):**

- Rebase over #30: R-DID/M-DID/C-DID/P-DID vocabulary throughout the diff becomes declared-scope language.
- Privacy item 7 currently recommends issuing VDCs "against an R-DID rather than an M-DID." Under three scopes the honest value is **`directed`, not `pairwise`**: a VDC is presented to arbitrary verifiers, each of whom sees the delegator's identifier, so it is known to a holder-chosen set by construction. #30 makes exactly this argument for the witness identifier ("`directed` at minimum"); the delegator's identifier follows the same precedent — a context-scoped `directed` identifier per delegation.
- Fold in the review feedback from @sankarshanmukhopadhyay and @bmiller59: acceptance unconditionally required, fail-closed `maxDepth` confirmed, delegate eligibility per VTC governance, VDC scoped to delegation only (guardianship/succession excluded).
- The digest-encoding change stays in this PR and becomes the vehicle for the settled `digestMultibase` decision — see D-A. On rebase it must widen to cover **both** digest members now on `main` (#12 added the member-issued VMC acknowledgement's `digest` alongside the VWC's), and carry #12's canonicalization clause (top-level `proof` excluded from the hashed representation), which the current diff predates.
- Undraft once the above are pushed.

**#29 (VAC):**

- Drop the `community_did.md` edit. The sequencing comment already concluded the C-DID amendment "has nothing left to amend," but the diff still modifies the file #30 deletes — an edit-vs-delete conflict waiting for whoever merges second.
- The node-type editor's note ("the four VID types cover neither service nodes...") is written against the taxonomy #30 retires. Under declared scope the answer is trivially "a DID with a declared scope," so the note should be deleted rather than rewritten.
- Reconcile the VDC↔VAC cross-references. #19's delegation-vs-authority table says authority is "not defined in this specification" and deliberately leaves the word free; once #29 merges, that row and the "left free" note are false. Neither PR's diff can fix this today (the VDC is not on `main`), so #29's rebase carries it.
- Place the VAC per the outcome of D-B, or carry an editor's note if D-B is still open.

## Decisions that belong to no single PR

**D-A — Digest encoding: settled, `digestMultibase` is the standard.** Recording it here because the agreement was reached among the cred spec editors and is not fully visible in any one thread: WD02 adopts Multibase/Multihash digest values per VC Data Integrity §2.6, replacing `sha256:`+hex. This is consistent with the direction already on the record — #17 items 1–2, the implementation in #18, and the Trust Tasks framework's own adoption of the mechanism as §4.9.3 (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#236) — so both layers agree on the encoding. What remains is only carriage: with #18 parked, **#19's Digest Encoding section becomes the vehicle**, exactly as @stormer78's preview branch resolved it. On rebase it applies to all three digest-valued members (the VWC `digest`, the member-issued VMC acknowledgement's `digest` from #12, and the VDC's `parent`/`accepts`), preserves #12's exclude-`proof` canonicalization clause, and #17 can then close at #19's merge with a comment noting that item 3 (`DataIntegrityProof` suites) travels with the #18 split.

**D-B — Credential taxonomy after eight types (resolves #28).** No open PR implements #28, and its proposed fix (two categories, VIC standalone) is overtaken by the new credentials. The deciding variable is the question #29 deliberately left open — where the VDC sits:

- **VDC in Edge Credentials** (as #19 proposes, and as the delegation-is-not-authority sections of both PRs argue): Edge = VRC, VMC, VDC; Annotation = VPC, VWC, VEC; VIC and VAC each stand alone — recreating the single-subsection problem #28 exists to fix, twice.
- **VDC in Authority Credentials** next to the VAC: three well-formed categories plus standalone VIC — structurally clean, but it files a delegation credential under a heading both PRs spend real effort distinguishing it from.

The categories are informative, so a third option is open: keep the semantic split (VDC = edge) and fix the outline editorially — promote VIC and VAC to top-level sections named for their credential, per @talltree's rule in #28 that no section should have exactly one subsection. My lean is that third option. Whichever way, it is a WG call to make here, not a side effect of merging.

**D-C — Consideration-list structure.** #27, #30, #19, and #29 all append to the Security and Privacy lists; the preview showed Security reaching fifteen items, and every later PR renumbers again. Proposal: the **last** PR in the sequence (#29) restructures both lists under short subheadings in the same push, so the churn happens once. Volunteers welcome to disagree with the grouping there rather than in five rebases.

**D-D — Disposition of #24.** #26's per-verifier definition answers #24's three questions in principle (different VTNs → the anchor sets the verifier accepts; deliberately unanchored → verifiable as far as those anchors reach; external verifier → the definition's home case), and @mitchuski endorsed that resolution on both threads. But #26 does not say "closes #24," and the answers are implicit. Proposal: when #26 merges, close #24 with a comment stating the three answers explicitly, unless anyone wants them added to the normative text first.

## What this plan closes, and what stays open

| Issue | Disposition |
|---|---|
| #21 | Closed by #26 |
| #22 | Closed by #30 (add the keyword on rebase) |
| #23 | Closed once #27 and #30 are both in |
| #24 | Closed at #26 with an explicit comment (D-D) |
| #28 | Closed by the D-B decision, implemented in #29's rebase or a small follow-up |
| #9 | **Stays open — and gains weight.** After this merge, four things lean on the unencoded common-control linkage: both existing ZKP constructions (the community-anchored one now crossing identifiers by default under #30), the VAC's shared-subject rule, and the VDC's delegation predicate. #26's note marks the dependency honestly; the resolution is cross-TF work with the ZKP task force. |
| #17 | Closed at #19's merge (D-A): items 1–2 land there; item 3 (`DataIntegrityProof` suites) travels with the #18 split, noted in the closing comment |
| #11 | Stays open with parked #18 / the vti-spec split |
| #25 | Stays open — proposes a new discovery mechanism no PR implements; orthogonal to this merge |

If the order and the four decisions look right, #26 can rebase immediately — nothing in it waits on anything above.

title: Name the property and @context term that carry a correlation-scope declaration
body:
## Summary

WD02 says every identifier has a declared [correlation scope](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/blob/main/spec/body.md#correlation-scope) of `pairwise`, `directed` or `public`, and §Declaring scope settles *where* the declaration lives: in the credential, made by the issuer about its own identifier. What it does not settle is the property that carries it or the `@context` term for that property. The editor's note at the end of the subsection records that:

> The property that carries the declaration, and its `@context` term, are not yet named. Until they are, the requirements of this section bind a declaration that has been made and do not require one; the examples in this specification carry no declaration.

This issue tracks naming it. The decision was taken in #30's rebase (review item 4) and recorded in the #31 merge plan; neither is a place anyone will look once #31 closes.

## Why it matters

- **The section is normative in form and void in practice.** The reuse check, the ordering rule and the verifier rules all key off a declared value, and no conforming credential can carry one. An implementation today cannot declare a scope and cannot be non-conforming for failing to.
- **The examples are silent.** Every example in the specification omits the declaration, so none demonstrates the mechanism the section defines. The readability note in the introduction already says the reused member identifier is `directed`; once the property exists the examples should say so themselves.
- **Downstream text assumes it exists.** The witness `directed` minimum, the VDC delegator guidance (Privacy Consideration 10), the VMC acknowledgement item, and the common-control discussion in #9 all reason about declared scopes as if a verifier can read them.

## What has to be decided

1. **The property name**, and whether it sits at the top level of the credential or inside a structure alongside the issuer identifier. The declaration is a property of the identifier rather than of the credential (§Declaring scope, first consequence), which argues for a placement that reads that way.
2. **The `@context` term** under `https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1`.
3. **Whether the reciprocal credential in a bidirectional edge may restate the counterparty's scope** for readability, or whether each half carries only its issuer's own declaration, as the second consequence in §Declaring scope currently implies.
4. **Populate the examples** with computed declarations, and delete the editor's note.

Placement in the DID document is already ruled out and should not be reopened: `did:key` and `did:peer` numalgo-0 documents are derived from the identifier value, and those are the methods the specification recommends for the two narrow scopes.

## Migration note carried over from #30

#30's description records that Keyring Wallet fixtures (`ref-07-dtg-edge-semantics`) were built against the earlier four-value draft of #22 and declare `community`, a value that does not map onto one scope; each has to be re-decided as `pairwise` or `directed` per fixture. `rDid` is also a DIDComm wire field in the VRC reference implementation, so retiring it is a peer-compatibility change. #31 asked that the fixture owner be told before WD02 was cut. WD02 has since been cut (#44) and nothing records the outcome. Since the property named here is what those fixtures will declare, this is the natural place to confirm the fixtures have been re-decided, or to record that they have not.

title: feat(rooms): read and browse a room's records through this wallet's own agent
body:
`rooms/records/*` is served by the room's **host**, and this console cannot address one. `carrierParams` passes `{type, payload}` and the offscreen document supplies its own agent as the recipient, so a `service` naming a host is silently dropped and the call lands somewhere that does not serve it.

That narrowing is deliberate — the offscreen document mints and signs rather than counter-signing a document composed in a page — so the answer is the one `roomsKeysBackfill` already took: **ask the agent to do it.** `roomsKeysRead` and `roomsKeysBrowse` ([tt#426](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/426), `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.18.3) are that ask.

## The agent verifies; this renders

The check is deliberately **not** re-implemented here. The epoch key never leaves the agent, so it is the only party that can open a record — and the only party on the member's side that remembers what this host said last time. `verification` is its account of both, and a second verifier here would be a second thing to keep in step.

**`verification` is a verdict, never a failure**, and the doc comments say so where a caller will read them. An adverse value **still returns the record**: a member's own agent refusing because the *host* misbehaved would punish them for somebody else's act, and lock them out of the room holding the records that would show what happened. The consequence belongs on the write path. A surface that treats an adverse verdict as an error has inverted the design.

Two things documented at the call site because they are easy to get wrong:

- **`limit` is the page size to ask the host for, never a cap on the result.** The agent follows the cursor and reports `complete`.
- **`verification.count` is narrow.** It means something only when `complete` is true and neither `prefix` nor `sinceVersion` was set. Anything else is `notComparable`, which will be the common answer and is not a fault.

## Resyncing the task surface exposed a break this library already had

Not part of the plan, and worth flagging rather than folding in quietly.

`vta-sdk` cut `rooms/keys/present` and `rooms/owner/issue-authority` over to **0.2** (VTI#1365) and nothing here followed. Both calls named versions the agent no longer serves — and `present` is the load-bearing one, since **every host task takes a presentation and nothing else produces one**. The rooms panes' host calls were broken against current VTI and nothing said so, because the task-surface snapshot was stale enough not to notice.

Cut over here. `issue-authority/0.2` is shape-identical (`validUntil` became REQUIRED, which this always sent). `present/0.2` **removed `audience` and `nonce`**, and neither was doing what its name suggested:

- `audience` at the task layer names the document's **destination** — the agent being asked — not the host the presentation is later shown to.
- A room presentation needs no `nonce`: a host binds it to whoever signed the envelope, not to a challenge it issued.

The payload is `additionalProperties: false`, so a caller still sending either is refused. **The test that asserted `nonce` was sent now asserts it is not** — the same test doing the same job against the shape that exists.

## Checks

- `npm run build` — clean
- `npm test` — **1,188 tests, 0 failures** across all four workspaces
- Task-surface census resynced against `vta-sdk` 0.34.1; `expected` moved 201 → 204 with the reason recorded inline

Depends on VTI serving the two tasks (in flight) — this is the client half, and nothing calls it yet.

title: chore(deps): take trql-client 0.17 and collapse the trust-tasks duplicate
body:
## What

`trql-client` 0.16 → **0.17**. One line, plus the lockfile and the manifest comment it makes stale.

0.17.0 published today. It is the registry's release of commit `d99228a` ("take trust-tasks 0.19.4, tdk 0.13 and vta-sdk 0.35", #133), so it declares `trust-tasks-rs ^0.19.4` — the same line `vta-sdk` 0.35 resolves.

## Why

#38 knowingly left a duplicate behind: `trql-client` 0.16 declared `^0.18` while `vta-sdk` 0.35 declared `^0.19.4`, so the tree carried 0.18.11 and 0.19.4 together. That was the narrowed, tolerable shape — `did-git-sign` has no `trql-client` edge, so it never reached a graph where a type had to unify — but tolerable is not clean. This closes it:

```
trust-tasks-rs v0.19.4
├── affinidi-messaging-sdk → affinidi-tdk → {verify-trust, vta-sdk}
├── trql-client v0.17.0 → verify-trust
└── vta-sdk v0.35.0
```

`cargo tree -i trust-tasks-rs` and `cargo tree -i vta-sdk` each resolve a **single node**, and the lockfile still carries **no git sources** (`grep -c 'source = "git' Cargo.lock` → 0).

Worth recording that holding at 0.16 in #38, rather than taking the then-merged-but-unpublished 0.17 as a git `rev`, was the right side of the trade — a rev would have re-blocked `cargo publish` at the manifest to buy a duplicate that was already harmless. The wait cost two days and nothing else.

## Testing

`cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo check --workspace`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace` (136 pass), `cargo +1.95.0 check --workspace` for MSRV — all clean. **No source change needed.**

## Still outstanding from #38

Neither is touched here:

- [ ] **OpenVTC is on `vta-sdk` 0.34.1 / TDK 0.12** while this workspace leads on 0.35. Until it moves, anything building `did-git-sign` and `vta-sdk` together resolves both copies, and `vti-common`'s re-exported `vta_sdk::acl` types will not unify across them.
- [ ] **`vgi-core` needs republishing** — the crates.io 0.4.7 predates `signer_did` / `conflicting_signer_dids`, so `cargo publish --dry-run -p verify-trust` still fails and no dependent can be released.

title: Structural issues in categorization of DTG credentials
body:
In reviewing @martipos PR https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/16, I realized we have an issue with spec as currently structured in Working Draft 01. 

We refer to "three functional categories" of DTG creds because at the proposal stage, we actually had three categories (with multiple members in each category). However, once we realized we only needed one verifiable invitation credential (VIC), we don't actually have three categories, only two:

1. Edge Credentials (VRCs and VMCs) 
2. Annotation Credentials (VWCs, VPCs, VECs)

Fixing this would also address the editorial issue that section "8. Invitation Credentials" currently only has just one subsection, "8.1. VIC (Verifiable Invitation Credential)". As a general rule, a spec should never have a section with only one subsection.

My proposed fix:

1. Move what is currently (in Working Draft 01) section "9. Annotation Credentials" to become the new section 8 (so it immediately follows section "7. Edge Credentials"). That way we cover the two categories of DTG credentials first in sections 7 and 8.
2. Change what is currently section "8. Invitation Credentials" to become the new section 9.
3. Change the name to "9. VIC (Verifiable Invitation Credential)".
4. Just include in section 9 the content of what is currently section 8.1.

title: chore(deps): move the workspace to the published head (trql-client 0.16, vta-sdk 0.35, TDK 0.13)
body:
## What

Moves the workspace onto the published head of the stack. Two commits:

1. **`trql-client` git `rev` → `"0.16"`** — retires the pin now that the registry has published, and removes the last git dependency from the lockfile.
2. **`vta-sdk` 0.34 → 0.35, `affinidi-tdk` 0.12 → 0.13** — the line VTI main runs and the registry merged onto in #133.

Plus `cargo update` for the transitive set. **No source change was needed for either step.**

## Commit 1 — retire the git pin

`trql-client` was pinned to a git `rev` because the last published version (0.14.0) declared `trust-tasks-rs ^0.9` against a stack on ^0.17. The registry has now published through 0.16.0. The rev → 0.16.0 diff touches only `trql-client/src/client.rs`, and only to route builder failures through one `payload_build_error` helper — none of the symbols `verify-trust` imports changed.

`cargo publish` rejects git dependencies outright, so `publish.yml` could not have got past the manifest on a release tag while the rev stood. That blocker is gone (see caveats for the one that remains).

## Commit 2 — vta-sdk 0.35 / TDK 0.13

⚠️ **This one leads the consumer instead of following it** — knowingly, and the manifest now records it as a temporary, known break rather than a new licence to lead.

| Workspace | vta-sdk | TDK | trust-tasks |
|---|---|---|---|
| VTI `main` | 0.35 | 0.13 | 0.19.4 |
| this PR | **0.35** | **0.13** | 0.19.4 (+0.18.11, below) |
| **OpenVTC `main`** | **0.34.1** | **0.12** | **0.18.5** |

OpenVTC is still a minor behind with no branch in flight. Until it moves, a build taking both `did-git-sign` and `vta-sdk` directly resolves 0.34.1 and 0.35.0 together — and `vti-common` re-exports `vta_sdk::acl::{ActScope, ApproveScope, ContextDirection}` as its own public API, so those copies carry types that cannot unify. **OpenVTC needs a follow-up move to 0.35; that debt is the thing to clear next.**

## Known duplicate

`trust-tasks-rs` splits as a side effect — `trql-client` 0.16 declares `^0.18`, `vta-sdk` 0.35 declares `^0.19.4`:

```
trust-tasks-rs v0.18.11
└── trql-client v0.16.0
    └── verify-trust
```

with every other consumer on 0.19.4. This is the narrowed, historically tolerated shape: `verify-trust` passes no trust-tasks type across `trql-client`'s HTTPS transport, and `did-git-sign` — the crate OpenVTC consumes — has no `trql-client` edge at all (`cargo tree -p did-git-sign | grep -c trql` → `0`), so the duplicate never reaches a graph where a type has to unify.

**`trql-client` 0.17.0 is the fix**: merged upstream as registry `d99228a` (#133), declares `^0.19.4`, collapses the tree to one copy. It is *not* taken here as a git `rev` — that would re-block `cargo publish` at the manifest, which commit 1 just cleared, to buy a duplicate that is already tolerable. Bump to `"0.17"` when it reaches crates.io; I verified the coupled move locally (single `trust-tasks-rs` 0.19.4, clippy and tests green, no source change).

## Testing

`cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo check --workspace`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace` (136 pass), and `cargo +1.95.0 check --workspace` for MSRV — all clean.

## Pre-existing, not fixed here

Both present on `main`:

- `cargo audit` reports **RUSTSEC-2023-0071** (`rsa` 0.9.10 via `pgp` 0.20 and `ssh-key` 0.6). No upstream fix available; not a CI gate.
- `cargo publish --dry-run -p verify-trust` still fails: the published `vgi-core` 0.4.7 predates `signer_did` / `conflicting_signer_dids` while the packaged build resolves it from crates.io. **`vgi-core` needs republishing before any dependent can go out.**

## Follow-ups

- [ ] Move OpenVTC to `vta-sdk` 0.35 / TDK 0.13 (clears the leading-the-consumer debt)
- [ ] Bump `trql-client` to `"0.17"` once published (collapses the trust-tasks duplicate)
- [ ] Republish `vgi-core` (unblocks releases)

title: feat(rooms): browse and read a room's records, and say what was checked
body:
The last rooms UI piece. A room's records are served by its **host**, which this console cannot address — so `rooms/keys/{browse,read}` ask the wallet's own agent to make the call, being the party with a channel to the host, the credentials, and the only copy of the epoch key.

Stacked on #222, which adds the client functions.

## The verdict is the feature, and it is copy before it is code

Every answer carries what the agent checked. The rule those checks feed — **a client that catches a host serves reads and refuses writes** — is one nobody would guess. A member shown a warning icon dismisses it; a member later refused a write with no explanation concludes their own agent is broken. **A detection the member attributes to the wrong party is worse than no detection.**

So `Verdict` says what was *observed*, never how alarmed to be, and always says both halves of what follows:

| observed | what the pane says |
|---|---|
| two roots at one version | *"two different answers about this room… one of them is wrong, and a write would explain neither — a write moves the version"* |
| a short listing | the count served against the count committed to: a contradiction **inside a single answer**, needing no anchor and no second member |
| a trace that misses its own root | *"either its bookkeeping is broken or the path was made up, and from here those look the same"* |

Each ends with the same two sentences: reading still works, writing to this host will be refused.

## The other failure is on the reassuring side

A verified trace says the record is under the root the host asserted and **nothing about whether that root is the room's** — a host serving a private view of a room builds a consistent tree over it and traces every record in it perfectly.

The pane never lets it stand alone. `a verified trace never stands alone as though it settled the question` asserts the qualification is on screen, and that the alarming words are *not*.

A host that keeps no tree is reported as **making no claim** rather than as failing, with why that matters: a record it left out would look exactly like a room that never held one.

## Tests

Six render tests, every one **against the words** rather than the props — a pane that computed the right verdict and drew none of it would pass a test written the other way. That is the same reasoning `rooms-pane.render.test.mts` already gives for asserting the three standings on screen rather than against `standing()`.

Included deliberately: a **retracted** record. A tombstone is an answer, and a member told only "no body" reads a retraction as a fault.

Also asserted: every call made from this pane goes to the wallet's own agent. A host verb from here would be dropped by the bridge and land somewhere that does not serve it, which is the defect this whole shape exists to avoid.

## Checks

- `npm run build` — clean
- `npm test` — **1,194 tests, 0 failures**

title: feat(rooms): browse and read a room's records, and say what was checked
body:
feat(rooms): browse and read a room's records, and say what was checked

The last rooms UI piece. A room's records are served by its host, which this
console cannot address — so `rooms/keys/{browse,read}` ask the wallet's own agent
to make the call, being the party with a channel to the host, the credentials,
and the only copy of the epoch key.

**The verdict is the feature, and it is copy before it is code.** Every answer
carries what the agent checked, and the rule those checks feed — a client that
catches a host serves reads and refuses writes — is one nobody would guess. A
member shown a warning icon dismisses it; a member later refused a write with no
explanation concludes their own agent is broken. A detection attributed to the
wrong party is worse than no detection.

So `Verdict` says what was OBSERVED, never how alarmed to be, and always says
both halves of what follows:

- two roots at one version — "two different answers about this room… one of them
  is wrong, and a write would explain neither, because a write moves the
  version"; reading still works, writing will be refused;
- a short listing — the count it served against the count it committed to, which
  is a contradiction inside a single answer and needs no anchor and no second
  member to catch;
- a trace that does not reach its own root — "either its bookkeeping is broken or
  the path was made up, and from here those look the same".

The reassuring side is where the other failure lives, and it is guarded too: a
verified trace says the record is under the root the host asserted and **nothing
about whether that root is the room's**, because a host serving a private view of
a room traces every record in it perfectly. The pane never lets it stand alone —
`a_verified_trace_never_stands_alone` asserts the qualification is on screen.

A host that keeps no tree is reported as making no claim rather than as failing,
with why it matters: a record it left out would look exactly like a room that
never held one.

Six render tests, every one against the words rather than the props — a pane that
computed the right verdict and drew none of it would pass a test written the
other way. A retracted record is included because a tombstone is an answer, and a
member told only "no body" reads a retraction as a fault.

title: feat(rooms): read and browse a room's records through this wallet's own agent
body:
feat(rooms): read and browse a room's records through this wallet's own agent

`rooms/records/*` is served by the room's **host**, and this console cannot
address one: `carrierParams` passes `{type, payload}` and the offscreen document
supplies its own agent as the recipient, so a `service` naming a host is dropped
and the call lands somewhere that does not serve it. That narrowing is
deliberate — the offscreen document mints and signs rather than counter-signing
a document composed in a page — so the answer is the one `roomsKeysBackfill`
already took: ask the agent to do it.

`roomsKeysRead` and `roomsKeysBrowse` (dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#426,
`@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.18.3) are that ask.

**The agent verifies; this renders.** The check is deliberately not
re-implemented here. The epoch key never leaves the agent, so it is the only
party that can open a record, and the only party on the member's side that
remembers what this host said last time — `verification` is its account of both
and a second verifier here would be a second thing to keep in step.

**`verification` is a verdict, never a failure**, and the doc comments say so
where a caller will read them. An adverse value still returns the record: a
member's own agent refusing because the *host* misbehaved would punish them for
somebody else's act and lock them out of the room holding the records that would
show what happened. A surface that treats it as an error has inverted the
design.

`limit` is documented as the page size to ask the host for, never a cap: the
agent follows the cursor and reports `complete`, and `verification.count` means
something only on a complete unfiltered listing.

**Resyncing the task surface exposed a break this library already had.**
`vta-sdk` cut `rooms/keys/present` and `rooms/owner/issue-authority` over to
`0.2` (VTI#1365) and nothing here followed, so both calls named versions the
agent no longer serves — and `present` is the load-bearing one, since every host
task takes a presentation and nothing else produces one. Cut over here, with
`validUntil` unchanged and the two members `present/0.2` removed now absent:
`audience` at the task layer names the document's *destination*, which is the
agent being asked rather than the host it is later shown to, and a room
presentation needs no `nonce` because a host binds it to whoever signed the
envelope.

The test that asserted `nonce` was sent now asserts it is **not**, which is the
same test doing the same job against the shape that exists.

`npm run build` clean; 1,188 tests, 0 failures.

title: fix(vocabulary): stop saying "disclosure" and "fact" on screen
body:
Three rendered strings still used words `design-docs/persona-vocabulary.md` retires. This console is the reference implementation for that table, so its copies are what every other surface gets checked against — and one of them had already been copied out.

## How this surfaced

The TUI took the gated family's note verbatim while porting the attribute grouping (openvtc#290), and **its** banned-word guard rejected the string. A guard in another repository caught a word this one's guard was not looking for.

## What changed on screen

| Where | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `attribute-family.ts` — gated family note | "the registry gates these — a disclosure needs your approval each time" | "…— your agent asks you again before one of them leaves" |
| `persona-editors.tsx` — release explainer | "binds the approval to that one disclosure" | "…to that one departure" |
| `background.ts` — step-up approval card | action "approve this disclosure"; "N **facts**"; "covers this one disclosure" | "let this leave"; "N **attributes**"; "covers this one departure, and nothing else" |

`fact` was not in the original report and is the more serious of the two. It is retired twice over — it asserts a truth a self-asserted value does not have, and `Facts` already names a *verified* policy input in the VTC ceremony engine, which is very nearly the opposite. The table's standing rule is to change it on sight. This card is the holder's own screen; in the step-up flow it is the only thing they read.

## The guard

`disclosure` and `fact` join `BANNED` in `manager-vocabulary.render.test.mts`. Neither can be a claim type, so any appearance in rendered text is prose and there is nothing to whitelist — the distinction that file's header draws for `profile`.

The guard also now mounts **`AttributeEditor`**, which was reachable by no vocabulary check at all despite carrying the longest stretch of prose in the persona family — both Decision explainers, one of which is fixed above. Both new patterns are exercised in the non-vacuous test.

## Deliberately untouched

The table governs *the words a person reads*, and is explicit that the spec's words stay in code, on the wire, in audit records and in engineering discussion. So these stay:

- every `Disclosure*` type, `personaDisclosureHistory`, `disclosureId`, `history.data.disclosures`
- the **disclosure triangle** in `context-tree.ts` — a different word with a different meaning
- the refusal text in `page-task-policy.ts`, whose reader the file states outright is the developer
- `background.ts`'s page-facing `"user declined the disclosure"` — its reader is a relying party, not the holder
- `facts` in `network-pane.tsx` / `trust-graph.tsx` — diagnostics about a DID or service, not attributes of a holder, the same separate meaning the table preserves for the ceremony engine

## Checks

`tsc -b` clean; `manager-vocabulary.render.test.mts` 7/7, and 64/64 across the vocabulary, persona-pane and attribute-family suites.

One unrelated failure exists in the full run — `rooms-owner.render.test.mts` expects `issue-authority/0.1` and gets `0.2`. It is untouched by this diff (four files, none rooms-related) and comes from the `present/0.2` cutover; worth confirming against a clean install on `main`.

chore(deps): take trql-client 0.16 from crates.io and retire the git pin

The registry has published through trql-client 0.16.0, which is what the
`rev` pin was scaffolding for. 0.16.0 declares `trust-tasks-rs ^0.18` — the
line vta-sdk 0.34 already resolves — so this goes back to a plain version
requirement and the workspace holds one copy of trust-tasks again:

    trust-tasks-rs v0.18.11
    ├── affinidi-messaging-sdk -> affinidi-tdk -> {verify-trust, vta-sdk}
    ├── trql-client v0.16.0 -> verify-trust
    └── vta-sdk v0.34.1

Previously 0.17.3 (via the pinned rev) and 0.18.6 sat in the tree together.
The lockfile now carries no git sources at all, so `publish.yml` can get
past the manifest on a release tag; a separate, older blocker remains, noted
below.

The 0.15.0 rev -> 0.16.0 diff touches only `trql-client/src/client.rs`, and
only to route builder failures through one `payload_build_error` helper. No
symbol verify-trust imports changed, and no source change was needed here.
0.16.0 also drops the AWS SDK's legacy hyper-0.14 client from the registry's
graph, and with it the h2 0.3 / rustls 0.21 advisories it was suppressing.

`cargo update` alongside it, which floats vta-sdk 0.34.0 -> 0.34.1 and
refreshes the usual transitive set (reqwest, rustls, tokio-rustls, uuid,
wasm-bindgen, zerocopy).

vta-sdk 0.35 and affinidi-tdk 0.13 are published and deliberately not taken.
The follow-never-lead rule in the manifest cuts both ways: OpenVTC is on
vta-sdk 0.34.1 / TDK 0.12, so moving here would put two vta-sdk copies in its
binary — the break that comment exists to prevent, caused from this side. It
would also re-split trust-tasks, since vta-sdk 0.35 wants ^0.19.4 against
trql-client 0.16's ^0.18. That bump belongs in the step where OpenVTC moves.

fmt, clippy -D warnings, check and all 136 tests pass. Two things this does
not fix, both pre-existing on main: `cargo audit` reports RUSTSEC-2023-0071
(rsa 0.9.10, via pgp 0.20 and ssh-key 0.6, no fixed version available), and
`cargo publish --dry-run -p verify-trust` fails because the published
vgi-core 0.4.7 predates `signer_did` / `conflicting_signer_dids` while the
packaged build resolves it from crates.io — vgi-core needs republishing
before any dependent can go out.

title: docs: promote the VIC to a top-level section (closes #28)
body:
> **Stacked on #29, #39, #40, #41 and #42.** Cut from `feat/zkp-dependencies`. Until those land, the diff against `main` carries their commits; the change under review is the single commit `aad2665`. Draft until the stack below it merges.

## What this decides, and whose call it is

This implements **decision D-B of #31** along the third option recorded there, which was @geoffturk's stated lean: keep the semantic split, with the VDC an edge credential, and fix the outline editorially rather than by moving credentials between categories.

#31 is explicit that D-B *"is a WG call to make here, not a side effect of merging"*. This PR does not pre-empt that. It exists so the option has a diff to look at rather than a paragraph, and it is trivially closed if the group prefers one of the other two. Nothing in it is normative.

## The change

#28 exists to remove sections that have exactly one subsection. "Invitation Credentials" containing only the VIC was the original case that prompted it. The VAC arrived in #29 as a top-level section for precisely that reason, which left the VIC as the last one standing.

The VIC is now its own section, so neither credential is filed under a category invented to hold a single member. Two functional categories remain, **edge** and **annotation**, three credentials each:

| | |
|---|---|
| Edge | VRC, VMC, VDC |
| Annotation | VPC, VWC, VEC |
| Outside both | VIC, VAC |

The VIC sits outside because it bootstraps a node *into* a community rather than connecting or annotating nodes already in the graph, which is what the old one-member category was really saying. The VAC sits outside because it neither forms an edge nor annotates existing structure.

The taxonomy diagram, the introduction's category list and its "three categories" note, and the VAC's placement note all follow. The placement note becomes ordinary prose, since it no longer records an open question.

## One thing I went slightly beyond the ask for

"Formal W3C Type Hierarchy" was the last heading in the document that was an only child. Nothing linked to it, so it is now a labelled paragraph inside the taxonomy section. Leaving it would have satisfied #28's letter while breaking the rule it states, and I would rather not close an issue against a document that still contains an instance of what it describes.

Verified after the change: no section in the specification has exactly one subsection.

## Scope

Editorial. No normative rule changes, no schema changes, no reference changes, and every anchor and JSON example still validates. The categories are informative, so what this moves decides nothing about any credential.
