title: docs: say plainly what the ZK predicates are waiting on
body:
> **Stacked on #29, #39, #40 and #41.** Cut from `feat/vac-invocation`. Until those land, the diff against `main` carries their commits; the change under review is the single commit `114a050`. Draft until the stack below it merges.

## Why

The Zero-Knowledge and Selective Disclosure section lists the predicates the schemas are deliberately shaped to support, then closes with *"Detailed ZK protocols and registry-ZK interactions are left to future work."* A reader cannot tell from that which predicates are constructible today, which depend on work nobody has done, or where that work lives. The predicate list reads like an inventory of available machinery. It is not one.

That gap gets worse as the catalogue grows. #19 added two delegation predicates, #29 added two more for authority, and the correlation-scope change altered when the oldest of them needs the missing primitive at all. Four separate PRs each added a line to a list whose status nobody had stated.

## What the note says

**One primitive carries four predicates.** A proof that two credentials, or two identifiers, are under common control, without disclosing either. No DTG specification defines it. It is tracked in #9, and it carries:

- the community-anchored proof, wherever a party's VMC identifier and its VRC identifier differ;
- the shared-subject requirement that stops two parties pooling one's membership with the other's authority;
- proving a VDC chain valid without disclosing it;
- proving a VAC chain valid without disclosing it.

**Declared scope promoted the first of these from edge case to ordinary case.** A member who declares `pairwise` toward their community and `pairwise` toward a counterparty holds two identifiers that differ by construction, so a community-anchored proof must cross them rather than read one identifier out of both credentials. The body already says this in the construction itself; the note makes the consequence for #9 explicit rather than leaving it to be inferred two sections apart. This is the point #31 flagged when it said #9 *"stays open, and gains weight"*.

**The unsalted digest binders sit with the same task force**, per #38, and now cover five members rather than the three that issue was filed against.

## The part I most wanted written down

**Nothing in this specification is unverifiable while that work is outstanding.** Every requirement here can be checked by presenting the credentials themselves, which is exactly what a holder must do today to satisfy any predicate in the list. The cost is privacy, not correctness, and it falls hardest where a chain is involved because the disclosure boundary is the whole chain rather than the credential presented.

So the note ends with a SHOULD NOT: implementations should not defer shipping a rule of this specification on the grounds that its zero-knowledge form is unspecified. Without that sentence, "left to future work" is readable as "this part is not ready", which is not true of any normative rule here.

## Scope

Editorial and informative. No normative rule changes, no schema changes. It replaces one vague bullet with a note that names the dependency, the issues tracking it, and the interim position.

title: feat: state that a VAC is not a bearer credential
body:
> **Stacked on #29, #39 and #40.** Cut from `feat/vac-attenuation-limit`. Until those land, the diff against `main` carries their commits; the change under review is the single commit `df222cb`. Draft until the stack below it merges.

## The gap

The VAC had no counterpart to the VDC's [Invocation Binding](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/29/files), which opens *"A VDC is not a bearer token"* and requires the presenter to demonstrate control of the subject's verification method. The VAC said nothing, and its `audience` field is OPTIONAL with its absence documented as meaning **any holder may present it**. So a VAC without `audience` was a bearer credential, and nothing in the specification recorded that as a decision rather than an omission.

Even with `audience` set, the field was unenforceable. It named the DID that must present the credential, but no rule required a verifier to establish that the presenter controlled it. A constraint with no check.

**This is sharper for a VAC than for a VDC**, because a VAC chain is presented in full on every use. A captured presentation is a captured chain. A specification that let a holder be identified by possession alone would make every verifier a distribution point for the authority it had just been shown.

## It also closes an inconsistency already in the text

[Relationship to Capability Models](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/29/files) says the mechanics the VDC borrows from ZCAP-LD and UCAN are *"attenuation-only re-delegation, chains resolving to a recognized root, and binding to a demonstration of key control at invocation"*, and adds that *"chained permissions are the VAC's territory, and its Attenuation rules apply the same mechanics to authority."*

The VAC applied the first two. The third was never written down. So the specification already claimed this rule existed. This PR makes it true rather than adding something new, which is also why "is bearer intentional here?" has no good answer in the current text: both readings are supported, by different sections.

Worth noting that the comparison does not push the other way either. UCAN requires the invoker to sign the invocation and ZCAP-LD requires proof of control, so neither of the models cited is bearer at invocation.

## The rules

- A verifier MUST NOT accept a party as holding the authority a VAC confers unless that party demonstrates control of the verification method associated with the presented VAC's `credentialSubject.id`, at the time of the request.
- Where the presented VAC carries `audience`, the party that demonstrated control MUST be the DID it names. The two checks answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other: key control establishes that the presenter is the subject, `audience` establishes that this subject is the one the issuer expected to be presenting here.
- **Only the presented VAC's subject demonstrates anything.** The links above it are not present and are asked for nothing. Requiring otherwise would defeat attenuation, whose whole purpose is that the party who attenuated is not in the loop when its agent acts.

How the demonstration is requested and carried is left to the planned DTG Core Trust Task Protocols specification, exactly as the VDC leaves it. That is the same dependency #11 tracks, and this PR adds no new one.

## Also in the diff

Security Considerations gain bearer use of a VAC. Conformance Target 3 gains the key-control rule alongside the chain and status rules. The `audience` schema text no longer says any holder may present, and the attenuation SHOULD explains what setting `audience` buys. CONTEXT.md follows.

All `[[ref:]]` references, anchors and JSON examples validated. Every commit carries a DCO sign-off.

title: feat: let a governing party bound or forbid attenuation of a VAC
body:
> **Stacked on #29 and #39.** Cut from `feat/vac-withdrawal`, because the section it changes exists only there. Until both land, the diff against `main` carries their commits too; the change under review is the single commit `c106e8c`. Draft until #29 and #39 merge, at which point this rebases onto `main`.

## The asymmetry

A [[VDC]] forbids re-delegation unless `maxDepth` explicitly authorises it — *"Setting `maxDepth` above 0 is the delegator's explicit authorisation to re-delegate; there is no other."* A VAC permits attenuation unconditionally, bounded only by the chain-depth ceiling of 8, which #29 is explicit is *"a resource bound, not a stylistic one"* — a denial-of-service control, not a policy one.

So a governing party could not decline to have an action re-granted, however sensitive it was. And neither section argued for the difference, which is what made it read as an oversight rather than a decision. It came up on #39 and this settles it.

## The defaults should differ, and now the specification says why

Extending the two chains does different things.

A further **delegation** adds a party who may act *in the principal's name*, so the principal has to keep the register of who can speak for it, and a delegate that needs help can ask the principal for a fresh root delegation. Failing closed costs little.

A further **attenuation** only narrows, and its subject acts *as itself*, so nothing new is attributed to the governing party or to the attenuating holder. More to the point: **forbidding attenuation does not stop a holder equipping an agent.** It makes them lend their own key instead, which confers everything they hold rather than a subset, lasts as long as their own authority does, and is indistinguishable to a verifier from the holder acting in person. Attenuation is the safer of the two things a holder will actually do, and a default that pushed holders toward the other would buy nothing.

That argument is why this PR does **not** simply copy `maxDepth` across.

## What it adds instead

**`authority.maxAttenuation` (OPTIONAL)** bounds how far a chain may extend below the VAC that carries it. `0` forbids attenuation outright, for an action sensitive enough that the governing party wants to decide personally who holds it. Absent means attenuation is permitted as far as the depth ceiling allows.

A link MAY lower a limit, or set one where its parent set none, and MUST NOT raise one — so the effective limit on a chain is the strictest any of its links imposes, in keeping with attenuation never widening what it derives from. A verifier MUST reject a chain in which any VAC lies more than *n* steps below an ancestor bearing `maxAttenuation` *n*.

**It is deliberately not called `maxDepth`.** One name that fails open in one credential and closed in the other is a mistake waiting to be made by an implementer who has read only one of the two sections. The section also states that the ceiling and this limit are separate controls and that a chain must satisfy both: five links under a root bearing `maxAttenuation` `2` is within the ceiling and still invalid.

## A second gap, surfaced by the first

The VAC had no counterpart to the VDC's third check (*"Must the delegate independently qualify?"*). A valid chain establishes that authority was narrowed by parties entitled to narrow it. It does not establish that the party now holding it is one the scope is willing to deal with — and because that party acts as itself rather than in its attenuator's name, it may be one the governing party has never encountered. A member granted write access could derive write access for an outside contractor, who then writes in the room as itself.

A governing party MAY now require the subject of an attenuated VAC to independently qualify, and a verifier enforcing that policy MUST reject a chain whose subject does not, however well formed the chain is. That is recorded as a governance determination alongside the equivalent one for delegates.

## Also in the diff

The agent example carries `"maxAttenuation": 0`, which is what equipping an agent ordinarily wants and shows the opt-out in place. Security item 15 gains the limit among its rejection reasons, the zero-knowledge chain predicate gains depth, and CONTEXT.md and the glossary entry follow.

All `[[ref:]]` references, anchors and JSON examples validated. Every commit carries a DCO sign-off.

## [0.35.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-sdk-v0.34.1...vta-sdk-v0.35.0) — 2026-09-09 ### Added - **rooms**: Cut over to present/0.2 and issue-authority/0.2 ([#1365](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1365)) The consuming half of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#415 and #418, unblocked by affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#784. `trust-tasks-rs` 0.19 carries both new spec versions, but this workspace could not take it: `affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.22.0` required 0.18, so pinning 0.19 put two `trust-tasks-rs` nodes in the graph and broke `vta-sdk` on `expected MediatorAcl, found a different MediatorAcl`. TDK #784 moved the messaging family to 0.19 and 0.23.0. Taking it exposed pins that had drifted apart underneath: `vta-sdk` was on messaging-sdk 0.22 while `vta-service` and the e2e tests were on 0.21, and three `trust-tasks-rs` versions were resolving at once. All of it is now consolidated: the lockfile holds exactly ONE `trust-tasks-rs` and ONE `affinidi-messaging-sdk`, where before it held three of each. `rooms/keys/present` 0.1 -> 0.2 and `rooms/owner/issue-authority` 0.1 -> 0.2. Both 0.1s are retired upstream. Neither is dual-accepted, deliberately: for `present`, 0.1's extra members are exactly the two nothing could honour; for `issue-authority`, accepting 0.1 means accepting a request with no `validUntil`, which is the thing 0.2 exists to refuse. The hand-rolled `validUntil` guard in `room_owner.rs` is deleted. 0.2 makes the member REQUIRED, so the generated payload types it as a `DateTime` and the envelope schema rejects a request without one before dispatch. Same rule, one layer up, which is where a shape constraint belongs. `every_witnessed_task_round_trips_through_its_generated_types` refused two witnesses that had been green for as long as they existed: 1. The `issue-authority` witness carried no `validUntil` — a chain root with no expiry, the exact request 0.2 forbids, and one this service could have sent. 2. The `present` witness carried `"audience": "did:key:z6MkHost"` — a HOST DID, the precise shape #414 reported as impossible to satisfy, since the field named the party that had to PRESENT the credential. `room_oracle` emitted `membership` and `authority[]` as JSON **objects**; `AuthorityPresentation` types both as strings, and the host's opener reads base64url or bare JSON text. So the oracle's output could not deserialize at a host at all — `rooms/keys/present` had never worked end to end. It went unseen because 0.1's response typed `presentation` as an opaque object; 0.2 names the shared component, which turned a runtime refusal nothing exercised into a type error. The oracle now serialises each credential. That is the first half of have caught all three of these years earlier. - **sdk**: A no-I/O verifier resolves did:peer too ([#1364](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1364)) - **sdk**: The client verifies the replies it receives ([#1341](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1341)) Completes the arc #1334 and #1335 began. Both services sign their responses; until now nothing checked one, so the signature was decorative. This is the surface that matters most — the CLI, cierge and the services all dispatch Trust Tasks through `VtaClient`. A reply is bytes off a socket. Nothing else in this path establishes who produced them: the transport proves a connection, and over REST not even that beyond TLS to a host name. Without the proof an intermediary can rewrite an ACL listing, flip a policy decision, or answer for an agent that never spoke, and every check downstream passes — because the checks downstream are about shape. Two checks, and the second is the one easy to omit: the proof must verify, **and its proven signer must be the agent this client is talking to**. A proof by somebody else's key verifies perfectly well, so skipping the binding turns "signed by somebody" into "signed by the agent". The expected signer is `ClientIdentity::vta_did`, which the client already holds. A client with no identity does not verify, because there is nothing to bind against — such a client cannot produce a conforming request either and is refused at the agent for a missing `recipient`. A loopback client likewise: its sink answers ahead of the transport and returns a value rather than a signed document. Error documents are exempt, from the specification rather than for convenience: `trust-task-error`'s own proof requirement is RECOMMENDED (SPEC §8.1), so demanding one would make every conforming refusal unreadable, including the ones carrying the reason a caller needs. `trusting_unsigned_replies()` is a staging control, not a preference. An agent that predates #1334/#1335 sends nothing to verify, so a client upgraded ahead of its agent would refuse every answer; this exists so that ordering can be chosen rather than endured. It weakens the check to almost nothing while set — an attacker who can rewrite a reply can also strip its proof — so a present proof is still verified and still bound. The resolver is built once per client and shared by clones. A `DIDCacheClient` is a cache; one per call would defeat it. - **persona**: Serve persona/facet — the holder's arrangement of their identity ([#1338](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1338)) Implements the three tasks specified in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#405, published in trust-tasks-rs 0.18.9. A holder who uses this model for a while ends up with twenty profiles, and a flat list of twenty is a list nobody reads. A facet is the arrangement over them — "Work", "Home", "Play" — and it is agent-scoped, like the pool and the profiles it groups. **An arrangement, not a container.** Nothing is stored inside a facet, and `delete_facet` touches no profile and no attribute. There is no cascading form because there is no cascading form of the idea: a grouping that could take its members with it is a folder, and a holder who reads it as a folder is right to be afraid of it. `releasedFaces` reports what now belongs nowhere, which is what a screen needs to say what it will look like afterwards. `deleting_a_facet_deletes_nothing_it_named` pins it. **Membership lives on the facet.** A `facet_id` on `Attribute` would be the obvious alternative and is the wrong shape: `attribute/put` REPLACES, and a well-behaved consumer does not hold the values it would have to resend — `attribute/list` withholds `sensitivity: high` plaintext unless asked by name. It would either request every sensitive value the holder owns to perform an arrangement that has nothing to do with values, or send a put without one and destroy them. ### Changed - **sdk**: Move the Trust-Task proof verifier down from vti-common ([#1340](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1340)) Pure move plus re-exports; no behaviour changes. It exists so the next change can be small: `VtaClient` needs to verify the responses it receives, and the verifier it needs already exists one layer up where a client cannot reach it. `vti-common` was the right home while services verifying their *inbound* requests were the only consumer. A client verifying its *replies* is the same operation over the same document shape, and `vta-sdk` is the layer both can see. **The part worth not duplicating is the verification-method resolver.** Resolving one looks trivial and is not: a DID document may name its methods absolutely (`did:webvh:…:glenn#key-0`) or relatively (`#key-0`), while a proof always names them absolutely, so a resolver accepting only the spelling it expects refuses perfectly good documents from conforming peers. A second copy would drift, and drift in a verifier means refusing honest documents or accepting dishonest ones. Writing that copy is what this move avoids. Behind a new `proof-verify` feature rather than `client`, because `vti-common` takes `vta-sdk` with `default-features = false` and must not acquire reqwest to keep verifying. It adds no dependency to `vti-common` — that crate already depended on `affinidi-data-integrity` and the DID resolver directly. `client` enables it: a client that cannot verify its replies is the gap being closed. The resolver rides in the feature deliberately. Verification is only as good as the party it resolves — a `did:key` signer needs no I/O, and a `did:webvh` one, which is what a real agent is, cannot be verified without resolving its document. Call sites that used the module path (`vti_common::auth::di_proof::…`) now use the flat re-export, so there is one canonical path rather than an alias to go stale. Two doc comments naming the old location updated with them. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` clean; `vta-service --lib` 1063 passed; `vta-sdk` + `vti-common` suites pass, including the four resolver tests that moved with the code. ### Fixed - **rooms**: A presentation is bound to its presenter — and dtg-credentials 0.6 → 0.9.1 ([#1356](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1356)) * fix(rooms): bind a presentation to its presenter, not to the host `pnm-cli rooms --host-did …` could never work. Every request it made was refused as `WrongAudience`, and omitting the flag "worked" only by skipping the check it exists to perform — so the flag's two states were broken and unprotected. `audience` is not who a presentation is addressed to. `dtg_credentials::authority::verify_chain` compares it to the PRESENTER — "the leaf must be presentable by whoever is presenting it" — so it is holder binding, and its whole job is to make a captured presentation worthless to whoever captured it. Filled with the host's DID it named a party no presenter can ever match. The value to bind to was already named a few lines away: `RoomSigner`'s doc says "a room request is signed by the party the presentation was minted for". This passes exactly that. There is no unbound case left, so the warning about one goes, and `--host-did` keeps its real job of naming the document's recipient.

## `vti-rooms`
## [0.2.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vti-rooms-v0.1.3...vti-rooms-v0.2.0) — 2026-09-09 ### Added - **rooms**: Traces, and a response type for the single-record read ([#1368](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1368)) A commitment lets a reader catch a host that equivocates. A trace proves a particular record sits under the root that host just asserted. This serves them — and fixes the conformance defect that adding them uncovered. Implements trust-tasks-tf#419, released as trust-tasks-rs 0.19.1. `rooms/records/get` has never conformed to its published schema. Both hosts answered a read by serialising `vti_rooms::Record` — the *storage* record — and adding `dataCommitment` to whatever came out: "c2VhbGVk" is not of type "object"; Additional properties are not allowed ('author','epoch','nonce','pinned','status','updatedAt' were unexpected) It survived because `vti_rooms::wire`'s rule — every wire type appears in tests/schema_conformance.rs — can only be applied to types that exist. A response that was never a type had no line to be missing from, and a storage record reached the wire because nothing stood between them. The consumer is not hypothetical: `@openvtc/pnm-core`'s `roomsRecordsGet` is typed on the generated payload, so a caller reading `sealed.ciphertext` got `undefined` from a live host, with a green type-check on both sides. The leaf preimage was not reproducible either. `leaf_hash` canonicalised the storage record, so every root it produced was unreachable by any reader: `updatedAt` is unix seconds in storage and RFC 3339 on the wire, `epoch` and `nonce` are flat in storage and inside `sealed` on the wire, and `epoch` serialises as `null` on an open room where the wire has it absent. Survivable while the only use was comparing two roots from the same build; not survivable once a trace has to be computable by someone else. - **rooms**: Hosts compute and serve the data commitment ([#1351](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1351)) * fix(rooms): a commitment is a DigestMultibase, not bare hex Owed from #1346. The spec that landed with it (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#411) types `dataCommitment` as the framework's `DigestMultibase`, and the helper shipped emitting hex. Bare hex hard-codes SHA-256 into the wire contract, which is precisely what `DigestMultibase` exists to prevent: multihash names the algorithm in-band, so moving off SHA-256 later is a change of value rather than another schema revision. `0x12 0x20` then the digest, base58btc with the `z` prefix — the same shape `sealed_transfer::bundle_digest_multibase` already produces, so the two agree by construction rather than by memory. `from_multibase` refuses anything that is not a sha2-256 multihash. A commitment is what a comparison turns on, so silently accepting an algorithm this build cannot compute would turn "these two roots differ" into "these two roots are not comparable" without saying which. Two tests, both about the encoding being a contract rather than a detail: a commitment decodes to the 34-byte multihash and round-trips, and bare hex, a foreign algorithm, a truncated digest and non-multibase are each refused. The tree, the leaves and the proofs are untouched — this is the wire boundary only. - **rooms**: A browser can be a room member ([#1347](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1347)) * feat(rooms): a `host` feature, so a room's member half reaches wasm `vti-rooms` already had two halves and no name for them: `vta-service` imports `mls`/`sealed`/`wire` and nothing else, while `vtc-service`, `room-host` and `vti-rooms-dtg` import `storage`/`authz`/`audit`. This names the second half `host`, on by default, and makes `vti-common` optional behind it. `vti-common` describes itself as server-side infrastructure and pulls axum, fjall and tokio, so it was the whole of what kept a room's member code off `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. With it optional, `--no-default-features --features mls` builds there — which is what lets a browser hold a room's keys itself rather than ask an agent to. See `docs/05-design-notes/data-rooms-demo-site.md`. The member half needed **no source changes** to get there. That is a property of `error.rs`, which deliberately does not use `vti_common::error::AppError` because key material is not a service's concern; a decision made for its own reasons that paid for itself here. `lifecycle` is deliberately left ungated: only hosts consume it today, but it needs nothing from `vti-common`, and a member computing a room's lifecycle state to explain it on screen should not need a host's dependencies. Three things about the wasm plumbing, each of which reports as a `compile_error!` that reads like an unsupported target: - OpenMLS 0.9 has a first-class `js` feature (`web-time` for the `SystemTime` wasm lacks, plus getrandom's JS backend). Declared per-target rather than as a feature of this crate, so building for wasm just works — verified wasm-only: `web-time` appears in the wasm tree and not the native one. - There are two getrandom majors in the graph. The 0.4 is ours; the 0.2 arrives transitively under `openmls_rust_crypto` via RustCrypto's elliptic-curve stack, so no feature declared here could reach it. `getrandom_02` is a feature shim, not a dependency this crate calls. - With both declared per-target, **no `RUSTFLAGS` are needed** — the `wasm_js` feature alone selects the backend. CI gains two steps in the `features` job: clippy on the member half with no host, and a wasm32 `--lib` check, so neither property rots silently. `vta-service` now takes `default-features = false`: a VTA holds room keys and is never a room's host, so it no longer compiles one. * feat(rooms): vti-rooms-wasm — a data room's member half, in a browser The MLS group, record sealing and the epoch key chain, compiled to WebAssembly, so a tab can *be* a member rather than drive an agent that is one. `vti-rooms` supplies all of it; this crate is only the boundary, and its job is deciding what crosses. **Secrets do not cross.** Everything returned is public — a KeyPackage, ciphertext, an epoch number — with one deliberate exception: the snapshot, which is key material because OpenMLS persists a group through its provider rather than as a value. It goes in IndexedDB and nowhere else; the docs say so at the method, since it is the one thing here a caller could reasonably mishandle.

This needs a floor of 0.18.10 — the spine validates OUTGOING responses, so under an older schema an analysis that fully succeeded would come back 500 `responseSchemaViolation` — and no longer moves one: main reached 0.18.11 while this sat open, which satisfies it. The bump this branch carried is dropped rather than resolved downward. **Severity is how linkable. Facets are whether the holder minds.** Nothing here touches `severity`, and that is the design rather than an omission. A value shared between two profiles in one facet still links them for anyone who sees both — the holder's filing changes nothing a counterparty can do — so softening severity on intent would report a false all-clear. What the facets add is a second axis: which of these findings the holder would actually want to act on. **Absent is unknown, not false.** `crosses_facets` is `Option` and is `None` when the holder keeps no facets, because `false` asserts these identities sit in one part of a life and an agent with no facets has made no such finding. `FacetIndex::any` is what carries that distinction, which is why the index is a struct rather than a map. **An unarranged profile is not a second facet.** Only distinct, named facets count toward a crossing. title: Promote the VIC to a top-level section (closes #28)
body:
Promote the VIC to a top-level section (closes #28)

Implements decision D-B of #31 along the third option recorded there,
which was @geoffturk's stated lean: keep the semantic split, with the VDC
an edge credential, and fix the outline editorially rather than by moving
credentials between categories.

#28 exists to remove sections that have exactly one subsection, and
"Invitation Credentials" containing only the VIC was the original case.
The VAC arrived as a top-level section for the same reason, which left
the VIC as the last one. It now stands as its own section, and neither
credential is filed under a category invented to hold one member.

Two functional categories remain, edge and annotation, with three
credentials each. The VIC and the VAC stand outside them: neither forms a
graph edge, and neither annotates structure already in the graph. The
taxonomy diagram, the introduction's category list, and the VAC's
placement note follow. The placement note becomes ordinary prose, since
it no longer records an open question.

Also folds "Formal W3C Type Hierarchy" into the taxonomy section as a
labelled paragraph. It was the one remaining heading that was an only
child, nothing linked to it, and leaving it would have satisfied #28's
letter while breaking the rule it states.

No normative rule, schema, or reference changes. The categories are
informative, so what this moves decides nothing about any credential.

title: Say plainly what the ZK predicates are waiting on
body:
Say plainly what the ZK predicates are waiting on

The Zero-Knowledge and Selective Disclosure section listed predicates the
schemas are shaped to support and closed with "detailed ZK protocols and
registry-ZK interactions are left to future work". A reader could not tell
which predicates are constructible today, which depend on work not yet
done, or where that work lives.

Four of them rest on one primitive no DTG specification defines: a proof
that two credentials or two identifiers are under common control without
disclosing either. It carries the community-anchored proof wherever a
party's VMC and VRC identifiers differ, the shared-subject requirement
that stops membership and authority being pooled by two parties, and the
zero-knowledge form of both the delegation and the authority chain. That
is #9, and the declared-scope change makes the first of them the ordinary
case rather than an edge case: two `pairwise` identifiers differ by
construction, so the proof has to cross them.

The unsalted digest binders are recorded alongside it as the same task
force's work, per #38, now covering five members rather than three.

The note also says what holds in the meantime, which was the part most
open to misreading: nothing here is unverifiable without zero knowledge.
Every requirement can be checked by presenting the credentials, which is
what a holder must do today. The cost is privacy, not correctness, and
implementations should not defer shipping a rule because its
zero-knowledge form is unspecified.

title: Address review: remove the audience field, fix a comma
body:
Address review: remove the audience field, fix a comma

Review made the point that `audience` is vestigial under this PR's rules
and that it had to be settled here rather than in a follow-up, since it
is a schema change either way.

It is. The presented VAC's subject MUST demonstrate control of
`credentialSubject.id`, and where `audience` is present the demonstrating
party MUST be the DID it names. So `audience` is either equal to
`credentialSubject.id`, adding nothing the subject check did not already
establish, or different, in which case no presentation can satisfy both.
The example had it set to the subject, which is the only value that ever
verifies.

Removed rather than redefined. Giving it the conventional meaning — the
verifier a credential is intended for — would restrict where a
presentation may be made, which is a trust task concern rather than
something the credential should carry, and `scope` already binds the
credential to the resource. The VDC has no counterpart field. A
paragraph in Invocation records the removal and the reasoning, so the
question is not reopened later, and Security item 20 no longer offers
`audience` as a fallback for a verifier that skips the key-control
demonstration: there is deliberately no fallback.

Also fixes the missing comma in Conformance Target 3.

title: Let a governing party bound or forbid attenuation of a VAC
body:
Let a governing party bound or forbid attenuation of a VAC

A VDC forbids re-delegation unless `maxDepth` authorises it; a VAC
permitted attenuation unconditionally, capped only by the chain-depth
ceiling, which the specification is explicit is a denial-of-service bound
rather than a policy control. So a governing party could not decline to
have an action re-granted, however sensitive, and neither section argued
for the difference — it read as an oversight rather than a decision.

The defaults should differ, and the section now says why. A further
delegation adds a party who may act in the principal's name, so the
principal keeps the register and a delegate that needs help can ask for a
fresh root delegation; failing closed costs little. A further attenuation
only narrows, and its subject acts as itself. Forbidding it by default
would not stop a holder equipping an agent, it would make them lend their
own key instead — everything they hold rather than a subset, for as long
as they hold it, and indistinguishable to a verifier from the holder
acting in person.

So the default stays, and the control is an opt-out:

- `authority.maxAttenuation` (OPTIONAL) bounds how far a chain may extend
  below the VAC carrying it; `0` forbids attenuation outright. Absent
  means attenuation is permitted as far as the depth ceiling allows.
- A link may lower a limit or set one where its parent set none, never
  raise one, so the effective limit is the strictest on the chain. A
  verifier MUST reject a chain in which any VAC lies more than n steps
  below an ancestor bearing n.
- It is deliberately not called `maxDepth`. The same name failing open in
  one credential and closed in another is a mistake waiting to be made by
  an implementer who has read only one of the two sections. The ceiling
  and this limit are separate controls and a chain must satisfy both.

A second gap surfaced alongside it: the VAC had no counterpart to the
VDC's third check. A valid chain shows authority was narrowed by parties
entitled to narrow it, not that the party now holding it is one the scope
will deal with — and since that party acts as itself, it may be one the
governing party has never encountered. A governing party MAY now require
a derived subject to independently qualify, and a verifier enforcing that
policy MUST reject a chain whose subject does not.

The agent example carries `maxAttenuation: 0`, which is what equipping an
agent ordinarily wants. Security item 15, the ZK chain predicate,
Governance Considerations, CONTEXT.md and the glossary follow.

title: State that a VAC is not a bearer credential
body:
State that a VAC is not a bearer credential

The VAC had no counterpart to the VDC's Invocation Binding. `audience`
was OPTIONAL and its absence documented as meaning any holder may present
the credential, so a VAC without one was a bearer credential and nothing
recorded that as a decision. Even with `audience` the field was
unenforceable: it named the DID that must present the VAC, but no rule
required a verifier to establish that the presenter controlled it.

This is sharper for a VAC than for a VDC because a chain is presented in
full on every use. A captured presentation is a captured chain, so
identifying a holder by possession alone would make every verifier a
distribution point for the authority it was shown.

It also closes an inconsistency the specification already asserted.
Relationship to Capability Models says the mechanics shared with ZCAP-LD
and UCAN are attenuation-only derivation, chains resolving to a
recognized root, and binding to a demonstration of key control at
invocation, and says the VAC's rules apply the same mechanics to
authority. The VAC applied the first two. The third was never written
down.

- A verifier MUST NOT accept a party as holding the authority unless it
  demonstrates control of the verification method for the presented VAC's
  `credentialSubject.id` at the time of the request.
- Where `audience` is present, the party that demonstrated control MUST be
  the DID it names. Key control establishes that the presenter is the
  subject; `audience` establishes that this subject is the one expected to
  be presenting here.
- Only the presented VAC's subject demonstrates anything. Requiring it of
  the links above would defeat attenuation, whose purpose is that the
  attenuating party is not in the loop when its agent acts.

How the demonstration is carried is left to the planned Trust Task
Protocols specification, as it is for a VDC. Security Considerations gain
bearer use, Conformance Target 3 gains the key-control rule, and the
`audience` schema text and the attenuation SHOULD point at the new
section.

title: fix(vocabulary): stop saying "disclosure" and "fact" on screen
body:
fix(vocabulary): stop saying "disclosure" and "fact" on screen

Three rendered strings still used words `design-docs/persona-vocabulary.md`
retires. The console is the reference implementation for that table, so
these are the copies every other surface is checked against — and one of
them had already been copied.

- The gated family's note said "a disclosure needs your approval each
  time". The TUI took the string verbatim when it ported the grouping and
  its own banned-word guard rejected it, which is how this was found: a
  guard in another repository catching a word this one's guard did not
  look for.
- The attribute editor's release explainer bound the approval to "that one
  disclosure". Same journey, and the table's phrase for it is *letting it
  leave*.
- The step-up approval card said "approve this disclosure" and described
  what was leaving as "N facts". `fact` is retired twice over — it asserts
  a truth a self-asserted value does not have, and `Facts` already names a
  *verified* policy input in the VTC ceremony engine, which is very nearly
  the opposite. The table's standing rule is to change it on sight, and
  this card is the holder's own screen: in that flow it is the only thing
  they read.

`disclosure` and `fact` join the render guard's banned list. Neither can
be a claim type, so any appearance in rendered text is prose and there is
nothing to whitelist — the distinction the list's header draws for
`profile`. The guard now also mounts the attribute editor, which carries
the longest stretch of prose in the persona family and was reachable by no
vocabulary check at all; both new patterns are exercised in the
non-vacuous test.

Left alone deliberately: every `Disclosure*` type, `personaDisclosureHistory`,
`disclosureId`, the disclosure triangle in the context tree, and the
refusal text in `page-task-policy.ts` — the table governs the words a
person reads, and is explicit that the spec's words stay in code, on the
wire, in audit records and in engineering discussion. The page-facing
error in `background.ts` stays too: its reader is a relying party, not the
holder.

title: vta-service-v0.25.0
body:
### Added

- **persona**: Say whether a link crosses a part of the holder's life ([#1342](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1342))

Serves the members added in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#408, published in
  trust-tasks-rs 0.18.10: `crossesFacets` and `facetIds` on a finding,
  `facetId` on each `sharedWith` location. This needs a floor of 0.18.10 —
  the spine validates OUTGOING responses, so under an older schema an analysis
  that fully succeeded would come back 500 `responseSchemaViolation` — and no
  longer moves one: main reached 0.18.11 while this sat open, which satisfies
  it. The bump this branch carried is dropped rather than resolved downward.

  **Severity is how linkable. Facets are whether the holder minds.** Nothing
  here touches `severity`, and that is the design rather than an omission. A
  value shared between two profiles in one facet still links them for anyone
  who sees both — the holder's filing changes nothing a counterparty can do —
  so softening severity on intent would report a false all-clear. What the
  facets add is a second axis: which of these findings the holder would
  actually want to act on.

  **Absent is unknown, not false.** `crosses_facets` is `Option<bool>` and is
  `None` when the holder keeps no facets, because `false` asserts these
  identities sit in one part of a life and an agent with no facets has made no
  such finding. `FacetIndex::any` is what carries that distinction, which is
  why the index is a struct rather than a map.

  **An unarranged profile is not a second facet.** Only distinct, named facets
  count toward a crossing. Counting "no facet" as one would make every holder
  who has arranged one part of their life and not the rest see a crossing on
  everything they own — the dismissal problem arriving from the other
  direction.

  `facet_index` is built once per analysis for the reason `disclosure_index`
  is: `analyze_correlation` with no `attributeId` walks the whole pool, and
  the per-finding shape re-lists every facet for every finding.

  The conformance witness now exercises the three new members rather than
  merely permitting them — they are the ones added last, and an outgoing
  member the embedded schema has not caught up with is a 500 on a call that
  succeeded.

  vta-persona 118/118 (6 new, one per rule above), vta-service lib 1063/1063,
  clippy --all-targets clean.

- **rooms**: Cut over to present/0.2 and issue-authority/0.2 ([#1365](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1365))

The consuming half of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#415 and #418, unblocked

  not take it: `affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.22.0` required 0.18, so pinning 0.19 put
  two `trust-tasks-rs` nodes in the graph and broke `vta-sdk` on `expected

  to 0.19 and 0.23.0.

  Taking it exposed pins that had drifted apart underneath: `vta-sdk` was on
  messaging-sdk 0.22 while `vta-service` and the e2e tests were on 0.21, and three
  `trust-tasks-rs` versions were resolving at once. All of it is now consolidated:
  the lockfile holds exactly ONE `trust-tasks-rs` and ONE `affinidi-messaging-sdk`,
  where before it held three of each.

  `rooms/keys/present` 0.1 -> 0.2 and `rooms/owner/issue-authority` 0.1 -> 0.2.

  `present`, 0.1's extra members are exactly the two nothing could honour; for

  1. The `issue-authority` witness carried no `validUntil` — a chain root with no

body:
> **Stacked on #29.** This branch is cut from `feat/vac-authority-credential`, because the section it changes exists only there. Until #29 merges, the diff against `main` shows #29's commits too; the change under review is the single commit `5833d4f`. Draft until #29 lands, at which point this rebases onto `main` and is ready.

## The gap

A VAC could not be taken back other than by waiting, and `validUntil` was only RECOMMENDED — so a VAC issued without one conferred authority that nothing could ever withdraw. The schema said as much in passing (*"authority that does not expire is authority nobody can withdraw by waiting"*) without requiring anything of an issuer.

The [[VDC]] section works the same problem carefully: `validUntil` REQUIRED, `credentialStatus` CONDITIONAL on a governing freshness window, revocation latency in Security Considerations, status lookups as a correlation surface in Privacy Considerations. The VAC section had none of it.

**The gap is worse for a VAC than for a VDC, which is why this is worth a PR rather than an editorial pass.** A VDC has a remedy the VAC does not: its verifier re-asks the permission question of the delegator at the time of the act, so withdrawing the delegator's own authority stops every delegate at once without touching a single credential. A VAC *is* that answer rather than a pointer to it. Nothing about the subject's current standing is consulted at verification, so expiry and revocation are the only remedies that exist.

## What this adds

**`validUntil` REQUIRED has moved to #29**, since a working draft should not publish a rule under which a conformant VAC confers authority nothing can withdraw. That leaves expiry as the sole withdrawal mechanism in #29, which is coherent standing alone, and this PR adds revocation on top of it. #29 carries an editor's note pointing here.

**`credentialStatus` is CONDITIONAL** on the freshness window the party governing the scope defines, mirroring the VDC rule.

**A new `### Withdrawal` subsection.** Expiry is the primary mechanism: it costs a verifier no network access, discloses nothing, and cannot fail open or closed, so it is the only withdrawal mechanism that survives the offline verification the VAC is built around. Only a VAC's issuer may revoke it — an attenuating holder revokes what it issued, the governing party revokes what it issued, neither reaches the other's directly.

**The verification rule is self-describing, which is the design decision here.** A verifier MUST check the status of every link that carries `credentialStatus` and MUST reject the chain if any is revoked; a link carrying none is evaluated on its validity period alone, and its absence is not a defect. The alternative — a status check per link — would have cost the VAC the property #29 spent the most text defending. Network cost now stays proportional to what a chain actually claims: one check for a long-lived root over short-lived attenuations, none where every link is short-lived. The two examples show exactly that contrast, the six-month root gaining a `credentialStatus` and the four-hour agent attenuation carrying none.

**Revocation cascades, and the section says so in both directions.** Revoking a VAC withdraws everything attenuated from it, transitively, whether or not the revoking issuer knows those derivations exist. That is what makes attenuation safe to permit without the governing party's involvement: it withdraws the whole tree in one act and needs no register of what its holder went on to issue. The converse is stated as plainly rather than buried — a chain whose links carry no status cannot show that an ancestor was revoked, so a verifier will accept an attenuation whose parent was revoked an hour ago. Offline verification bounds that exposure by the shortest `validUntil` in the chain; it does not remove it.

## Everywhere else the VDC's rules already reach

- **Attenuation** gains a SHOULD for short validity, since an attenuating holder is often a person, a device, or an agent rather than an operator of a status list, and may be unreachable when its grant needs taking back.
- **Relationship to the VDC** no longer claims the VAC chain is wholly offline. It is precommitted, with status on the links that carry it as the one live dependency. Overstating this was a small inaccuracy in #29 that this change would otherwise have made larger.
- **Security Considerations** gain items 19 and 20: revocation latency, and the cascade together with its invisibility where status is absent.
- **Privacy Considerations** gain item 14. Status on a root gives back part of what bearer-side presentation bought: whoever hosts the root's status list learns that a verifier checked it and when, so a governing party observes the *timing* of activity by agents and devices it never issued to and cannot see. One lookup for a whole chain rather than one per link, and timing rather than content — but it is the honest reason the section prefers short validity to status wherever re-issuance is available.
- **Governance Considerations** gain item 7, which is also the first VAC entry in that list: action vocabularies, the status mechanism, the freshness window, and whether status is required outright, are the governing party's to define.
- **Conformance Target 3** covers the status-checking rule alongside the chain rule.
- **CONTEXT.md** and the glossary entry follow.

## Not in scope, deliberately

**Resolved in #40, stacked on this branch.** The asymmetry below is settled there: the defaults should differ, and the control is an opt-out (`maxAttenuation`) rather than the VDC's opt-in `maxDepth`. Left here for the record.

**Attenuation is permitted by default; re-delegation is not.** A VDC prohibits re-delegation unless `maxDepth` explicitly authorises it (*"Setting `maxDepth` above 0 is the delegator's explicit authorisation to re-delegate; there is no other"*). A VAC permits attenuation unconditionally, capped at depth 8. That asymmetry may well be right — attenuation only ever narrows, and the cascade rule this PR states means a governing party can always withdraw the whole tree — but it is a deliberate difference that neither section argues for, and a governing party currently has no way to say "this authority is not attenuable". Worth settling separately; withdrawal is the control it leans on in the meantime, which is part of why this PR matters.

All `[[ref:]]` references, anchors, and JSON examples validated. Every commit carries a DCO sign-off.

* Define how authority is withdrawn from a VAC

A VAC had no way to be taken back other than waiting, and `validUntil`
was only RECOMMENDED, so a VAC issued without one conferred authority
that nothing could withdraw. The VDC section works the same problem
through a CONDITIONAL `credentialStatus` and a REQUIRED `validUntil`;
the VAC section was silent.

The gap is worse for a VAC than for a VDC. A verifier re-asks the
permission question of a delegator at the time of the act, so
withdrawing a delegator's own authority stops every delegate at once
without touching a credential. A VAC is that answer rather than a
pointer to it: nothing about the subject's current standing is consulted
at verification, so expiry and revocation are the only remedies there
are.

- `validUntil` is REQUIRED, as it is on a VDC and for the same reason.
- `credentialStatus` is CONDITIONAL on the freshness window the party
  governing the scope defines, mirroring the VDC rule.
- A new Withdrawal subsection states that expiry is the primary
  mechanism, that only a VAC's issuer may revoke it, and that a verifier
  MUST check the status of every link that carries one and MUST NOT
  treat its absence as a defect. Network cost stays proportional to what
  a chain claims: one check for a long-lived root over short-lived
  attenuations, none where every link is short-lived.
- Revocation cascades. Revoking a VAC withdraws everything attenuated
  from it, which is what lets a governing party withdraw derivations it
  never saw and never registered. The converse is stated as plainly: a
  chain whose links carry no status cannot show that an ancestor was
  revoked, so exposure is bounded by the shortest `validUntil` in the
  chain rather than removed.

Attenuation gains a SHOULD for short validity, since an attenuating
holder is often a person, device, or agent rather than an operator of a
status list. Relationship to the VDC no longer claims the chain is
wholly offline; it is precommitted, with status as the one live
dependency. Security Considerations gain revocation latency and the
cascade, Privacy Considerations gain the timing channel a root's status
list opens onto activity by agents the governing party never issued to,
Governance Considerations gain the VAC decisions, and Conformance
Target 3 covers the status rule. CONTEXT.md and the glossary entry
follow.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Address review: digest rationale, revocation pointer, computed parent

Three points from review on this PR.

The Digest Encoding rationale said the two chain references "do not need
the digest for safety", on the grounds that a verifier re-checks every
link. That holds for widening, which was the only failure the paragraph
had in view. Withdrawal's cascade makes the digest load-bearing for a
second reason: it binds a child to the exact parent it was derived from,
so an issuer that revoked a VAC and re-issued it under the same id
cannot silently revive the attenuations beneath it. Stated there, with
the existing re-derivation cost re-framed as the same property seen from
the other side.

Security item 2 sent verifiers to the trust registry for revocation
status. That predates the VDC and the VAC, both of which carry status in
the credential's own credentialStatus; the registry holds the policy
around it — which mechanism, the freshness window, whether status is
required at all — which is what Governance items 5 and 7 say. Reworded
so the two are not confused, with pointers to the VAC and VDC rules.

The attenuated example's parent was a placeholder while every other
digest in the document is computed, and this PR changes the root example
it is taken over by adding credentialStatus. Computed per Digest
Encoding over the root example as it now stands, and a sentence added
saying what it is a digest of.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Stop the digest rationale contradicting the withdrawal cascade

The Digest Encoding paragraph said the two chain references "do not need
the digest for safety" and then, two sentences later, that the digest is
what makes the withdrawal cascade hold without a register. Both were true
of different threats. Say which: the digest is not needed to stop a chain
widening, and it is needed to stop a child being re-parented onto a
re-issued parent.

Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>

title: vta-persona-v0.3.1
body:
### Added

- **persona**: Say whether a link crosses a part of the holder's life ([#1342](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1342))

Serves the members added in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#408, published in
  trust-tasks-rs 0.18.10: `crossesFacets` and `facetIds` on a finding,
  `facetId` on each `sharedWith` location. This needs a floor of 0.18.10 —
  the spine validates OUTGOING responses, so under an older schema an analysis
  that fully succeeded would come back 500 `responseSchemaViolation` — and no
  longer moves one: main reached 0.18.11 while this sat open, which satisfies
  it. The bump this branch carried is dropped rather than resolved downward.

  **Severity is how linkable. Facets are whether the holder minds.** Nothing
  here touches `severity`, and that is the design rather than an omission. A
  value shared between two profiles in one facet still links them for anyone
  who sees both — the holder's filing changes nothing a counterparty can do —
  so softening severity on intent would report a false all-clear. What the
  facets add is a second axis: which of these findings the holder would
  actually want to act on.

  **Absent is unknown, not false.** `crosses_facets` is `Option<bool>` and is
  `None` when the holder keeps no facets, because `false` asserts these
  identities sit in one part of a life and an agent with no facets has made no
  such finding. `FacetIndex::any` is what carries that distinction, which is
  why the index is a struct rather than a map.

  **An unarranged profile is not a second facet.** Only distinct, named facets
  count toward a crossing. Counting "no facet" as one would make every holder
  who has arranged one part of their life and not the rest see a crossing on
  everything they own — the dismissal problem arriving from the other
  direction.

  `facet_index` is built once per analysis for the reason `disclosure_index`
  is: `analyze_correlation` with no `attributeId` walks the whole pool, and
  the per-finding shape re-lists every facet for every finding.

  The conformance witness now exercises the three new members rather than
  merely permitting them — they are the ones added last, and an outgoing
  member the embedded schema has not caught up with is a 500 on a call that
  succeeded.

  vta-persona 118/118 (6 new, one per rule above), vta-service lib 1063/1063,
  clippy --all-targets clean.

- **persona**: Serve persona/facet — the holder's arrangement of their identity ([#1338](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1338))

Implements the three tasks specified in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#405, published
  in trust-tasks-rs 0.18.9.

  A holder who uses this model for a while ends up with twenty profiles, and a
  flat list of twenty is a list nobody reads. A facet is the arrangement over
  them — "Work", "Home", "Play" — and it is agent-scoped, like the pool and
  the profiles it groups.

  **An arrangement, not a container.** Nothing is stored inside a facet, and
  `delete_facet` touches no profile and no attribute. There is no cascading
  form because there is no cascading form of the idea: a grouping that could
  take its members with it is a folder, and a holder who reads it as a folder
  is right to be afraid of it. `releasedFaces` reports what now belongs
  nowhere, which is what a screen needs to say what it will look like
  afterwards. `deleting_a_facet_deletes_nothing_it_named` pins it.

  **Membership lives on the facet.** A `facet_id` on `Attribute` would be the
  obvious alternative and is the wrong shape: `attribute/put` REPLACES, and a
  well-behaved consumer does not hold the values it would have to resend —
  `attribute/list` withholds `sensitivity: high` plaintext unless asked by
  name. It would either request every sensitive value the holder owns to
  perform an arrangement that has nothing to do with values, or send a put
  without one and destroy them.

title: vti-rooms-dtg-v0.2.0
body:
### Fixed

- **rooms**: A presentation is bound to its presenter — and dtg-credentials 0.6 → 0.9.1 ([#1356](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1356))

* fix(rooms): bind a presentation to its presenter, not to the host

  `pnm-cli rooms --host-did …` could never work. Every request it made was
  refused as `WrongAudience`, and omitting the flag "worked" only by
  skipping the check it exists to perform — so the flag's two states were
  broken and unprotected.

  `audience` is not who a presentation is addressed to.
  `dtg_credentials::authority::verify_chain` compares it to the PRESENTER —
  "the leaf must be presentable by whoever is presenting it" — so it is
  holder binding, and its whole job is to make a captured presentation
  worthless to whoever captured it. Filled with the host's DID it named a
  party no presenter can ever match.

  The value to bind to was already named a few lines away: `RoomSigner`'s
  doc says "a room request is signed by the party the presentation was
  minted for". This passes exactly that. There is no unbound case left, so
  the warning about one goes, and `--host-did` keeps its real job of naming
  the document's recipient.

title: vti-rooms-v0.2.0
body:
### Added

- **rooms**: Traces, and a response type for the single-record read ([#1368](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1368))

A commitment lets a reader catch a host that equivocates. A trace proves a
  particular record sits under the root that host just asserted. This serves
  them — and fixes the conformance defect that adding them uncovered.

  Implements trust-tasks-tf#419, released as trust-tasks-rs 0.19.1.

  `rooms/records/get` has never conformed to its published schema. Both hosts
  answered a read by serialising `vti_rooms::Record` — the *storage* record — and
  adding `dataCommitment` to whatever came out:

      "c2VhbGVk" is not of type "object";
      Additional properties are not allowed
      ('author','epoch','nonce','pinned','status','updatedAt' were unexpected)

  It survived because `vti_rooms::wire`'s rule — every wire type appears in
  tests/schema_conformance.rs — can only be applied to types that exist. A
  response that was never a type had no line to be missing from, and a storage
  record reached the wire because nothing stood between them. The consumer is not
  hypothetical: `@openvtc/pnm-core`'s `roomsRecordsGet` is typed on the generated
  payload, so a caller reading `sealed.ciphertext` got `undefined` from a live
  host, with a green type-check on both sides.

  The leaf preimage was not reproducible either. `leaf_hash` canonicalised the
  storage record, so every root it produced was unreachable by any reader:
  `updatedAt` is unix seconds in storage and RFC 3339 on the wire, `epoch` and
  `nonce` are flat in storage and inside `sealed` on the wire, and `epoch`
  serialises as `null` on an open room where the wire has it absent. Survivable
  while the only use was comparing two roots from the same build; not survivable
  once a trace has to be computable by someone else.

- **rooms**: Hosts compute and serve the data commitment ([#1351](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1351))

* fix(rooms): a commitment is a DigestMultibase, not bare hex

  Owed from #1346. The spec that landed with it
  (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#411) types `dataCommitment` as the
  framework's `DigestMultibase`, and the helper shipped emitting hex.

  Bare hex hard-codes SHA-256 into the wire contract, which is precisely what
  `DigestMultibase` exists to prevent: multihash names the algorithm in-band,
  so moving off SHA-256 later is a change of value rather than another schema
  revision. `0x12 0x20` then the digest, base58btc with the `z` prefix — the
  same shape `sealed_transfer::bundle_digest_multibase` already produces, so
  the two agree by construction rather than by memory.

  `from_multibase` refuses anything that is not a sha2-256 multihash. A
  commitment is what a comparison turns on, so silently accepting an algorithm
  this build cannot compute would turn "these two roots differ" into "these
  two roots are not comparable" without saying which.

  Two tests, both about the encoding being a contract rather than a detail: a
  commitment decodes to the 34-byte multihash and round-trips, and bare hex, a
  foreign algorithm, a truncated digest and non-multibase are each refused.

  The tree, the leaves and the proofs are untouched — this is the wire
  boundary only.

- **rooms**: A browser can be a room member ([#1347](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1347))

* feat(rooms): a `host` feature, so a room's member half reaches wasm

  `vti-rooms` already had two halves and no name for them: `vta-service`
  imports `mls`/`sealed`/`wire` and nothing else, while `vtc-service`,
  `room-host` and `vti-rooms-dtg` import `storage`/`authz`/`audit`. This
  names the second half `host`, on by default, and makes `vti-common`
  optional behind it.

  `vti-common` describes itself as server-side infrastructure and pulls
  axum, fjall and tokio, so it was the whole of what kept a room's member
  code off `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. With it optional,
  `--no-default-features --features mls` builds there — which is what lets
  a browser hold a room's keys itself rather than ask an agent to. See
  `docs/05-design-notes/data-rooms-demo-site.md`.

  The member half needed **no source changes** to get there. That is a
  property of `error.rs`, which deliberately does not use
  `vti_common::error::AppError` because key material is not a service's
  concern; a decision made for its own reasons that paid for itself here.

  `lifecycle` is deliberately left ungated: only hosts consume it today,
  but it needs nothing from `vti-common`, and a member computing a room's
  lifecycle state to explain it on screen should not need a host's
  dependencies.

  Three things about the wasm plumbing, each of which reports as a
  `compile_error!` that reads like an unsupported target:

  - OpenMLS 0.9 has a first-class `js` feature (`web-time` for the
    `SystemTime` wasm lacks, plus getrandom's JS backend). Declared
    per-target rather than as a feature of this crate, so building for
    wasm just works — verified wasm-only: `web-time` appears in the wasm
    tree and not the native one.
  - There are two getrandom majors in the graph. The 0.4 is ours; the 0.2
    arrives transitively under `openmls_rust_crypto` via RustCrypto's
    elliptic-curve stack, so no feature declared here could reach it.
    `getrandom_02` is a feature shim, not a dependency this crate calls.
  - With both declared per-target, **no `RUSTFLAGS` are needed** — the
    `wasm_js` feature alone selects the backend.

  CI gains two steps in the `features` job: clippy on the member half with
  no host, and a wasm32 `--lib` check, so neither property rots silently.

  `vta-service` now takes `default-features = false`: a VTA holds room keys
  and is never a room's host, so it no longer compiles one.

  * feat(rooms): vti-rooms-wasm — a data room's member half, in a browser

  The MLS group, record sealing and the epoch key chain, compiled to
  WebAssembly, so a tab can *be* a member rather than drive an agent that
  is one. `vti-rooms` supplies all of it; this crate is only the boundary,
  and its job is deciding what crosses.

  **Secrets do not cross.** Everything returned is public — a KeyPackage,
  ciphertext, an epoch number — with one deliberate exception: the
  snapshot, which is key material because OpenMLS persists a group through
  its provider rather than as a value. It goes in IndexedDB and nowhere
  else; the docs say so at the method, since it is the one thing here a
  caller could reasonably mishandle.

title: vti-common-v0.18.2
body:
### Changed

- **sdk**: Move the Trust-Task proof verifier down from vti-common ([#1340](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1340))

Pure move plus re-exports; no behaviour changes. It exists so the next
  change can be small: `VtaClient` needs to verify the responses it receives,
  and the verifier it needs already exists one layer up where a client cannot
  reach it.

  `vti-common` was the right home while services verifying their *inbound*
  requests were the only consumer. A client verifying its *replies* is the
  same operation over the same document shape, and `vta-sdk` is the layer both
  can see.

  **The part worth not duplicating is the verification-method resolver.**
  Resolving one looks trivial and is not: a DID document may name its methods
  absolutely (`did:webvh:…:glenn#key-0`) or relatively (`#key-0`), while a
  proof always names them absolutely, so a resolver accepting only the
  spelling it expects refuses perfectly good documents from conforming peers.
  A second copy would drift, and drift in a verifier means refusing honest
  documents or accepting dishonest ones. Writing that copy is what this move
  avoids.

  Behind a new `proof-verify` feature rather than `client`, because
  `vti-common` takes `vta-sdk` with `default-features = false` and must not
  acquire reqwest to keep verifying. It adds no dependency to `vti-common` —
  that crate already depended on `affinidi-data-integrity` and the DID
  resolver directly. `client` enables it: a client that cannot verify its
  replies is the gap being closed.

  The resolver rides in the feature deliberately. Verification is only as good
  as the party it resolves — a `did:key` signer needs no I/O, and a
  `did:webvh` one, which is what a real agent is, cannot be verified without
  resolving its document.

  Call sites that used the module path (`vti_common::auth::di_proof::…`) now
  use the flat re-export, so there is one canonical path rather than an alias
  to go stale. Two doc comments naming the old location updated with them.

  `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` clean; `vta-service --lib` 1063
  passed; `vta-sdk` + `vti-common` suites pass, including the four resolver
  tests that moved with the code.

title: vta-sdk-v0.35.0
body:
### Added

- **rooms**: Cut over to present/0.2 and issue-authority/0.2 ([#1365](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1365))

The consuming half of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#415 and #418, unblocked
  by affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#784.

  `trust-tasks-rs` 0.19 carries both new spec versions, but this workspace could
  not take it: `affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.22.0` required 0.18, so pinning 0.19 put
  two `trust-tasks-rs` nodes in the graph and broke `vta-sdk` on `expected
  MediatorAcl, found a different MediatorAcl`. TDK #784 moved the messaging family
  to 0.19 and 0.23.0.

  Taking it exposed pins that had drifted apart underneath: `vta-sdk` was on
  messaging-sdk 0.22 while `vta-service` and the e2e tests were on 0.21, and three
  `trust-tasks-rs` versions were resolving at once. All of it is now consolidated:
  the lockfile holds exactly ONE `trust-tasks-rs` and ONE `affinidi-messaging-sdk`,
  where before it held three of each.

  `rooms/keys/present` 0.1 -> 0.2 and `rooms/owner/issue-authority` 0.1 -> 0.2.
  Both 0.1s are retired upstream. Neither is dual-accepted, deliberately: for
  `present`, 0.1's extra members are exactly the two nothing could honour; for
  `issue-authority`, accepting 0.1 means accepting a request with no `validUntil`,
  which is the thing 0.2 exists to refuse.

  The hand-rolled `validUntil` guard in `room_owner.rs` is deleted. 0.2 makes the
  member REQUIRED, so the generated payload types it as a `DateTime` and the
  envelope schema rejects a request without one before dispatch. Same rule, one
  layer up, which is where a shape constraint belongs.

  `every_witnessed_task_round_trips_through_its_generated_types` refused two
  witnesses that had been green for as long as they existed:

  1. The `issue-authority` witness carried no `validUntil` — a chain root with no
     expiry, the exact request 0.2 forbids, and one this service could have sent.
  2. The `present` witness carried `"audience": "did:key:z6MkHost"` — a HOST DID,
     the precise shape #414 reported as impossible to satisfy, since the field
     named the party that had to PRESENT the credential.

  `room_oracle` emitted `membership` and `authority[]` as JSON **objects**;
  `AuthorityPresentation` types both as strings, and the host's opener reads
  base64url or bare JSON text. So the oracle's output could not deserialize at a
  host at all — `rooms/keys/present` had never worked end to end. It went unseen
  because 0.1's response typed `presentation` as an opaque object; 0.2 names the
  shared component, which turned a runtime refusal nothing exercised into a type
  error. The oracle now serialises each credential. That is the first half of
  have caught all three of these years earlier.

- **sdk**: A no-I/O verifier resolves did:peer too ([#1364](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1364))
- **sdk**: The client verifies the replies it receives ([#1341](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1341))

Completes the arc #1334 and #1335 began. Both services sign their responses;
  until now nothing checked one, so the signature was decorative. This is the
  surface that matters most — the CLI, cierge and the services all dispatch
  Trust Tasks through `VtaClient`.

  A reply is bytes off a socket. Nothing else in this path establishes who
  produced them: the transport proves a connection, and over REST not even
  that beyond TLS to a host name. Without the proof an intermediary can
  rewrite an ACL listing, flip a policy decision, or answer for an agent that
  never spoke, and every check downstream passes — because the checks
  downstream are about shape.

  Two checks, and the second is the one easy to omit: the proof must verify,
  **and its proven signer must be the agent this client is talking to**. A
  proof by somebody else's key verifies perfectly well, so skipping the
  binding turns "signed by somebody" into "signed by the agent". The expected
  signer is `ClientIdentity::vta_did`, which the client already holds.

  A client with no identity does not verify, because there is nothing to bind
  against — such a client cannot produce a conforming request either and is
  refused at the agent for a missing `recipient`. A loopback client likewise:
  its sink answers ahead of the transport and returns a value rather than a
  signed document.

  Error documents are exempt, from the specification rather than for
  convenience: `trust-task-error`'s own proof requirement is RECOMMENDED
  (SPEC §8.1), so demanding one would make every conforming refusal
  unreadable, including the ones carrying the reason a caller needs.

  `trusting_unsigned_replies()` is a staging control, not a preference. An
  agent that predates #1334/#1335 sends nothing to verify, so a client
  upgraded ahead of its agent would refuse every answer; this exists so that
  ordering can be chosen rather than endured. It weakens the check to almost
  nothing while set — an attacker who can rewrite a reply can also strip its
  proof — so a present proof is still verified and still bound.

  The resolver is built once per client and shared by clones. A
  `DIDCacheClient` is a cache; one per call would defeat it.

- **persona**: Serve persona/facet — the holder's arrangement of their identity ([#1338](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1338))

Implements the three tasks specified in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#405, published
  in trust-tasks-rs 0.18.9.

  A holder who uses this model for a while ends up with twenty profiles, and a
  flat list of twenty is a list nobody reads. A facet is the arrangement over
  them — "Work", "Home", "Play" — and it is agent-scoped, like the pool and
  the profiles it groups.

  **An arrangement, not a container.** Nothing is stored inside a facet, and
  `delete_facet` touches no profile and no attribute. There is no cascading
  form because there is no cascading form of the idea: a grouping that could
  take its members with it is a folder, and a holder who reads it as a folder
  is right to be afraid of it. `releasedFaces` reports what now belongs
  nowhere, which is what a screen needs to say what it will look like
  afterwards. `deleting_a_facet_deletes_nothing_it_named` pins it.

  **Membership lives on the facet.** A `facet_id` on `Attribute` would be the
  obvious alternative and is the wrong shape: `attribute/put` REPLACES, and a
  well-behaved consumer does not hold the values it would have to resend —
  `attribute/list` withholds `sensitivity: high` plaintext unless asked by
  name. It would either request every sensitive value the holder owns to
  perform an arrangement that has nothing to do with values, or send a put
  without one and destroy them.



### Changed

- **sdk**: Move the Trust-Task proof verifier down from vti-common ([#1340](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1340))

Pure move plus re-exports; no behaviour changes. It exists so the next
  change can be small: `VtaClient` needs to verify the responses it receives,
  and the verifier it needs already exists one layer up where a client cannot
  reach it.

  `vti-common` was the right home while services verifying their *inbound*
  requests were the only consumer. A client verifying its *replies* is the
  same operation over the same document shape, and `vta-sdk` is the layer both
  can see.

  **The part worth not duplicating is the verification-method resolver.**
  Resolving one looks trivial and is not: a DID document may name its methods
  absolutely (`did:webvh:…:glenn#key-0`) or relatively (`#key-0`), while a
  proof always names them absolutely, so a resolver accepting only the
  spelling it expects refuses perfectly good documents from conforming peers.
  A second copy would drift, and drift in a verifier means refusing honest
  documents or accepting dishonest ones. Writing that copy is what this move
  avoids.

  Behind a new `proof-verify` feature rather than `client`, because
  `vti-common` takes `vta-sdk` with `default-features = false` and must not
  acquire reqwest to keep verifying. It adds no dependency to `vti-common` —
  that crate already depended on `affinidi-data-integrity` and the DID
  resolver directly. `client` enables it: a client that cannot verify its
  replies is the gap being closed.

  The resolver rides in the feature deliberately. Verification is only as good
  as the party it resolves — a `did:key` signer needs no I/O, and a
  `did:webvh` one, which is what a real agent is, cannot be verified without
  resolving its document.

  Call sites that used the module path (`vti_common::auth::di_proof::…`) now
  use the flat re-export, so there is one canonical path rather than an alias
  to go stale. Two doc comments naming the old location updated with them.

  `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` clean; `vta-service --lib` 1063
  passed; `vta-sdk` + `vti-common` suites pass, including the four resolver
  tests that moved with the code.



### Fixed

- **rooms**: A presentation is bound to its presenter — and dtg-credentials 0.6 → 0.9.1 ([#1356](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1356))

* fix(rooms): bind a presentation to its presenter, not to the host

  `pnm-cli rooms --host-did …` could never work. Every request it made was
  refused as `WrongAudience`, and omitting the flag "worked" only by
  skipping the check it exists to perform — so the flag's two states were
  broken and unprotected.

  `audience` is not who a presentation is addressed to.
  `dtg_credentials::authority::verify_chain` compares it to the PRESENTER —
  "the leaf must be presentable by whoever is presenting it" — so it is
  holder binding, and its whole job is to make a captured presentation
  worthless to whoever captured it. Filled with the host's DID it named a
  party no presenter can ever match.

  The value to bind to was already named a few lines away: `RoomSigner`'s
  doc says "a room request is signed by the party the presentation was
  minted for". This passes exactly that. There is no unbound case left, so
  the warning about one goes, and `--host-did` keeps its real job of naming
  the document's recipient.
