title: feat(rooms/owner/anchor): a room writes its own state where a host cannot
body:
Everything else in this family produces values a **host** asserts. An anchor is the one statement a host does not make, cannot forge, and cannot show two members two versions of — because witnesses co-sign the `did:webvh` log entry it rides, so it is **singular**.

Implements the shape decided in VTI's `data-rooms-epoch-anchoring.md` (§3a, a typed service entry) with the corrections from VTI#1378.

## Three attacks die together

- **A rolled-back room.** A host serving an older state is indistinguishable from a room that has not moved, because every value it serves is its own. An anchor pins where the room *was*.
- **A forked group.** The MLS epoch authenticator is derived independently by every member and by **no host**. A member whose own differs from the anchored one is in a different group than the room says it has.
- **Equivocation about contents.** `dataCommitment` is evidence only against a copy the host did not choose — and an anchored root is that copy **for every member at once**, needing neither a gossip channel rooms deliberately lack nor durable state in an agent.

## The owner holds one of the three values it publishes

This decides the shape of the task, and an earlier design note got it wrong before it got it right.

`rooms/epoch/mint` answers `{roomId, epoch}` — **no watermark**, and no reason there should be one: minting acts on the *epoch*, while the watermark and the commitment are facts about the room's **records**, which live at the host. So an anchor is assembled from a read, and all three head values **MUST** come from **one** response: a root and a version from two reads can straddle a write, and the pair is then individually correct and jointly false.

**That the owner anchors a value the host gave it looks circular and is not.** The owner does not vouch for the root — it did not compute the tree. The anchor makes the root singular and witnessed. That is Certificate Transparency's arrangement exactly: the log operator's own signed tree head is what gets published, and gossip is what makes equivocation fatal.

## The rule that will look wrong at first glance

A recipient **MUST NOT** refuse to anchor when reconciliation fails.

An owner that withheld an anchor from a suspect room would leave it with **no witnessed statement at all** — which is precisely the position a misbehaving host benefits from. So: publish what the host claimed, and record in `reconciled` that it had already been caught claiming something inconsistent. `false` is a finding, not a failure.

## `notWitnessed` is a refusal, not a warning

An entry nobody co-signed is the controller's own word. Publishing one produces something that *looks* like an anchor and carries none of the property — **worse than its absence**, because a member checking it would believe they had checked something.

It also constrains a configuration that is otherwise legal: a room whose DID is **host-controlled** cannot anchor honestly, since the party being checked would be writing the check.

## The cost, stated where an operator will read it

`vta/webvh/dids/update/1.0` needs nothing added. But its own description says supplying a `document` **rotates the DID's update key** and refreshes its pre-rotation commitments — so each anchor is a witnessed update *and* a rotation, with witness co-signing each time.

**Cadence is therefore an operational decision rather than only a freshness one.** A room anchoring on every write would rotate its own DID's update key on every write. It also brushes succession: a transfer landing between anchors aims at a key that has moved.

## Privacy, said plainly

An anchor is **public by design** — that is what makes it singular. It discloses that a room exists, roughly how much it holds, and how often it moves. On a `private` room that is real and it is what the tier can afford: it says nothing about *who* is in the room or *what* any record says. A room for which even the shape is sensitive should anchor rarely or not at all, **knowingly**.

Also kept true deliberately: to the host, this read is indistinguishable from any other. A host that could tell an anchor was imminent could serve a flattering answer to that one read.

## Checks

- Scaffolded with `npm run new-spec`
- `npm run build` — clean
- `npm run check-bindings` — **422** specifications against 422 TypeScript and 417 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test --workspace` — green
- Both generators re-run and committed

  those checks a FIRST-TIME reader can make — no history, no peer, no gossip —
  and the only place a **rollback** is visible: a host serving a state older than
  the room's own published statement is `behind`, and nothing else in this family
  catches that. `notChecked` is deliberately not a synonym for `none`: one says
  the room published nothing, the other says nobody looked.
- **`anchorCadence`** on `rooms/create`, which makes silence legible. A room that
  says `renewal` and has not anchored in ten epochs is telling a member
  something, and a member who did not know what to expect could not have noticed.
  Deliberately not a duration: a room promising "daily" would make a claim its
  owner's availability cannot keep, and a member comparing against a clock would
  read an owner's holiday as a host's misbehaviour.

title: feat(manager): the console opens forms where you clicked, and worlds hold faces
body:
The console's persona surface, reworked. Five things landed together and the
first is the one people actually reported.

## An editor opened ~1700px below the fold

Every form on the identity map rendered at the *end* of the JSX — after the
attributes band, the faces, the divider, the contexts and the selection strip.
On a populated wallet that put the first field around 1700px down a 2450px
scroller whose `scrollTop` never moved, with focus left on the button. Pressing
**Add an attribute** changed nothing a person could see.

Measured in a real tab, on the shipping bundle:

```
mainScrollTop: 0     mainClientH: 866     mainScrollH: 2454
fieldTopWithinMain: 1722    fieldBelowFoldBy: 856
activeElement: BUTTON
```

The list and worlds screens had the opposite failure — they *replaced* the list
with the form, so the thing being worked on vanished. Three surfaces, three
behaviours, none of them "a form appeared where I clicked".

`popover.tsx` is now the one behaviour: positioned `fixed` against the anchor
(measuring against a scroll container means knowing *which* container, and being
wrong glues the popover 800px from its trigger), focus moved into the first
field, `Escape` closing it and handing focus back. `Editing` therefore carries
the element it was opened from — not decoration, the mechanism.

## The Worlds tab is gone; worlds are bubbles on the map

A grouping you cannot see beside the things it groups is a list of names, and
arranging faces on one screen while looking at them on another is the same act
performed twice. Faces sit inside tinted world bubbles and move by dragging.

The world's hue lives on the bubble's **ground** — a surface face cards do not
use — so a card's border still means selection and reach, its stripe still means
claim family, and its pills still mean status. A fourth categorical channel that
costs none of the three already spent.

`movePlan` (`world-model.ts`, tested) owns the two writes a move needs **and
their order**: `facet/put` replaces, and the agent refuses to place a face that
is already placed, so the source is rewritten without it before the destination
is rewritten with it. Every write carries live membership via `seedMembership` —
a put echoing a dangling id is refused `unresolvedReference` and leaves the world
permanently uneditable (the defect that shipped as #216).

The delete confirm moved intact. It still says what **survives** before what
goes, which is the most load-bearing copy in the feature now that a bubble
literally looks like a folder.

## Released is a peer view, not a footer

The disclosure history — what your agent has handed over, across every context —
used to render below *every* view, reachable only by scrolling past the whole
map. It answers a question the size of the other two. The toggle is now
**Map / List / Released**.

## Cards are closed until you select one

An attribute card draws its type and one of three words — `shown`, `hidden`,
`held back` — and never the value; selecting it expands it in place. Thirteen
values drawn before anyone asked for one was both the density complaint and a
shoulder-surfing surface.

The three states stay three. *hidden* is a value in hand behind a mask;
*held back* is one the agent never sent. Collapsing them is exactly the defect
the reveal path exists to end, reintroduced one layer up.

The detail strip **no longer renders the value at all** — two `AttributeValue`s
for one attribute is two *Show* buttons and two reveal states, and the second is
always the one that stops being maintained.

## A hand-drawn icon set, and a rail that folds to it

The four sections under *Authority & graph* are all "security", so any four
shield-and-padlock variants collapse into each other at 18px — the size they are
actually rendered at. They are drawn as four different **kinds of thing**: a
person beside a list, a check, a fork, a clock. Rooms is a vault rather than a
door, because a door outline is an empty rectangle at that size and a room is
storage whose host cannot read it. DIDs is a tag — an identifier that resolves.

Collapsed, the icons carry their act's colour; the 3px edge alone cannot hold
four groups together, which is the same reason the expanded rail colours its
headings. Labels return as tooltips on hover and focus. State is remembered in
`localStorage`, `⌘\` toggles it.

Context **standing is a shape** now, not only a hue: filled / dashed / struck
through. `identified` is a real state and a reader who cannot separate green
from amber still reads three different shapes.

## Also

- Link edges draw only once something is selected — `reachOf` has no answer to
  draw before that, so at rest they were twenty low-contrast curves crossing the
  page answering nothing.
- The whoami banner folds four never-changing fields behind a disclosure and
  keeps the two an operator acts on. An authority **error** is never folded.
- Panel explanations clamp to their opening claim with a *Why this matters*
  toggle — clamped by line count, because splitting prose on full stops breaks
  on `did:webvh:…` and on `0.3`.
- The context column filters at eight contexts or more. A filter that matched
  nothing gets its own sentence, never the "ask for a grant" one.
- The New key form asks for a context instead of rendering itself with a dead
  button. Only for the missing *context* — a form withheld for missing authority
  would say the agent has no such feature.

## One rule that is load bearing

`[role="dialog"] * { min-width: 0 }` in `manager-theme.css`. Grid and flex items
default to `min-width: auto` and refuse to shrink below their content, so one
long help paragraph sized the editors past the popover and clipped them at the
border. A rule rather than a prop because the editors are several layers of
nested inline-styled grids.

## Tests

530 pass. New: `movePlan`'s ordering and dangling-id handling; the popover's
dialog / focus / Escape behaviour (layout cannot be asserted in happy-dom, so
these assert the three things that are true of a popover and false of a form
appended to the page).

**13 existing render tests were rewritten, not deleted.** They asserted values
were on screen; a card must now be opened first. Every property they pinned —

title: fix(manager): pin the detail strip, so a selection's actions are reachable
body:
Follow-up to #220, from a report against it: *"editing a face still shows a form
at the bottom vs the popup box?"*

## What was actually wrong

The popover was working. The **button that opens it** was not reachable.

Selecting anything on the identity map renders the detail strip, and the strip
is the last element of a document two or three screens tall — so its *Edit* and
*Delete* sat below the fold. Clicking a face looked like it had merely
highlighted something, and the form only appeared once you had scrolled to the
bottom and found the button.

Measured on the shipping bundle, with a face selected:

```
strip top: 1466    viewport height: 997
```

That is the same defect #220 fixed for editors, arrived at from the other
direction.

## The fix

The strip is now `position: sticky; bottom: 0` inside the pane.

- **`sticky`, not `fixed`** — it belongs to the pane, so it must not hang over
  the rail or the context column, and it must stop at the pane's own bottom edge
  rather than the window's.
- **Capped at `46vh` and scrollable** — a context with many personas makes a
  tall strip, and a detail panel that eats the map it describes is worse than
  one that scrolls.
- **It carries its own dismiss.** "Click the card again" stopped being an
  acceptable only-way-out the moment the panel became persistent.

Fixing it here fixes it for attributes, faces *and* contexts at once, rather
than by adding an Edit button to three kinds of card.

## Tests

Two rendered, both on the reported path:

- selecting a face and pressing *Edit* opens a dialog — end to end, the exact
  thing that was reported
- the strip's dismiss clears the selection

`position: sticky` itself cannot be asserted in happy-dom, which has no layout —
so these pin the behaviour it unblocked rather than the property, which is the
same choice the popover tests make and for the same reason.

532 pass. Verified in a real Chrome tab against the built bundle: the strip sits
inside the viewport on selection, and *Edit* opens the face editor as a popover
flipped above the anchor, since the anchor is near the bottom of the screen.

title: test(room-host): pin the reply threading a mediator cannot check for you
body:
Stacked on #1373.

That PR closed with the listener's round trip uncovered, because the fixture mediator is a `did:peer` and a host cannot mint a resolvable identity against one. On reflection that framing was too pessimistic.

The part of the listener that was *wrong* is not the packing or the routing — those are library code with their own tests. It is **the parsing of an inbound frame and the framing of the answer**, and neither needs a mediator.

## The regression, pinned

`unwrap_request` is now a pure function: protocol plus payload in, document plus thread out. Over TSP the thread is the **document's own `id`**, never the frame's — that is the only id the caller ever saw. Threading on `frame.message.id` produces a reply that is sent, accepted by the mediator, and matched by nobody: the caller waits out its full timeout while the answer sits unclaimed, and *neither end logs anything wrong*.

Verified by putting the defect back:

```
test a_tsp_request_threads_on_the_documents_own_id ... FAILED
  assertion `left == right` failed: the caller correlates on the id it put on
  the document, and saw no other
    left: "the-frames-own-id"
   right: "urn:uuid:1111…"
```

## Also covered

- DIDComm threads on the **envelope** id instead, because that is what its caller correlates on. The two carriers reading it from different places is why this is one function rather than an `if` at the call site.
- A DIDComm message under any other type is ignored, not answered — a problem report (answering one feeds the mediator's policy back into the loop and spins), an un-unwrapped forward, and the near-miss: a caller sending the **task** type instead of the binding's envelope type. That is the mistake the shared `ENVELOPE_TYPE` constant exists to prevent, and a conformant peer drops it *silently*, so it has to drop here too.
- A payload with no id to correlate by is refused. Replying on a thread nobody sent is the same failure as replying on the wrong one.
- `tsp_reply` puts the thread where a caller looks and leaves the document untouched — a caller ignoring the wrapper reads the same bytes the other two carriers deliver.

## Still open

The full round trip through a mediator remains uncovered, for the reason in #1373. This covers the class of bug that actually occurred, which is the part a mediator would not have checked for you anyway.

title: feat(manager): the console opens forms where you clicked, and worlds hold faces
body:
feat(manager): the console opens forms where you clicked, and worlds hold faces

Five things reached the live console together, and the first is the one
people reported.

**An editor opened ~1700px below the fold.** Every form on the identity map
rendered at the end of the JSX — after the attributes, the faces, the divider,
the contexts and the selection strip — so on a populated wallet the first field
landed near the bottom of a 2450px scroller whose `scrollTop` never moved, with
focus left on the button. Pressing "Add an attribute" changed nothing anyone
could see. The list and worlds screens had the opposite failure: they replaced
the list with the form, so the thing being worked on vanished. `popover.tsx`
gives all of them one behaviour — anchored to the control that summoned it,
focus moved into the first field, Escape closes and hands focus back.

**The Worlds tab is gone; worlds are bubbles on the map.** A grouping you
cannot see beside the things it groups is a list of names, and arranging faces
on one screen while looking at them on another is the same act done twice.
Faces now sit inside tinted world bubbles and move by dragging. The world's hue
lives on the bubble's *ground* — a surface face cards do not use — so a card's
border still means selection and reach, its stripe still means claim family,
and its pills still mean status. `movePlan` owns the two writes a move needs and
their order: `facet/put` replaces, and the agent refuses to place a face that is
already placed, so the source is rewritten before the destination.

**"Released" is a peer view, not a footer.** The disclosure history — what your
agent has handed over, across every context — used to render below every view,
reachable only by scrolling past the whole map. It answers a question the size
of the other two, so it sits beside them.

**Cards are closed until you select one.** An attribute card draws its type and
whether the value is `shown`/`hidden`/`held back`, never the value; selecting it
expands it in place. Thirteen values drawn before anyone asked for one was both
the density complaint and a shoulder-surfing surface. The three states stay
three: "hidden" is a value in hand behind a mask, "held back" is one the agent
never sent, and blurring them is the defect the reveal path exists to end. The
detail strip no longer renders the value at all — two `AttributeValue`s for one
attribute is two Show buttons and two reveal states.

**A hand-drawn icon set, and a rail that folds to it.** The four sections under
Authority & graph are all "security", so any four shield-and-padlock variants
collapse into each other at 18px; they are drawn as four different kinds of
thing instead — a person beside a list, a check, a fork, a clock. Rooms is a
vault rather than a door, because a door outline is an empty rectangle at that
size and a room is storage its host cannot read. Collapsed, the icons carry
their act's colour: the 3px edge alone cannot hold four groups together.

Also: link edges are drawn only once something is selected (`reachOf` has no
answer to draw before that); the whoami banner folds four unchanging fields
behind a disclosure and keeps the two an operator acts on; panel explanations
clamp to their opening claim with a "Why this matters" toggle; the context
column filters once there are eight or more; and the New key form asks for a
context instead of rendering itself with a dead button.

The `[role="dialog"] *` min-width rule is load bearing: grid and flex items
default to `min-width: auto` and refuse to shrink below their content, so one
long help paragraph sized the editors past the popover and clipped them.

Tests: `movePlan`'s ordering and dangling-id handling; the popover's dialog,
focus and Escape behaviour; the worlds tests ported onto the two surfaces that
replaced the pane, delete-confirm copy intact. The harness gained the bare
window globals (`addEventListener`, `innerHeight`, …) that any browser
component uses, and a `key` helper.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.19.3
body:
### Added

- **rooms/keys**: Read and browse — a member's agent fetches, checks, and opens ([#426](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/426))

The last unbuilt piece of the rooms surface, and the missing half of verified
  reads. Both were the same piece, as `data-rooms-read-through.md` works out: the
  console cannot address a host (its carrier drops the recipient, deliberately),
  and a `dataCommitment` is inert without a party that keeps the last root. The
  member's own agent is the answer to both.

  `rooms/keys/read` is four acts that today belong to three parties — mint the
  presentation, ask the host, check what came back, open it. The fourth decides
  where the other three go: the epoch key never leaves the key holder, so a member
  doing the middle two themselves holds a half-verified record in between and
  still makes two more round trips.

  What the recipient checks, and each is stated because each has a way of being
  skipped:

  1. the reply is signed by the host that was ADDRESSED — the proof verifies and
     the proven signer binds to the `host` named, or it is a reply from somebody
     else;
  2. the trace reaches the commitment served BESIDE IT, with the leaf preimage
     reassembled from the response itself — never a root kept from an earlier read;
  3. the root against what the agent has seen at this `headVersion`, which is the
     comparison no other party on the member's side can make.

  **A verdict is never an error**, and `ReadVerification` says so in the shared
  schema rather than in two places. A member's own agent refusing a record because
  the HOST misbehaved punishes the member for somebody else's act, and locks them
  out of the room holding the records that would show what happened. The
  consequence belongs on the write path. `priorRoots` is REQUIRED so an agent that
  keeps no history has to answer `notChecked` rather than omit the question —
  which is not a synonym for `noneHeld`: one says nothing was found, the other
  says nothing was looked for.

  `rooms/keys/browse` carries the check that only a listing can do. A reader
  cannot recompute a root from a listing — a leaf commits to a whole record and a
  listing returns a projection — but it can COUNT, and a host that omits a record
  while committing to a tree holding it contradicts itself inside one exchange,
  with no second party and no anchor. The condition is narrow and stated: no
  prefix, no `sinceVersion`, and `complete: true`. `complete` exists because a
  page bound and a withheld record produce the same shorter array, and a consumer
  that could not tell them apart would either cry wolf on every paged listing or
  learn to ignore the one that mattered.

  Both specs say the part that decides whether any of this works: *serve reads,
  refuse writes* is a rule nobody would guess, so an adverse verdict MUST be
  surfaced in words naming what was observed rather than as a status colour. A
  member who dismisses an icon here is a member who later reads a refused write as
  their own agent malfunctioning, and a detection attributed to the wrong party is
  worse than no detection.

  Scaffolded with `npm run new-spec`. Both generators re-run: 421 specifications
  against 421 TypeScript and 416 Rust modules, all agreeing; `cargo test
  --workspace` green.

title: docs(rooms): the root memory is keyed by room, which buys a fourth comparison
body:
The one question `data-rooms-read-through.md` §5 left open, and the one I said was worth deciding *before* the implementation rather than during it. Working it out turned a storage question into a design one.

## Key it by room, not by host

This is the part worth not getting wrong. **A room's tree at version `V` is a fact about the room**; who served it is not part of that fact. Keying by `(room, host)` files two hosts of one room in two drawers and never compares them — and a room may deliberately have several, a mirror serving reads while its primary takes writes.

Keyed by room, a member who reads the same room from two of its hosts gets the comparison for free. Two hosts reporting **different roots at one `headVersion`** is exactly as damning as one host disagreeing with itself: one of them is wrong. A mirror that merely *lags* reports a lower `headVersion` and is correctly not compared at all.

## That is a fourth comparison

`rooms/records/list` lists three ways a root becomes evidence: another member's root, the same member's earlier root, the witnessed anchor. The first needs a gossip channel rooms deliberately lack — on a `private` room a member list is the thing being withheld — and the third is unbuilt.

***Another host of the same room*** needs neither. No gossip, no anchor, no second member — only a caller who names a different `host`, which `rooms/keys/read` already lets them do, because nothing maps a room to its host and the caller always names one.

It falls out of keying by room. It would have been invisible if the memory had been keyed the other way, which is the reason to write this down rather than leave it to whoever types the storage key.

## How much

**A small map from `headVersion` to root**, most-recent-N by version, plus the highest `headVersion` ever seen.

One slot is weaker than it looks in a specific way, and stronger than it looks in another. It **does** catch a host that alternates: `(V, A)` then `(V, B)` is same version, different root, caught — and caught again on the way back to `A`. What it misses is a head that **advances and then goes backwards**:

```
(V, A)  →  (V+1, X)  →  (V, B)
```

With one slot the agent holds `V+1` and has nothing to compare `V` against. That is the mirror case and the rollback case — the two this exists for — so one slot is not enough.

N = 16 versions is more history than a member reads across in a session and costs a few hundred bytes. The highest-ever value is separate because it answers a question no single pair can: *has this room gone backwards?*

## Bounded by membership, not by time

Dropped when the member leaves the room. It carries no record content, but it **is** a record of when this member read this room, and an agent that keeps that after the membership ends is keeping a diary of a room its principal can no longer open.

Documentation only. Closes the last open question in the read-through note, so §5's two questions are both answered.

title: docs(rooms): the owner cannot anchor from what it holds, and an anchor rotates a key
body:
Two corrections to `data-rooms-epoch-anchoring.md` §6, now that the shape is decided and it is a note somebody will build from. Both checked against the specifications rather than reasoned about — the note asserted the opposite for two days.

## The owner holds one of the three values it publishes

§6 said the work "sits entirely on the owner's side". **Publishing does; assembling does not.**

`rooms/epoch/mint`'s response is `{roomId, epoch}` — no version watermark, and no reason there should be one: minting acts on the epoch, while the watermark is a fact about the room's *records*, which live at the host. The data commitment lives there too, and always did.

So the owner must read the room's head from the host, presenting its own credentials like any other member. That makes the anchor **downstream of the read-through work** rather than parallel to it — [`rooms/keys/browse`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/426) is that read, and its response carries `head.dataCommitment`, `head.headVersion` and `head.recordCount` from one snapshot.

**That the owner anchors a value the host gave it looks circular and is not.** The owner is not vouching for the root — it did not compute the tree. The anchor makes the root *singular and witnessed*: a host that claimed root `R` at version `V` in a witnessed log cannot claim `R'` at `V` to anybody else. That is exactly Certificate Transparency's arrangement, where the log operator's own STH is what gets published and gossip is what makes equivocation fatal.

An owner **SHOULD** still reconcile before anchoring. A complete unfiltered browse whose `verification.count` reads `short` is a host contradicting itself, and anchoring that is publishing a number already known to be wrong.

## Publishing needs no new task — and costs a key rotation

`vta/webvh/dids/update/1.0` already exists and takes the new `document` plus a witness configuration, so an anchor can be published today with nothing added.

What that task's own description says, and what changes how §5's cadence question should be read:

> Supplying this **ROTATES the DID's update key** and refreshes its pre-rotation commitments, as a parallel consequence of the change.

So an anchor is not a cheap append. Each one is a witnessed DID update **and** a rotation of the room DID's update key, with witness co-signing and a fresh pre-rotation commitment each time.

That is manageable — the owner's VTA holds the key and does this for every webvh DID it controls — but it makes **cadence an operational decision rather than only a freshness one**. A room anchoring on every write would be rotating its own DID's update key on every write. It also brushes §10 succession: a transfer landing between an anchor and its successor is aiming at a key that has moved. Not a new problem (every webvh update has it), but worth knowing before scheduling anchors densely.

§5's cadence bullet now cross-references §6.2.

Documentation only.

Four acts that today belong to three parties — mint the presentation, ask the host, check what came back, open it. The fourth decides where the other three go: **the epoch key never leaves the key holder**, so a member doing the middle two themselves makes two more round trips and holds a half-verified record in between.

What the recipient checks, each stated because each has a way of being skipped:

1. **The reply is signed by the host that was _addressed_.** The proof verifies *and* the proven signer binds to the `host` named — otherwise it is a reply from somebody else. Unsigned or misattributed is `hostRefused`, never a success with a caveat.
2. **The trace reaches the commitment served _beside it_**, with the leaf preimage reassembled from the response itself (exactly `CommittedRecord`). Never a root kept from an earlier read.
3. **The root against what the agent has seen at this `headVersion`** — the comparison no other party on the member's side can make. A tab does not outlive itself; a CLI keeps nothing.

## A verdict is never an error

`ReadVerification` lives in `rooms/_shared` so this is said once rather than twice.

**None of these findings fails the task**, including the ones reporting a host caught out. A member's own agent refusing a record because the *host* misbehaved punishes the member for somebody else's act — and locks them out of the room holding the records that would show what happened. The consequence belongs on the **write** path, where continuing to hand material to a party you have caught is what compounds the damage.

`priorRoots` is **REQUIRED**, so an agent that keeps no history has to answer `notChecked` rather than omit the question. That is deliberately not a synonym for `noneHeld`: **one says nothing was found, the other says nothing was looked for.**

The read spec carries a worked example of `trace: "verified"` beside `priorRoots: "conflict"`, because reading that as a contradiction is the mistake the shape exists to prevent. The trace proves the record sits under *the root the host just asserted*; the conflict says that root is not the one this host asserted for the same state before. **A host serving a private view of a room can build a consistent tree over it and trace every record in it perfectly.**

## `rooms/keys/browse` — the check only a listing can do

A reader **cannot** recompute a root from a listing: a leaf commits to a whole record and a listing returns a projection without the body. But it can **count**. A host that omits a record while committing to a tree that holds it contradicts itself **inside one exchange** — no second party, no anchor, no other member. The example in the spec catches a host on a `priorRoots: "noneHeld"` first read.

The condition is narrow and a consumer MUST respect it: no `prefix`, no `sinceVersion`, and `complete: true`. Everything else is `notComparable`, which will be the common answer.

**`complete` exists because a page bound and a withheld record produce the same shorter array.** A consumer that could not tell them apart would either cry wolf on every paged listing or learn to ignore the one that mattered. `limit` is the page size to ask for, never a cap on the result.

## The part that decides whether any of this works

Both specs say it: *serve reads, refuse writes* is a rule **nobody would guess**. So an adverse verdict **MUST** be surfaced in words naming what was observed — *two different record sets, both claimed as this room at version N* — rather than reduced to a status colour. A member who dismisses an icon here is a member who later reads a refused write as their own agent malfunctioning, and **a detection the member attributes to the wrong party is worse than no detection.**

## Shape notes

- **`plaintext` vs `cleartext`**, exactly one present, mirroring `rooms/records/get`. Carried differently on purpose: a member ought to be able to tell that this room's host can read what they just read.
- **`cannotOpen` is its own error**, naming the epoch, with `rooms/keys/backfill` as the repair. A member told only "could not read" cannot tell a missing epoch key from a host refusing.
- **A `retracted` record is an answer, not a failure.** The tombstone, its version and its verdict are returned.
- **`host` is named by the caller** — nothing maps a room to its host, a room is portable, and a room may have more than one. Presenter binding is what makes that safe: naming a host transfers no standing, only *sight* of the presentation.

## Checks

- Scaffolded with `npm run new-spec` rather than copied from a neighbour
- `npm run build` — clean
- `npm run check-bindings` — **421** specifications against 421 TypeScript and 416 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test --workspace` — green
- Both generators re-run and committed

## Next

VTI implements them on the `rooms/keys/backfill` pattern (six census sites each). Per the design note's sequencing, `read`/`browse` may ship **verifying-and-reporting** before the durable root memory exists — `priorRoots: "notChecked"` is the honest answer until it does — but a write task may not ship *refusing* without it, since a refusal that lasts only as long as the process that noticed is not a refusal.

title: feat(rooms)!: a tree head, so two roots can be compared at all
body:
Implements [trust-tasks-tf#422](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/422), released as `trust-tasks-rs` 0.19.2. It is the last implementation piece of verified reads: a reader now gets a root, **the state that root describes**, and a path from their record to it.

## Why a root alone was not enough

The commitment shipped as a bare root, and the prose claimed a host showing two members two different roots "cannot claim a transient". It can: a room moves on every put, curate and retraction, so the host answers *there was a write between your reads* and nothing contradicts it. The comparison the whole member exists for could not be performed by anybody.

Certificate Transparency does not have that problem because **a signed tree head is a root _and a size_**. This family shipped the root and dropped the rest.

## `merkle::TreeHead`

```rust
pub struct TreeHead {
    pub root: Hash,
    pub record_count: u64,
    pub head_version: u64,
}
```

One type, produced by one function from one pass over one set — and that is a **correctness requirement rather than tidiness**. `head_version` read from the room's own `next_version` counter would be a *second* read, and two reads are not a snapshot:

```
member A:  scan records → S1                    … counter → V+1
member B:              [write lands]  scan → S2 … counter → V+1
```

Both report `headVersion: V+1` over different trees. Two honest members, two different roots, one version — which reads as **equivocation and is not**. Ordering the reads the other way admits the mirror case; only taking both from one set closes it. A false accusation discredits the mechanism rather than the host, which is the worst outcome this machinery has.

The type makes it structural rather than remembered:

```rust
pub fn of(record: &Record, head: Option<&TreeHead>, trace: Option<InclusionProof>) -> Self
```

A caller cannot serve a root without its head, or a head from a different moment, because there is no way to spell it.

## What moved

| before | after |
|---|---|
| `storage::data_commitment` | `storage::tree_head` |
| `storage::data_commitment_with_trace` | `storage::tree_head_with_trace` |
| host helper `room_commitment` | `room_head` |
| `merkle::commit_records` | now `tree_head(...).map(\|h\| h.root)` — one implementation of the walk |

Both hosts serve `dataCommitment`, `recordCount` and `headVersion` on **both** read paths, from the head they already computed.

## Tests

`the_head_reports_the_set_it_committed_to` pins the part that would otherwise rot:

```rust
assert_eq!(head.head_version, get_room(&rooms, "r1").await.unwrap().next_version - 1,
    "with no erasure the committed maximum is the room's last assigned version");
```

The two agree — and the test exists to say *why we do not read the counter*, so that nobody later simplifies it into one. It then retracts a record and checks the count stays at 3 (a tombstone is still a record) while the head advances and the root moves.

Conformance gains assertions that a served head carries all three, and that a host with no tree asserts **none** of them — `dataCommitment`, `recordCount` and `headVersion` all absent, alongside `pinned: false` being spelled by absence.

## The erasure corollary

A host that *erases* a record — as distinct from retracting it, which leaves a tombstone in the tree — moves the root without necessarily moving `head_version`. I checked rather than assumed: `vti_rooms::storage::purge_record` exists and has **no caller outside its own tests**, so nothing exposes it. Documented on `TreeHead` as something a family that exposes one would owe another look.

## Checks

- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace` — green
- Verified twice: against a local `[patch.crates-io]` while 0.19.2 was in the release queue, then again against the published crate with the patch removed.

`!` for `vti-rooms`' own API, which is alpha and has no external consumers.

## Next

With this in, verified reads is complete as a mechanism. What remains is what turns a root into evidence rather than the host's own assertion:

- the **witnessed anchor** — now unblocked, shape 3a decided (`data-rooms-epoch-anchoring.md`);
- the **agent's root memory**, and the rule that a client which catches a host **serves reads and refuses writes** — decided, and it makes the memory a prerequisite of the refusal rather than an optional second increment, since a refusal that lasts only as long as the process that noticed is not a refusal.

title: docs(rooms): record the three decisions, and what each one obliges
body:
Both open questions in the rooms design notes are answered. Recorded where the reasoning lives rather than only in a conversation — which is exactly what left the anchoring note marked "open question, not a plan" for two days, by its own admission ("it was blocking in a conversation rather than in the repository").

## One: a client that catches a host serves reads and refuses writes

It was asked **twice, in two vocabularies** — `data-rooms-read-through.md` §5 (two roots at one `headVersion`) and `data-rooms-epoch-anchoring.md` §5 (an anchored authenticator that does not match the member's own) — and it is one question. Answered once, in both notes.

Reading is how a member gathers the evidence, and the records that would prove what happened are inside the room a refusal would lock them out of — by their own agent, over somebody else's act. Writing to a host you have caught is what compounds the damage.

Two consequences the notes now carry, because neither falls out of the rule by itself:

**The refusal is the mechanism; the flag is not.** "Serve reads, refuse writes" is a rule nobody would guess, so a member who hits it and is shown only a failure reads it as their agent malfunctioning — and a detection the member blames on the wrong party is worse than no detection. The refused write owes an explanation in the room's own words, at the point of refusal: *two different record sets, both claimed as this room at version N*. A pill will not carry that. It is a copy problem before it is a code problem.

**The agent's root memory is a prerequisite, not a second increment.** §6 originally sequenced it after the tasks as an additive extra. It cannot be: a refusal that lasts only as long as the process that noticed is not a refusal — an agent that catches a host, restarts, and happily writes has a detection and no consequence. A read task may ship verifying-and-reporting without durable `(headVersion, root)` state; a write task may not ship *refusing* without it. §6's sequencing is amended.

Both rejected answers are kept rather than deleted, with why.

## Two: anchoring takes shape 3a

A typed service entry. §3b and §3c stay, because a shape chosen with its rejected siblings deleted is one nobody can argue with later.

This unblocks something outside §9 as well. The data commitment now shipped on both read paths offers three comparisons, and **the anchor is the only one needing neither a gossip channel rooms deliberately lack nor durable state in a member's agent** — so until it exists, a root is comparable only by an agent that has read the same room before. The commitment rides the same `serviceEndpoint` slot this note settles, as `data-rooms-verified-reads.md` §3.2 anticipated; it is one more member of that map, not a second mechanism.

## Three: `vti-rooms` has no external consumers

Not a note change. Recorded because it is the standing answer to whether its API breaks need batching — they do not, while it is alpha, and three consecutive PRs have relied on that being true without ever having asked.

## Also

§14 items 7 and 9 follow. Item 7 additionally gains tt#422: a root names no state, so two of them differing is a room that moved as readily as a host that equivocated — which the shipped prose had got wrong, and which is fixed by `headVersion` and `recordCount`.

Documentation only. Stacks alongside #1375, which implements the tree head.

title: test(rooms): an invitation's window, which neither gate was checking
body:
There are two copies of the room-invitation gate — `vta-service`'s and the browser member's in `vti-rooms-wasm` — and they were both a test short, on the same clause.

Five clauses covered on both sides. The **validity window** exercised on neither.

## Why this one is worth catching

It is the quiet failure. A regression here breaks nothing visibly: expired invitations simply keep working, and the party who would care — whoever issued one and expected it to lapse — has no way to find out. Contrast the forgery clause, whose absence at least lets an attacker in loudly.

A room invitation is given an hour on the grounds that it is *an act somebody is about to perform rather than a standing entitlement*. That reasoning is only true while the window is enforced.

## Covered now, on both sides

- **expired** — `validUntil` in the past.
- **not yet valid** — `validFrom` in the future.
- **no `validUntil` at all**, asserted as *accepted*. The credential type permits it, so a room can issue one that never lapses; a verifier refusing it would be overruling the issuer's decision rather than checking it.

Verified by deleting the expiry clause from each gate in turn — the new test is the only one that fails, on both sides:

```
test tests::an_invitation_outside_its_window_is_refused ... FAILED
test operations::room_invitation::tests::an_invitation_outside_its_window_is_refused ... FAILED
```

## Why it went untested

The fixture could not express it. Both `an_invitation` helpers hardcoded a good window, so no test could have written the case even if someone had thought of it. Each now has an `an_invitation_valid` taking the window explicitly — which is the whole reason a reachable clause was never reached.

## The duplication itself

Still there, and still worth closing, but not here. Sharing the gate needs `vti-rooms-dtg` to build for `wasm32`, and it cannot: it takes `AppError` from `vti-common`, `AppError` implements `IntoResponse`, and so it is axum-bound by design (`vti-rooms-dtg` currently fails to compile for wasm on tokio's net stack). Splitting that is a workspace-wide change to the central error type, not something to fold into a test PR.

## Testing

`vti-rooms-wasm` 10 passed; `vta-service --lib` 1070 passed, 0 failed. Clippy clean.

title: fix(room-host): refuse to mint an identity no member could resolve
body:
I set out to add the integration test #1369 was missing, and found a defect in the thing I was trying to test.

## A host could come up unreachable and say it was fine

A `did:peer:2` carries its services **inside** the identifier, so advertising a mediator costs roughly that mediator's DID again, once per service. Two services:

| mediator | host DID | resolvable? |
|---|---|---|
| `did:webvh` (production, and the demo) | ~460 bytes | yes |
| `did:peer` | ~1685 bytes | **no** — every `DIDCacheClient` refuses over 1000 |

The host minted it, logged that it was reachable, and was not. And neither end says why: the member fails its websocket connect as `isActive? command timed out` (reads as a hang), the mediator answers `403 authcrypt requires sender public key` (reads as a key problem). Only `affinidi_did_authentication` logs the real reason, on one side.

This workspace has been here before — CHANGELOG, *"Watch the DID size"*, where the transport harness hit the identical trap — and closed it by asserting the length at mint. Same fix: the host now refuses to start, names the limit and what to do about it, and leaves nothing half-written on disk to be loaded next time.

## CI was building none of it

The listener is behind a non-default feature, so `cargo test --workspace` skipped it: **not tested, not even compiled.** A workspace change could have broken it silently. That is precisely the hole the transport harness sat in ("CI now **runs** the harness — `transport-harness` is not a default feature").

A Feature-combos step now runs `cargo test -p room-host --features didcomm`. Tested rather than only checked, deliberately: the one bug this module has had was a reply threaded on the wrong id, which compiles perfectly.

## What is covered, and what still is not

`tests/carrier.rs` runs against a real `TestMediator` and asserts the failure lands where somebody can act on it, plus the ordinary case: a `did:webvh` mediator leaves a host inside the limit, the identity survives a restart (a member's saved address names it), and pointing it at a different mediator refuses rather than advertising where it no longer listens.

**The round trip through the listener still has no automated cover**, and the reason is in the file: the fixture mediator is itself a `did:peer`, so a host pointed at it cannot mint a resolvable identity — the very thing this PR asserts. Covering it needs a fixture with a short DID. The path has been exercised by hand against a live `did:webvh` mediator over both carriers.

`HostIdentity` also gains a hand-written `Debug`: `expect_err` wants one, and a derived one prints the secrets — a log line, a panic message and a test failure being exactly where key material must not appear.

one and a derived one would print the secrets — a log line, a panic
message and a test failure being exactly where key material must not
appear.

**And CI never built any of this.** The listener is behind a non-default
feature, so `cargo test --workspace` skipped it entirely: not tested, not
even compiled. That is the hole the transport harness sat in too. Now a
Feature-combos step runs its tests — tested rather than checked, because
the bug this module has already had was a reply threaded on the wrong id,
which compiles perfectly.

The round trip through the listener still has no automated cover, and the
reason is in `tests/carrier.rs`: the fixture mediator is itself a
`did:peer`, so a host pointed at it cannot mint a resolvable identity —
which is the very thing being asserted here.

* test(room-host): pin the reply threading a mediator cannot check for you

#1373 closed with the round trip uncovered, because the fixture mediator
is a `did:peer` and a host cannot mint a resolvable identity against one.
That framing was too pessimistic: the part of the listener that was
*wrong* is not the packing or the routing — those are library code with
their own tests — it is the parsing of an inbound frame and the framing
of the answer. Neither needs a mediator to test.

So `unwrap_request` is now a pure function: protocol plus payload in,
document plus thread out. The bug it had is pinned by a test that fails
when reintroduced — over TSP the thread is the **document's own id**,
never the frame's, because that is the only id the caller ever saw.
Threading on the frame's produces a reply that is sent, accepted by the
mediator, and matched by nobody: the caller waits out its whole timeout
while the answer sits unclaimed, and neither end logs anything wrong.

Verified by putting the defect back: two tests fail, and they fail saying
what is wrong rather than where.

Also covered: DIDComm threads on the envelope id instead, since that is
what its caller correlates on; a message under any other type is ignored
rather than answered — including a caller sending the *task* type instead
of the binding's envelope type, which is the near-miss the shared
`ENVELOPE_TYPE` constant exists to prevent and which a conformant peer
drops silently; and a payload with no id to correlate by is refused,
because replying on a thread nobody sent is the same failure as replying
on the wrong one.

The mediator round trip is still uncovered and still for the same reason.
This covers the class of bug that actually occurred.

title: fix(room-host): refuse to mint an identity no member could resolve (#1373)
body:
fix(room-host): refuse to mint an identity no member could resolve (#1373)

Setting out to test the mediator listener found a defect in it instead.

A `did:peer:2` carries its services **inside** the identifier, so
advertising a mediator costs roughly that mediator's DID again, per
service. Against the `did:webvh` production uses, a host lands around 460
bytes. Against a `did:peer` mediator it lands at about 1685 — and every
`DIDCacheClient` refuses a DID over 1000 before it parses it.

The host came up regardless, logged that it was reachable, and was not.
Neither end says why: the member fails its websocket connect as
`isActive? command timed out`, which reads as a hang, and the mediator
answers `403 authcrypt requires sender public key`, which reads as a key
problem. Only `affinidi_did_authentication` logs the real reason, on one
side.

The workspace has been here — CHANGELOG, "Watch the DID size" — and closed
it by asserting the length at mint. Same here: the host now refuses to
start, names the limit and what to do about it, and leaves nothing on
disk to be loaded next time.

one and a derived one would print the secrets — a log line, a panic
message and a test failure being exactly where key material must not

title: docs(rooms): a room's DID names its mediator, never its host
body:
`vta-sdk/templates/room.json` said a room is portable because you "re-point its service endpoint and the room has moved". That points at a mechanism the document does not have — a room's DID names its **mediator**, and nothing maps a room to a host at all.

The data-rooms design note flagged this as its one genuine nit (§4.1, and delivery-sequence item 3) precisely because it had misled that design on its first pass: the reading it invites is that the service endpoint *is* the host pointer, so resolving a room DID ought to yield somewhere to send records.

## It is a wrong pointer, not a stale one

A room may be registered with more than one host — a mirror serves reads while its primary takes writes. So a host pointer in the document would not merely go out of date; it would be incorrect while everything was working. `rooms/owner/register/0.1` and `rooms/keys/backfill/0.1` both require the caller to name the host, and both say why.

Portability actually comes from the room issuing its own credentials: a host authorizes room operations against what the room issued, never against its own records, so a member names a different host and nothing is reissued. That is what the sentence was reaching for, and it is now what it says — with a pointer to the two specs that carry the reasoning.

## Also

Marks the two delivery-sequence rows this closes:

- **item 3** — done, this change.
- **item 8** — superseded by §10.3. A reader following the table would otherwise build `rooms/join/*` as a Trust Task family, which that section explains is the wrong shape: a Trust Task is an instruction to your own agent, and a would-be member is a stranger asking an owner to decide.

Description text only — no schema change, no field added or removed. `vta-sdk` builds and its 73 template tests pass; nothing asserts on the wording.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.19.2
body:
### Specifications

- **rooms/records/list**: A root names no state, so give it a tree head ([#422](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/422))

`dataCommitment` shipped as a bare root, and the section explaining what it is
  worth ended:

      A host that shows two members two different roots for the same room has
      been caught, and cannot claim a transient.

  That is false. A room moves — every put, curate and retraction changes the tree —
  so two roots taken at two moments differ for the most ordinary reason there is. A
  host shown to have served two different ones answers *there was a write between
  your reads*, and with a bare root nothing contradicts it. The comparison this
  member exists for could not be performed by anybody.

  The error came from taking half of the analogy the same paragraph draws.
  Certificate Transparency does not have this problem because **an STH is a root
  and a tree size**; this family shipped the root and dropped the rest.

  So two members travel with it, both from the snapshot the root was taken over:

  - `headVersion` — the room's highest assigned record version. A version advances
    on exactly the mutations that change the tree, so it names the *state* the root
    describes. Two roots at the same `headVersion` that differ is a host caught,
    with no write to attribute the difference to; two at different ones are two
    moments and a reader must draw nothing from them.
  - `recordCount` — how many records the room held, tombstones included. A reader
    cannot recompute the root from a listing (a leaf commits to a whole record and
    a listing returns a projection), but it can **count**: a host that omits a
    record from a complete unfiltered listing while committing to a tree holding it
    contradicts itself inside one response, with no second party and no anchor.

  Both OPTIONAL in exactly the sense the root is — a host maintaining no tree
  asserts none of it. A host serving `dataCommitment` SHOULD serve both, and a
  reader receiving a root without them MUST NOT compare it against another root.
  Such a root is still usable against a witnessed anchor, where the epoch pins the
  state, which is why it is not simply refused.

  A host can understate both together. That is the point rather than a hole: the
  omission stops being silence and becomes a specific claim about how many records
  the room holds and how far it has been written — which any other member's view,
  and any writer's signed put acknowledgement (vti #1334/#1335), contradicts
  directly. Making an omission attributable is the whole of what this machinery
  buys; it never claimed to make one impossible.

  Not a timestamp: a time is host-asserted and unverifiable, and two roots a second
  apart are not evidence of anything while two roots at one version are.

  `checkCommittedRecordMirror` — added last change — caught both new members on the
  first build and named the two ways to resolve it. That is the guard doing the job
  it was written for, on a question nobody would have got from reading two files.



  Amended after checking how a host would actually compute it: `headVersion` is
  the highest version among the records the root **covers**, derived from the same
  set, and NOT read from the room's own `next_version` counter.

  The two agree for any host that has never erased a record. They are not
  interchangeable, because a root and a counter are *two reads*, and two reads are
  not a snapshot. A write landing between them labels a root with a version from a
  different moment — so two honest members end up holding roots over different
  trees under one version, which reads as equivocation and is not. **A false
  accusation discredits the mechanism rather than the host**, which is the worst
  outcome available here, and it is the same reasoning that put the root and its
  trace in one scan.

  Ordering the two reads does not help, in either direction: whichever is taken
  first, a write in the gap admits a pair that is individually correct and jointly
  false. Only deriving both from one read closes it.

  Stated corollary: a host that **erases** a record — as distinct from retracting
  it, which leaves a tombstone in the tree — moves the root without necessarily
  moving this value. `vti_rooms::storage::purge_record` exists and today has no
  caller outside its own tests, so nothing exposes it; a family that exposes one
  owes this definition another look.

title: spec(rooms/records/list): a root names no state, so give it a tree head
body:
`dataCommitment` shipped as a bare root. The section explaining what it is worth ended with a sentence that is **false**:

> A host that shows two members two different roots for the same room has been caught, and cannot claim a transient.

A room moves. Every put, curate and retraction assigns a new version and changes the tree, so two roots taken at two moments differ for the most ordinary reason there is. A host shown to have served two different roots answers *there was a write between your reads*, and with a bare root **nothing contradicts it**. The comparison this member exists for could not be performed by anybody — not by two members, not by one member over time.

The error came from taking half of the analogy the same paragraph draws. Certificate Transparency does not have this problem because **an STH is a root _and a tree size_**. This family shipped the root and dropped the rest.

## The two members

Both computed from the snapshot the root was taken over, on both read responses.

**`headVersion`** — the room's highest assigned record version. A version advances on exactly the mutations that change the tree, so it names the **state** the root describes.

| observation | verdict |
|---|---|
| two roots, **same** `headVersion`, different | host caught — there is no write to attribute the difference to |
| two roots, different `headVersion` | two moments; a reader must draw nothing from them |
| a root with **no** `headVersion` | not comparable to another root at all |

**`recordCount`** — how many records the room held, tombstones included. A reader cannot recompute the root from a listing (a leaf commits to a whole record; a listing returns a projection without the body — established in #419), but it can **count**. A host that omits a record from a complete, unfiltered listing while committing to a tree that holds it now contradicts itself *inside one response*, with no second party and no anchor involved.

The count is over the **room, never the page** — the same rule and the same trap as the root. It is only comparable against a listing read to the end with no `prefix` and no `sinceVersion`; against a filtered one it is a discrepancy the reader manufactured.

## Optional, and what a bare root is still good for

Both OPTIONAL in exactly the sense the root is: a host maintaining no tree asserts none of it. A host serving `dataCommitment` **SHOULD** serve both, and a reader receiving a root **without** them **MUST NOT** compare it against another root.

It is not simply refused because a bare root retains one real use: the **witnessed anchor**, where the epoch pins the state, so all members are comparing roots taken over the same thing by construction. That is the line — the head members are what the *peer* and *over-time* comparisons need.

## Yes, a host can lie about both

That is the point rather than a hole. The omission stops being **silence** and becomes a specific claim about how many records the room holds and how far it has been written — which any other member's view contradicts, and which any writer's **signed put acknowledgement** (vti #1334/#1335) contradicts directly, since `headVersion` is the same counter `expectedVersion` and `sinceVersion` ride on. Making an omission *attributable* is the whole of what this machinery buys; it never claimed to make one impossible.

**Not a timestamp.** A time is host-asserted and unverifiable. Two roots a second apart are not evidence of anything; two roots at one version are.

## The guard from #419 earned its keep immediately

`checkCommittedRecordMirror` failed on the first build after I added the members, naming both and both ways to fix:

```
- specs/rooms/_shared/0.1/room.schema.json: the rooms/records/get response carries
  'recordCount' but CommittedRecord does not define it — the preimage is stated to be
  that response minus dataCommitment, trace, ext, so this member is either part of the
  leaf (add it to CommittedRecord) or a verification member (add it to
  NON_COMMITTED_RESPONSE_MEMBERS in this script, and say so in the prose).
```

They are verification members, so the list and the prose both moved. That is a question nobody would have got right from reading two files.

## Checks

- `npm run build` — 419 specs, clean
- `npm run check-bindings` — 419 specs against 419 TS and 414 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test --workspace` — green
- both generators re-run and committed

Additive: no existing document changes validity (the `dependentRequired` entries only constrain documents carrying the new members).

## Next

VTI serves them — `Room::next_version` is already the head, and `data_commitment_with_trace` already does the single scan where the count comes free. That rides on top of #1368, which is in flight.

title: docs(rooms): what building the demo site changed
body:
The design note predicted the shape of a browser member. Two of its conclusions did not survive contact with a running one.

Kept as an added **§10** rather than edits, for the reason the note itself gives for keeping §4.1's wrong turn: the reasoning that turned out wrong is the useful part, and a reader arriving fresh will make the same mistakes. §4 now carries a pointer so nobody reads the stale conclusions without the correction.

## §4.2's premise was wrong

The note says a browser tab "has no DIDComm address and no inbox". The first half is false — a tab can mint a `did:peer:2`, connect to a mediator, and be addressed there for as long as it is open.

The conclusion survives, and that is the interesting part: the ceremony still has to invert, but **because a tab cannot be addressed *between* sessions**, not because it cannot be addressed. An owner pushing a Welcome to a closed tab has pushed it nowhere, at an address that will never exist again.

The distinction matters beyond the demo. "Cannot be reached" implies a browser member needs a permanent agent somewhere. "Cannot be reached between sessions" means it needs a way to ask for what it missed — much smaller, and it is what commit delivery turned out to be.

## §4.3 and §8's item 8 point the wrong way

§4.3 correctly finds that `rooms/*` has no join request, and proposes closing it as a `rooms/join/*` Trust Task family. That is the wrong shape.

A Trust Task is an instruction you give **your own agent**, authorised by your control of it — `vta-service` gates `rooms/owner/{invite,issue-membership,issue-authority}` on `CredentialWrite` and never asks who the subject is, because the caller is the principal and the subject is a field. A would-be member is a stranger asking an owner to *decide* something about them. As a Trust Task that says the stranger may instruct the room's agent.

The gap is real; it is a **request protocol between two parties**, closer to a VTC's `join-requests/*` — and the resemblance is not a coincidence.

## The contrast is the lesson

The record path went the other way with no design work at all, because a record operation genuinely is a Trust Task: a member asking a host to act. The framework already binds it to every carrier, so `room-host` gained a carrier and not a protocol (#1369).

**Asking a service to act is a Trust Task; asking a person to decide is not.** Both travel the same wires.

## Also in §10

- **Two identities, and the split is forced** — the transport key must be in the page (authcrypt and TSP need an X25519 secret in the caller's hands), the room key must not be (that is why it lives in wasm). Hence a request proves both and binds them: drop the binding clause and a signed request becomes a bearer artefact anybody who saw it could replay from their own connection.
- **§9's open questions answered** from the built thing — the epoch chain does reach a browser member; the pooling defence is unweakened and now asserted; and commit delivery, which was the sharpest edge: the first cut routed on the demo's own room slug, which addressed rooms do not have, so a room you were handed a link to would join, fall behind at the next admission, and fail to open records with nothing saying why. That reads as corruption.
- **The broker got smaller than §5 predicted** — catalogue and page only.
- **A room says which carriers it serves**, rather than a client discovering it by succeeding.

Docs only; no code in this PR.

title: ci: a broken vendor apt repo must not take out the build, or the release
body:
Every Rust job on this repo is currently red, and none of it is ours:

```
E: Failed to fetch https://dl.google.com/linux/chrome-stable/deb/dists/stable/main/binary-amd64/Packages.gz  Hash Sum mismatch
E: Some index files failed to download. They have been ignored, or old ones used instead.
##[error]Process completed with exit code 100.
```

`apt-get update` exits non-zero when **any** configured source fails, and the GitHub runner image ships Google's Chrome repository. When that mirror serves a `Packages.gz` whose hash does not match its `Release` file — which it does periodically — the `&&` short-circuits and the step fails, taking `cargo test`, `cargo clippy` and `cargo package` with it.

Ubuntu's own archive fetched fine in the same run (`Fetched 11.9 MB in 1s`, no error). The only thing that failed is a vendor repo **no job here uses**.

Confirmed on all three failing jobs of #422, and it survived a `--failed` re-run, so it is not the kind of transient that waits itself out.

## `publish.yml` runs the same line twice

That is the part worth pausing on. This is not only an inconvenience on PRs: **a Release PR merged while Google's mirror is unhappy fails to publish.** The release path should not be gated on a third party this repository has no relationship with.

## The fix

```yaml
sudo apt-get update || true
sudo apt-get install -y libdbus-1-dev pkg-config
```

These jobs need Ubuntu's archive and nothing else, so a failed update is not informative. **The install is the check that matters**, and it still fails loudly if the headers are genuinely absent — so tolerating the update's exit code loses nothing and stops an unrelated third party from gating this repository.

## Two fixes I did not take, and why

- **`rm -f /etc/apt/sources.list.d/google-chrome.list`.** Names one vendor. The next image to break will be a different one, and the fix would have to be rediscovered from the same red build.
- **`apt-get update -o Dir::Etc::sourceparts=/dev/null`** (restrict to `/etc/apt/sources.list`). Correct on 22.04 and wrong on 24.04, where the archive moved to `sources.list.d/ubuntu.sources` — it would fetch nothing and fail the install for a new reason that reads like the same one.

Five sites: three in `rust.yml`, two in `publish.yml`. Both files still parse.

title: feat(room-host): serve Trust Tasks over DIDComm and TSP
body:
A host was reachable only at a URL — and that is a requirement on the **member**, not on the host: they have to be somewhere that can open it. A public name, a certificate, an origin the browser is permitted to call. A browser member frequently is not, and a host on a laptop or behind NAT is not reachable at all.

`--mediator-did` makes a host reachable the way a phone is. It connects as its own `did:peer:2`, and a member who resolved that DID dials the same mediator; neither side has to be able to reach the other.

## Nothing about authorization changes, and that is the design

A host takes the presenter from the request document's own `eddsa-jcs-2022` proof and the authority from the chain the room issued. **Neither comes from the carrier.** So the same bytes are exactly as authorized over a socket as over a POST, and a transport that authenticates its sender confers nothing extra.

That is what lets `dispatch` be one function rather than one per wire, and `one_dispatch_answers_the_same_over_any_carrier` asserts it: the same signed document, once through the router and once straight into `dispatch`, must agree on `type`, `payload`, `threadId`, `recipient` and `issuer`. A host with a per-carrier authorization model would have as many as it has wires, and the difference would surface as "it works over HTTP but not over DIDComm" — a report with nowhere to start.

(The test also guards itself: it asserts each compared field is *present* first. Written against `inResponseTo` it would have passed vacuously — the field is `threadId`.)

## Shape

`reject`/`respond` now return `Answer { status, document }` instead of an `axum::Response`. The document is the answer — self-describing, carrying its own `type` and a framework `code` when it refuses — and the status is that same fact restated for the one carrier that wants it out of band. DIDComm and TSP drop it, exactly as `vta-service`'s DIDComm handler already does.

## One socket, both protocols

A mediator permits one websocket per DID and sniffs the TSP magic byte, so this listens through the delivery layer's `DidCommTransport`, whose inbound stream surfaces both tagged by protocol. A second socket is not an alternative: the mediator evicts one of the pair as a duplicate channel.

- **DIDComm** — the framework binding: one reserved envelope `type`, `body` is the document. Sourced from `trust_tasks_didcomm::ENVELOPE_TYPE` rather than a fifth hand-written copy of the URI.
- **TSP** — the payload *is* the envelope, byte-identical to the HTTP body, no wrapper. The **reply** is wrapped as `{ thid, document }`, because TSP has no headers and correlation is the one thing a document cannot carry about itself.

The reply threads on the **document's own `id`**, not the frame's. Threading on `frame.message.id` produced a reply that was sent, accepted, and matched by nobody — the caller waited out its full timeout while the answer sat unclaimed. Found live, and it is the kind of thing that only shows up against a real mediator.

## Opt-in, and stable

Behind a `didcomm` feature and a flag, both off by default — matching `--resolve-dids` and `--allow-origin`. A capability here is a decision an operator makes rather than one they inherit, and opening a standing outbound connection to a third party is a larger one than either. A host not asked to be reachable opens no socket and mints no identity.

The identity persists in the data directory, because a member's saved address names it. If it changed on restart, every kept link would point at a host that no longer exists and the failure would be a timeout — which reads as "the host is down", not "the host is now somebody else". Verified stable across a restart.

The stored file records **which mediator** it was minted for rather than re-deriving it from the DID. The first cut rebuilt the service block's base64 and looked for it in the identifier; that fails whenever the encoder orders or omits a field differently from the guess, and it did — a host refused to start against the very mediator it had been minted for.

## Testing

24 tests pass with the feature on and off; clippy clean. Validated live against a `did:webvh` mediator: a browser member with **no HTTP access to the host at all** (started without `--allow-origin`, so `fetch` fails) sealed, wrote, listed and re-opened records, and walked the epoch chain, entirely over TSP.

title: docs(rooms): read-through — the agent as the room's memory
body:
The last unbuilt piece of the rooms UI and the missing half of verified reads turn out to be the same piece. This works it out far enough to be argued with.

## Two threads, one party

**The console cannot read a record.** Not a missing feature: `manager/carrier.ts`'s `carrierParams` passes exactly `{type, payload}`, and the offscreen document supplies `vtaDid: active.conn.vtaDid` as the recipient — so a `service` naming a **host** is silently dropped and the call lands at the wallet's own agent, which does not serve `rooms/records/*`. Nothing type-checks as wrong, and the render harness answers by task URI regardless of recipient, so tests pass.

That narrowing is deliberate — the offscreen document mints and signs the envelope rather than counter-signing one composed in a page — so widening the carrier trades a real property for a convenience. The answer is the one `rooms/keys/backfill` and `rooms/owner/register` already took.

**And `dataCommitment` is inert.** A root read once proves nothing; it becomes evidence compared against a copy the host did not choose. Of the three the spec offers: the witnessed anchor is blocked on `data-rooms-epoch-anchoring.md`'s open question, and another member's root needs a gossip channel rooms deliberately do not have — on a `private` room a member list is the thing being withheld. The third, *the root the host gave the same member earlier*, needs only somewhere to keep it.

A tab cannot keep it. A CLI cannot. The agent already keeps per-room state at `room-group:{roomId}`.

## What it keeps

`(headVersion, root)` pairs — not roots. A bare root is not comparable to another bare root, because a room moves and two roots differing is the most ordinary observation there is (the correction tt#422 makes). With the pair:

> Two roots at the **same** `headVersion` that differ is a host caught. There is no write to attribute the difference to.

And the agent is the only member-side party that saw both reads.

## What it does not catch

Stated plainly in the note, because the mechanism is easy to oversell: a consistently lying host that understates `recordCount` to match; a host that never stored the record; and anything at all on a first read. What changes is that an omission stops being silence and becomes a specific claim — which a writer's signed put acknowledgement (#1334/#1335) contradicts directly.

## Recommendation

`rooms/keys/{read,browse}` with verification **first** — they unblock the console immediately and trace verification is worth having on its own. The root memory **second**, as a strictly additive change to a task that exists by then. `rooms/keys/write` last; it composes two things that already work and unblocks nothing reading does not.

A read-through is four acts — mint a presentation, ask the host, check the answer, open the ciphertext — and the fourth is only ever the agent's, which is what makes one task the right shape rather than three round trips with a half-verified record held in between.

## The open question, left open on purpose

**What does an agent do when it catches a host?**

- **Refuse the read.** Honest, makes the detection load-bearing — and locks a member out of their own room through their own agent, plausibly including the records that would prove what happened.
- **Return it flagged.** They keep working; a flag that blocks nothing gets dismissed, and the room's vocabulary has no word for *this host has been caught* stronger than a pill.
- **Refuse writes, serve reads.** Has some logic — writing to a host you have caught compounds the damage, reading gathers evidence — and is a rule nobody would guess.

I have not picked one. It is the kind of decision that should be made deliberately rather than fall out of an implementation.

## Also

§14 item 7 was stale — it ended "what remains unbuilt is the commitment itself", which stopped being true across #1346, #1349, #1351, tt#411, tt#419 and #1368. Updated, including the two things traces flushed out: `rooms/records/get`'s response had never conformed to its published schema, and the shipped prose claimed a host showing two members different roots "cannot claim a transient", which is false while a room moves.

Documentation only.
